speechtext: TEMPLEMAN (Minister of Inland Revenue) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 110) respecting agricultural fertilizers. He said: The present Act has been found unworkable and ineffective as a protection to the purchaser of fertilizers. It is proposed to repeal the present Act and substitute this one. There are some very important changes but the Bill is along the lines of the existing Act. It is desired to give greater security to farmers in purchasing fertilizers. It requires that all .manufacturers of fertilizers shall register and that they shall sell their products under registered numbers. It also provides that a guaranteed analysis shall be placed on every package of fertilizer sold and provides penalties for contraventions of the Act. A Bill was prepared last session, submitted to the Senate, brought to its second reading and circulated with a view to bringing it before the farmers and others interested in fertilizers. We have had a great many replies and criticisms of the proposed measure and they have been almost unanimously in favour of making a change. The present Bill therefore is in the form of a Bill introduced in the Senate last year with certain modifications and changes to meet the criticisms we have received.

Could not the minister insert a clause in this Bill or introduce another Bill making similar provision with reference to the sale of feed for stock ? I have had many complaints from farmers that when they purchased feed, seeds and other things which they did not purchase were found.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The question of an Act regulating the sale of food for stock has been under consideration since last session. Several delegations have visited Ottawa and had interviews with the Min-

ister of Agriculture and myself, and the question of preparing and submitting a Bill at the present session, something along the line of this Bill, is receiving consideration. I hope to come to a conclusion in a week or so with regard to it.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
On the order for the consideration of an amendment made by the Senate to Bill (No. 8) to amend the Dominion Lands Act.-Mr. Oliver.

speakeroldname: Hon. FRANK OLIVER (Minister of the Interior).
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The amendment proposed by the Senate is made at the suggestion of the department and is intended to meet a condition which has arisen by reason of the very large numbers of patents now being granted. Section 90 of the Act relates to the preparation and signing of patents. Provision is made that the patent shall be transmitted to the Secretary of State, by whom, or by the Under Secretary of State, it shall be countersigned. The number of patents has become so great that the signing of them becomes too great a tax upon the time of either the Secretary or the Under Secretary of State and the amendment prepared by the Senate and offered for the assent of the House provides that the patents may be countersigned either by the Secretary of State, the Under Secretary of State as at present, or by ' some other person thereunto specially authorized by the Governor in Council.5 That is the whole amendment and its purpose.
Amendment concurred In.

Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair I desire to bring to the attention of the House a letter which I received this morning as follows :
36 Craig Street West, Montreal.
Dear sir,-I want to ask you to help me to get my money refunded from the Grand Trunk Railway. I came from Toronto and left there Tuesday last. They sold me a second-class ticket and checked my luggage. No one said a word or stopped me getting on the 10.15 p.m. train, but when the conductor came round he demanded $3.35 from me or to make me leave the train. I paid under protest and send you the receipt. I know you are the man who is fighting this question and can get what is right for me.
Hear, hear.
Sometimes we do get a little compliment outside of this House. The letter continues:

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I have travelled by the same train, 10.15 p.m., from Toronto to Montreal, three times before and they have always taken my second-class ticket without a word. I am told that the company are bound to carry second-class passengers by that train. Will you put me right on this matter? Thanking you in anticipation.
Yours truly,

The receipt is enclosed. My contention is, as I have often said in this House, that this man or any other person was entitled to travel for two cents a mile on that Grand Trunk train. His right to travel on a Grand Trunk train at that rate has been vindicated by the highest court in this realm. We had a judgment the other day from the Privy Council in England which declared that the Grand Trunk Railway Company was bound to give a penny a mile service at least once a day on its line from Toronto to Montreal. We know also that this has been confirmed by the Railway Commission of this country and by all the courts, and still the Grand Trunk compelled that man, when he endeavoured to travel for two cents a mile, to pay first class fare and threatened to eject him from the train if he did not pay it. I want to know who is looking after the public interest in this matter. I am getting rather tired of it; at least I am willing to continue the work but I would call upon the government, upon the Minister of Railways and Canals, or upon some official of this country to see that the public get what they are entitled to. For the last few days I have had to devote my time to preparing a case in order to bring another action be fore the Railway Commission so as to try and get this penny a mile service between Toronto and Montreal, or, in fact, to get it for all of the province of Quebec. According to my interpretations of the law, and according to the advice I get from eminent counsel, the people of the province of Quebec and certainly of Ontario up to Toronto are entitled to this penny a mile service. But instead of that this man is refused the right to travel at that rate. He is threatened with being put off the train and he is compelled to pay the additional money. The government, the Minister of Railways and Canals, and the Minister of Justice should be busy at this moment seeing that this man gets his rights.	I
Had they no second-class accommodation on that train?

I am not in a position to say whether they had or not, but the man was entitled to travel at that rate. It makes every Canadian's blood boil with indignation at the thought that the Grand Trunk and Canadian Pacific Railway Companies carry all the travel that originates in the United States across Canada for

two cents a mile or less, gladly accepting that fare, and at the same time threaten to eject a Canadian who demands similar treatment. How long will we stand that in this country? Yet, it is going on every day.
I have investigated it, and I have had it proved time and time again that on travel which originates in Michigan or New York state, the same being true at the Soo and on the Manitoba border, it is carried for two cents a mile while a Canadian must pay three cents and he is not even given second class or third class accommodation. The conductor holds him up and says: If you do not pay this additional sum we will stop the train and put you off in the wilderness. They have done it. The case that we won in the Privy Council arose out of stoping a train and putting a reporter off because he would not pay the additional sum. I am not here to antagonize the railways of this country; I am not here to say or do anything against the Grand Trunk. But, I am here to ask these railways in the first place, to carry out their charter obligations, and, in the next place, to treat Canadians as well as they treat Americans. It is not antagonizing the railways. It is not making an, attack upon their credit or their capital ; but my contention is that they are bound to do this and that if they would agree to do it they would make more money and the people would appreciate it. At this very moment this same Grand Trunk Railway Company is a suppliant to parliament, asking this country to come to its relief in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, and we have already been told that it is to get relief. If the managers of that road are coming to parliament asking for relief is not this the time to put it up to them and say: You are not going to get any help until you carry out your charter obligations and until you agree to give as good treatment to Canadians as you give to people across the line. I know that Mr. Hays and some of his newspaper friends in this country say that I am making an unjust attack on the road and that the Canadian roads cannot live if they carry people at two cents a mile. It has been proved in the United States, as it has been proved wherever it has been tried, that cheap railway travel increases the revenue of the railways. I am prepared to stand here and prove that such is the case and that these roads are not going to be hurt. The attitude of Mr. Hays and of the railway companies is to give as little service as possible and to go at the public with a club. My contention is that they will make more money if they give a better and cheaper service. The people will spend as much money on railway travel but they will get a better service and there will be a better understanding between the railways and the public. I hope that I will 92
have the assistance of the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Railways in trying to get better treatment accorded to the Canadian travelling public and that no Canadian in future will be ejected from a train because he is asking for his rights and for equality of treatment.
Now, I want to pass to the question I raised the other day in this House with regard to the capitalization of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. I then told this House that the capitalization of railway companies was an important matter, that it bore directly on the traffic charges and I said that that had been found to be the case in the United States, and that if we would wait a few days we would hear the deliverance from the incoming president on the subject. Almost the first paragraph of President Taft's inaugural address the other day at Washington was to the effect that the time had come when the capitalization of interstate railways had to be regulated, and that the people who used the railways had to be protected with regard to tariff rates through the regulation of the capitalization of these railway companies. They have found it desirable in the United States that somebody should exercise a scrutiny over proposed increases in the capital of Tailway companies. Yet, here in Canada we have allowed the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to increase their capital by an immense amount, to divide over $60,000,000 amongst the shareholders, thus putting an unnecessary tax, I contend, on the traffic of this country to the extent of whatever the earnings on $60,000,000 may be. I was told that we had no concern with the capitalization. I have proved that we have by the statement of the President of the United States and by the law in existence in the state of New York, and I am now going to show something else which follows from over-capitalization. If we in this country are to establish the idea that this cutting of melons is to be the rule who will invest anything in railway securities unless a melon goes with it? And, strange to say, that very thing is being demonstrated in our own day. If the Canadian Pacific Railway cuts a melon, if it becomes the rule to issue stock in that way and if all the shareholders have the prospect of becoming-shall I say-millionaires, it will continue to do that business and nobody will buy any railway security that has not a bonus or a melon with it. What has happened? The Canadian Pacific Railway can sell all the stock they wish as long as there is a bonus or a melon to cut. The Grand Trunk cannot sell a dollar's worth of stock and they are to-day coming to this country for relief. If they had a melon to cut they would get their money, investors would take up their stock, but what the investor looks for is a security that has a melon attached to it and the Grand



Trunk Pacific cannot sell one of their securities. This man of melons, this man who is making this new class of melonaires, Sir Thos. Shaughnessy, is able to come to the relief of the government and buy some of these Grand Trunk securities that cannot be sold. That is the position of things in this country with regard to railway securities. It is high time that there was a change and that the government undertook to scrutinize all these issues of stock. The government ought to confine the Canadian Pacific Eailway to an issue of 4 per cent bonds. Then I was told by the Minister of Justice that instead of finding out what was the actual investment in the Canadian Pacific Eailway as provided for by the charter, the minister had agreed to hang up for an indefinite period the ascertainment of what the actual cost of the Canadian Pacific Eailway was. In other words, the Canadian Pacific Eailway having been sentenced to be hanged on a certain date, as long as it was pampered and allowed to issue melons it would not ask to be hanged. That is the position in regard to the regulation of its rates as we are entitled to have them regulated under the original agreement.
Then, I want to tell the Minister of Finance how far this bonus business has got to in this country. You cannot issue hardly a security of any kind in Canada unless there is a bonus of some kind with it, and we find our Canadian banks and some of the Canadian insurance companies parties to a new kind of what I consider dangerous financing in this country. They are raising money every day for the development of electrical industries in South America, Central America and Mexico, and all these securities are put on the market largely with the assistance of Canadian financing institutions, and the proposition is in the shape of bonds and with the bonds there goes bonus stock so that you buy a bond for $1,000 and you get $1,000 of bonus stock. That- kind of financing is producing a bad effect in this country and it is getting so that people will buy no security unless a bonus of stock goes with it. And while I say Canadian capitalists aTe free to invest in any way the-"' like, I do not quite think that the Canadian banks and the Canadian insurance companies with the savings of the Canadian people ought to be floating propositions for the development of foreign industries. We have enough industries at home to develop and enough necessity to keen our money here. I want to see the Grand Trunk Pacific built, and if there is Canadian money I would like to see it put in that enterprise. But you will never get investments of that kind taken by the Canadians if this practice of issuing bonus stock is continued. There was a gentleman defending the insurance companies the other day and he said he regarded the gov-Mr. W. P. MACLEAN.
ernment proposal to limit these companies so that they should not indulge in this purchase of bonds along with which went bonus stock, but I say the legislation in that direction is right and that the practice has got to be stopped in this country so far as public action can stop it. We have got to tell the Canadian Pacific Eailway Company that never again will they be allowed to cut a melon and to issue to their shareholders at par a security that is worth $170 and soon will be worth $200. We have got tc stop that once and for all, and in the name of the Canadian people I tell the government here to-day that that must never occur again, and later on I intend to test the feeling of the House on that very proposition. I want to tell the House here to-day that we must stop this financing of foreign corporations with the savings of the Canadian people on this basis of issuing bonus stock with bond securities. It is not in the interest of the Canadian people. Once we establish that habit in this country of dis-tiibuting bonuses of one kind or another with nublic securities, then we will have to give bonuses with all our securities and the first thing we know when this government goes on the London market to get a security issued it will be asked: What bonus are you going to give us; can't you give us some kind of common stock that some dav will be of some use to us, or cannot we get some kind of rights? So, the thing is going on and it is time it was stopped and it must be stopped. I am availing myself of this occasion when the Grand Trunk Pacific Eailway and the Canadian Pacific Eailway is here before us to-day asking for favours ; the Canadian Pacific Eailway is before us asking for an increase of its capital stock and the Grand Trunk Pacific is here as applicants for assistance.
I say now is the time to compel these great corporations to treat the people of this country fairly, and to give us a 2-cent passenger rate, as. they give to the American travel on their roads. Again I say that the Canadian Pacific Eailway financing of this kind must be stopped, and the [DOT]way to stop it is to tell them not only that they must come under the general Act under the control of the Eailway Commission, but that they must use the funds they now have in their treasury, that they must sell their lands, and abandon" that exemption clause which protects them in the west. Al' these privileges can be wiped away when they come here as suppliants, and some kind of concession can be got from them in this respect. Later on I intend to test the feeling of the House on this question. I have now got my facts fairly well before the House and I leave these facts with the House, and this letter which I have read from a common ordinary Canadian traveller on the Grand Trunk Railway, who was threatened with ejectment because he would not pay something he was not

entitled to pay, I commend to the consideration of the Minister of Railways and I hope he will compel the Grand Trunk Railway Company to treat that Canadian as he ought to have been treated and compel them to Tetum to him the three dollars and odd cents which he was forced to pay.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways).
speechtext: I will detain the House but for a moment. The question of the Canadian Pacific Railway issue of stock has already been discussed and I will not further discuss it now. My hon. friend (Mr. W. F. Maclean) tells us, and rightly, that there was something in President Taft's address in reference to the issuing of stock. I think his statement was fairly general on that point. .
Very.
President Taft carefully kept away from any detail; he was not as courageous as my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean). What he will do or what he will not do nobody on earth can know from reading his address.
I'll bet you what he will do.

As the hon. gentleman told us what President Taft was going to say perhaps he can tell us now what he is going to do. With that true newspaper instinct of his he had a scoop on the rest of us as to the contents of the address a day in advance, although if I were actively in the business now as I used to be perhaps I would be as fortunate as he was. However, the two cent rate matter was the gist of the hon. gentleman's remarks. I do not know the particulars of his complaint except that as he tells us a man got on the fast train of the Grand Trunk and his second-class ticket was not honored. Well, as I understand it, the judgment of the Privy Council only provides for one train a day between Montreal and Toronto at the two cent rate.
Was it there?

The judgment of the courts would not allow the man to select the fastest train for his two cent ticket and no railway in the world would give him a two cent rate on its fastest train. This train no doubt was selected for the purpose of showing that the road would not give him a second-class fare, but that train I understand does not carry a second-class car at all; it is one of the very fastest trains on the Grand Trunk.
I went up on that train the day before yesterday and a lady sitting on a seat in front of me had a second-class ticket was sent out to the second-class car.

This occurred on the night train going east?
92}
My experience was on the fast train going from Montreal west.

This occurred on the night train which carried the sleepers, and there was a train on the Grand Trunk which travelled in the same direction a short time before it and on which the second-class ticket would have been honoured. The fast train only carries the sleepers and the first-class car. It is very questionable to my mind whether the gentleman who wrote that letter had any grievance at all. It is questionable whether if the law were enforced to-day that gentleman would have any cause of complaint because the law only requires the Grand Trunk to put on one train per day for the accommodation of second-class passengers and surely they can run as many other trains as they like without a second-class car and not violate their charter. However, the question of a two cent rate is a very large one. My hon. friend will have noticed that within the last few days one of the states he quoted as having a two cent rate has had that law declared unconstitutional simply because the railways cannot carry people at two cents a mile and live. We forget often that the railways in this country are of as much importance to the country as this House itself is; the country cannot prosper without the railways; we are partners in the railways and while I believe in making them live up to their contracts and give the people a good service at a minimum price, we must not run away with the idea that every time we attack a railway we are doing something for the country, while the fact is that' we may be injuring the country in pursuing such a course. Perhaps I should not say so, but at the present moment I do not believe that the railways of Canada run through a population sufficiently dense and affording sufficient traffic to give the people a two cent rate with any kind of living profit to the railways. I believe that is the situation at the present time, and if parliament were asked to pass a law now to compel the railway companies to give a two cent rate I do not believe the House would consent to it. While I agree that my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) has a perfect right to adhere to his idea with regard to a two cent passenger rate, I am inclined at present to take the other view. We cannot compare Canada with the United States or with Great Britain in this respect. In Canada the rate for transportation cannot be governed by the density of population. Canada is a sparsely settled country, as long as the United States, with seven millions of population to feed railways extending from one end of the country to the other, while the United States has over eighty millions of population. It is out of the question, therefore, to expect as low a rate in Canada as there is in the United States. I do not know that I have anything

more to say. After all, if we compelled the Grand Trunk to adhere to what my hon. friend calls the terms of its charter and to the judgment recently given, I doubt if the gentleman who wrote that letter would have any claim at all.
: Hon. G. E. FOSTER (North Toronto). When a railway like th.e Grand Trunk has some trains on which it honours second-class tickets, is it not obliged to point that out by way of advertisement? A traveller may know generally that there is a two-cent fare on the railway, but he may get on the wrong train inadvertently. Is there not a duty on the railway to guard travellers against misapprehension of that kind?
1 Mr. GRAHAM. I think that on every time-table, including those posted on the walls of the stations, there are particulars that enable any one to glean that information; but at the city of Toronto the arrangements are so imperfect, too imperfect for a large city, that people are liable to get on the wrong train. I hold with my hon. friend that the railway should have a regulation to prevent people getting on the wrong train, such as there is at Chicago and elsewhere.
' Mr. FOSTER. When a ticket agent sells a second-class ticket, he should point out to the purchaser what the arrangements are.
The minister has missed my point, which is that there were Americans travelling at two cents a mile on the same train on which Canadians were given this unfair treatment.
I do not know that we have any proof of that.
I have, on every train.

There is this to be remembered in regard to railway travelling, that the rates are governed to a certain extent by the place where the traffic originates. That is true of passenger rates as well as freight rates. Traffic originating in the United States has to compete with the rates prevailing in the United States, and it can be sent either by the American route or by the Canadian route. The railways have to give these rates to comply with the laws of the United States. If they had any traffic originating in Canada, they would have in the same way to comply with the laws of Canada. This arrangement is perfectly feasible, and if brought before the Board of Railway Commissioners to-morrow, they would deal with it just as they deal with this proposition, and my hon. friend gets the benefit. A place like the city of Toronto gets a distributing rate which is not given to other places, and that is what enables the city of Toronto to become a wholesale centre.

If my hon. friend's idea were carried to its logical conclusion, that distributing rate would have to be abolished, and our larger cities would not be the wholesale centres they are at the present time. To nibble at the shell of the traffic problem gives one only a little information; but railway tariffs are based on scientific principles. You cannot take an isolated case and make a system out of it. You have to go through all the tariffs and ascertain the principles on which they are based, and then form your conclusion.

May I ask the hon minister a question? When the Canadian Pacific Railway Company disposes of $50,000,000 of stock, for what authority has been given by order in council, and distribute that stock among their own shareholders at par, which will be practically dividing $50,000,000 among their shareholders, as the stock is worth intrinsically $200, will they be in a position to say to the Railway Commission, we will no longer allow you to fix our rates, and we want this lawsuit brought to a conclusion?

I suppose they are able 'to force this law-suit to a conclusion at the present time, but the Canadian Pacific Railway will never do it. There is no question about their being in that position, and I see no great benefit to be derived to the people of Canada in having it pushed to a conclusion, so long as they do as at present, allow the rates to be governed by the Railway Commission. As I say, I think there is nothing to hinder them asking the case to be pushed to a conclusion, or the government doing the same thing.

I only arose to call the attention of the hon. minister to the case in hand, to which his attention was particularly called, and to remark that he had apparently overlooked the salient feature of that letter. 'The man applied for a ticket and checked his baggage for the 10.15 train, and when he did that, one would naturally think that he should have been made aware of the fact that he could not travel on that train on that ticket. A second opportunity is afforded when he comes to check his baggage. He must present his ticket, and when he did he should have been told that he could not have his baggage checked 'by that train. But they allowed him to purchase his ticket and check his baggage, and when he got on the train they put him off, although he made three previous trips under the same circumstances.
He knew better, then.

Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.

Intercolonial Railway-cut-off line at Moncton, N.B., $50,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext: This is an item I want to explain, because this small expropriation does not really cover what is meant. This line will cost about $357,000. It will be two and a half miles and double-tracked. The idea of this is to save running the heavy freight through the city where there are high grades.
What are you going to get by it?

We will reduce the distance quite a large extent and get rid of a very heavy grade and actually make a grade of five-tenths of one per cent that will save our going through the city with the heavy traffic.
How did you get along before ?

Our shops are moved west of that city quite a distance. Before they were in the city. We are going to out off a loop practically, and the Grand Trunk Pacific will connect with the Intercolonial just at that point.

This seems a large expenditure for something never wanted before. It is estimated to cost $350,000, but before completed it will cost half a million dollars, if the usual record on the Intercolonial Railway is not departed from.
Our engineer thinks it is absolutely necessary and we will save on the haul as well as on the distance.
When was it begun?
It has not been begun. It has always been the intention in the laying out of the yard.
$350,000 is a large amount for two and a half miles of railway.
It is a double-tracked line.
How much cutting and filling in to make it cost so much ?

I have the items here. 41-2 acres of land, right of way; 17 acres clearing right of way; 3 acres grubbing; 1,000 cubic yards solid rock excavation; 30,000 loose rock; 16,000 ordinary excavation; 200,000 earth excavation; 1,800 yards standard fence; 24 gates; 28 cattle guards; 30,000 lbs. of rails for culverts; 854,000 lbs. of steel trussel at Hall's Creek; one under crossing at north street; 5 miles track laid.
What do you estimate the cost of the land for right of way?
If that is intended to be used as a marshalling track, you will require more than two tracks.

It is not really a yard. We have an extension yard outside of this. We have constructed a new yard altogether and one shop west of the city. This will start where the Grand Trunk Pacific reaches our tracks and will not run through the city proper. We will escape the trade going down the city.
If you are to have 28 cattle guards, that means 14 street crossings on 2i miles of track.
There are 2 for each street, and then there are double tracks, which will make 7 streets all told and one viaduct.
Has the land been yet secured?
No.
Has the line through which this road is to run been decided ?
It has practically.
Then the hon. gentleman is in this position. He has laid down his railway tracks and has not taken any opportunity to secure the land. How does he propose to get the land now?-by expropriation?

We have really two lines surveyed, and we propose not to be tied up to either. We are getting a man to make an estimate and get offers from these people. If we do not get a fair price, we will expropriate the land.
But you make the whole matter public.
It was difficult not to do that, seeing that we had located our shops there.

We have had land transactions in Moncton before now. The minister was urged, I think by the present deputy minister, though I am not sure, both with reference to Moncton and Halifax land, that it would be better not to let a word get out concerning the government's intentions until they had options on the land. That was the whole argument, in fact, that, if the thing were known, the government would put itself in the hands of the land owners, and that the necessary course was to secure options in advance. Now, the department, with a different minister, but, I think, with the same deputy, thinks it well to come to parliament and advertise the matter of an expenditure of $354,000, although it is tied up within a very small radius of land. I cannot see the consistency of these two situations in the one department. Unless you are going to

expropriate in any event, it would seem not very wise to advertise the whole thing in this manner. We remember that in the matter of the purchase of the sand lands at Kentville for military purposes, we were told that it was necessary to get hold of these lands before it became known to the public that the department wanted them, or they would have to pay through the nose for them. Is this a new diplomacy that the Minister of Railways and Canals is introducing in the management of his department ? I would like to see how he works it out.

I will tell my hon. friend, and he will see it in a moment. The purchase of the sand lands, or even the purchase of a building site in Halifax, was a different case. The government could buy in one place or in another. But, in the case now before us, the range of choice is very little, for the railway has to go through from one point to the other.

The minister must go back further than that in order to make it clear. It must have been known several years ago that these shops were to be erected, and it must have been foreseen that, at some time, you would need moTe land there. Why did not the government, before the shops were built, take measures to secure the necessary land, and so apply the principle which has been so often advocated before, that of securing control before the public knowledge of the government's intentions makes the land immensely valuable? The minister can do what he likes, but, in this case, he will pay a great deal more for the land than he would have had to pay had he gone at it in a businesslike way. Even an expropriation court will give the owners a larger award now than it would have given before.
This line was not contemplated when the shops were built?

My deputy tells me that part of the surveys were made as long ago as two years. It has always been his idea to have this line connected in this way since the building of the new shops. And the building of the new shops was rendered necessary by the burning of the old ones.
I understand that the cut-off is 2J miles. What is the length of the existing line ?
Nearly a mile longer.
And what is the grade ? What is the ton-mile saving over that piece of road ?
The grades will be reduced about one-half.
How many cars can you take over that grade now with a hundred-ton locomotive such as you ordinarily handle freight with ?
The difference would be as between 1,000 tons and 1,800 tons.
Is this line to be used jointly by the Intercolonial and the Transcontinental ?

We expect that the terminals with which this connects will be used by the Grand Trunk as their Moncton terminals or, at least, as a portion of them; and as the freight starts east from there, it will use the double track with the lesser grade. It will be part of the eastern line from our shops.
Is the minister charging the whole of this amount to capital account of the Intercolonial or dividing it between the two lines ?
This is all ours. Should we make an arrangement with the Grand Trunk Pacific, they would pay for whatever rights they secured.
Is this improvement necessary for the traffic of the Intercolonial as it is at present ?

It could be got along without, but as we are doing the work we thought that we might as well make a complete job of it, instead of being compelled to go back and finish it. We are building our shops and getting them in splendid shape. The whole work will take us two or three years, as the committee will see by the amount asked for in this vote.

Does it not strike the minister that, particularly this year, this is a pretty large expenditure unless it is really necessary ? As I understand it, it i3 not really necessary for the traffic of the Intercolonial, but will only become necessary because the Grand Trunk Pacific is going there and it is believed you will want this cut-off when you get access to the traffic that you expect you will have when that road enters Moncton. The $350,000, which I suppose will run to nearly half a million before it is through, is a very large expenditure for a cut-off of 24 miles. The question would be, I would think, whether it is so necessary that it should be gone on with at once. You are making large expenditures at Moncton, I think the information was it would take $500,000 more to finish the shops. These shops of course would not be necessary simply for the Intercolonial Railway.
Oh, yes they are.

You are making them more expensive simply because you are looking to joint interests by the Grand

Trunk Pacific and the Intercolonial Railway.
The longer we leave this the more expensive the land will become. The moment the Grand Trunk Pacific gets to Moncton the city as a railway centre will increase in size.
What is the estimated cost of cattle-guards and is there a uniform pattern?
The estimate here is $25 each. They are a steel cattle-guard which we get from the Fairbanks Company. We use this kind in anything new we put in.
That is not a very heavy sum. What is it that will cost so much?
Here is a filling, 400,000 cubic yards, that will cost $80,000. Then we have a trestle, 854,000 pounds of steel trestle, that will cost $38,430. Eighty-pound rails and fastenings will cost $21,000.

In connection with cattle-guards, the other day we got a return as to the number of protected crossings in Canada. It is stated that there were 15,000 crossings in Canada of which 3,115 were protected, but we could not get particulars as to how they were protected. It now transpires that there has been a great mistake in that matter. The Grand Trunk Railway mistook protection for the people for cattle-guards and in reply to the question sent to them stated that they had 2,888 protected crossings, but this included all the cattle-guards on their line. They have only a couple of hundred protected crossings, and instead of 3,115 we have probably not 500 protected crossings in Canada. I hope the minister will amend his Bill because the cattle-guards do not serve the purpose of protecting the public in the way intended by the legislation before the House.
Who is making inquiry and looking after this land purchase?
The deputy has been negotiating himself for the purchase of this land. Some of the land belongs to the Moncton Land Company and some to Humphries. It is mostly vacant land.
One hundred dollars a lot should be a good price for the land.

I think so, some will run a little higher and some a little lower.
Original construction, $800.
What is that?
Every year little claims come up for damages on account of original construction that have not been presented or that have been overlooked. We generally have a small appropriation for that.
It seems to me this is worse than the United States pensions.
It is something on the same line I admit. There are some peculiar claims. Sometimes heirs return or something of that kind occurs. We carried last year $1,000 and paid out $634.84 on that account.
Before leaving the branci. lines, I would like to discuss for a few mo ments the general question of the acquisitions of branch lines by the Intercolonial Railway.

How can we do that in Committee of Supply on an individual item? I found the very same difficulty. I did not get off what I wanted to get off the other night, but I do not see how it is possible for me to get it off on individual items. I did not know that the minister was going into Supply this afternoon or before he had gone in I would have discussed with him some points. I think my hon. friend (Mr. Turriff) had better take some other opportunity. If we are all going to take up these general questions of policy and discuss them on individual items it will be unsatisfactory, and I do not see how we would get through with the estimates. I would like the minister to let me know the next time he is going into Supply, and then I will be prepared to take up some of these other questions.
I have a general one held over-the Trent canal.

I am quite prepared either to go on now for fifteen minutes or wait for a further occasion. The other night, when the matter was discussed generally, it was passed around that the minister would adjourn the debate, and I took it for granted that the question would not come up again, or that if it did come up again we would all have an opportunity of placing our views before the House. The particular reason for wishing to place my views before the House is that on that occasion all the members who spoke favoured the taking over of the branch lines, and I thought that if the matter did not come up again the government would likely come to the conclusion that in so far as members on this side of the House were concerned, they were all in favour of the proposition of additional branch lines in connection with the Intercolonial Railway. I was under the impression that possibly we could discuss it on these estimates, but if not we can discuss it on another occasion.

speechtext:
I would not like to refuse any discussion on this question of branch lines on any particular vote, but I have ascertained that the question the hon. gentleman wishes to refer to is still on the Order Paper, and may come up

again. A long discussion on branch lines and their merits would not be in order at this moment, especially as it is still on the Order Paper, although the question might be referred to.

If we had the assurance that we would have an opportunity of discussing it again on the resumption of the adjourned debate that would be quite satisfactory, although, in adjourning the debate, the minister took the opportunity of saying that he would refer to the policy of the government on branch lines when he made his statement in connection with the Intercolonial Railway.
So he did to a certain extent.
As long as I have the opportunity of discussing it later on that is all I want.
I think it would be better business to take up these matters when the minister next goes into Supply if he will be good enough to inform us when he next proposes to move the House into committee.
All right.
I would like to ask the minister why an examination was not made of the Dominion Atlantic Railway at the time the other branches were examined?

The Dominion Atlantic is in a somewhat different position from some of the other roads. I did not know that they had neglected to give us a report on that until my attention was drawn to it. It seems that the commissioners had some little difficulty with the Dominion Atlantic as to their transportation and that instead of facilitating them they put everything in the way of getting a report on the Dominion Atlantic. However, we have the sworn returns of the road every year, and have a pretty good idea of its value, its earnings, and that kind of thing. It is in a different position from some of the other lines because the Dominion Atlantic does not want to lease or sell and the other lines practically all do.

But >
the people living along that road may want it.
It would be a question how far you could go in expropriating a railway that did not want to sell or lease.

I do not think that it is
correct to say that the Dominion Atlantic people do not want to sell. There are too many shrewd business men in the company in London to say openly that they want to sell it. They prefer to hold off and be in a position to make the best bargain they Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
can. I was talking to the manager of that road and he said in one breath that they would not sell and in the next that anybody who bought the road must buy the steamers also. It has been in the air for the last five or six years that the Toad is for sale and that other companies have been after it. If the road were in the hands of anybody who would give encouragement to manufacturers and industries located upon it, it would pay more than it does now. The road is being run, not to the advantage of the country, of the farmers or of the manufacturers, but it is being run in order to skim all it can out of the country, being owned by a company which is out of Canada and which has no interest in it.
Is that the Evangeline route ?

That is the Evangeline route. I have received a letter from a manufacturer in one of the towns there complaining that the policy of the road is one of obstruction instead of assistance in the work of developing their trade. They are in continual trouble.
How much does that road pay?
The earnings over operating expenses are $280,586.
How many miles?
Counting the branches and sidings, 298 miles. I think the straight run is about 225 miles from Yarmouth to Halifax.
Who is the manager of the road?
The local manager is Mr. Percy Gifkins. The road is owned in London.
Do you not think it would be a good scheme to sell the Intercolonial Railway to that road or buy that manager?

I think it would be a good
thing to buy that manager.

This Dominion Atlantic Railway passes through my county and I think it is only fair to the corporation to say that it is a road owned by private individuals and is not owned by the government and run, as the Intercolonial is, for the purpose of carrying out the scheme of confederation or of promoting trade between the western and eastern parts of the Dominion, one of the objects for which the Intercolonial Railway was originally conceived and constructed. This railway is owned by private individuals. It must be run in such a way as to pay running expenses and something more or go into insolvency. It had its difficulties in its early years and more than once was on

the verge of insolvency, but I think that during the last 15 or 20 years it has paid running expenses and possibly some dividends. I am not prepared to say that the rates are higher than they ought to be, but I do know that the rates are higher than the rates on the Intercolonial Railway. And, I do know that the people in west* ern Nova Scotia have complained-in fact in former years I brought this matter to the attention of the House on several occasions-that they were placed at an unfair disadvantage in the city of Halifax their principal market, as compared with their friends in eastern Nova Scotia through whose counties the Intercolonial Railway runs. I do not intend to carry this discussion further, but I think it is only fair to the Dominion Atlantic Railway and its management to say that they are operating a railroad owned by private individuals! and built with private money. I do not' think it is fair to charge them with levying too high rates. Their rates are controlled; by the scale of rates adopted for all company owned railways, and they are subject to the control of the Railway Commission. If the rates are unduly high it is very easy for any one to make a complaint to the Commission and to have them adjusted. As to the taking over of this road and the policy of acquiring the branch lines which are feeders of the Intercolonial, should that policy ever be adopted I think there would be no very great difficulty in this case, because if I remember correctly in the original charter under which this road was constructed there is a provision by which the government can take it over at a price to be fixed by certain judges who are named in the charter for that purpose.
Do I understand the Minister of Militia to say that the government-owned road treats the public better than this private-owned road ?
Yes.
Well, I am glad to have that on record.
It is a fact, and we have a deficit on the Intercolonial Railway as a result.
You would not think of going back to private ownership later on.
No; it does not go through my county.

I had a letter from the chairman of the cotton company in the town in which I reside, and he gives me the schedule of rates paid by their company on the Dominion Atlantic Railway and on the Intercolonial Railway, and the last clause of his letter states that it will be seen by the schedule that his company
is paying six times as much for their cotton goods on the Dominion Atlantic Railway as on the Intercolonial Railway. Furthermore, I think I am right in saying that whatever financial difficulty the Dommion Atlantic road has had in years past wa3 not caused by the running of their railroad, but that the loss was made in purchasing steamers and attempting and succeeding in running a rival steamship off the route between Yarmouth and Boston. There was a local steamship line owned by the Eastern Steamship Company which had been in successful operation, and it came into the minds of the London management of that railway that they wanted to compete on that route, and they bought steamers and cut rates and finally ran the local steamship company off. In the end they bought the local company's steamers and then found they had too many boats on their hands.
I think that is about the only loss the Dominion Atlantic has made. I believe that the steamship route does not pay yet, and so it cuts down the large profits which are made on the railway itself. But, that the railroad is a paying concern there is no doubt, and that it could be made still more paying there is also no doubt. It could be made mutually to the advantage of the Intercolonial Railway and to the people along the road, because it runs through one of the richest fruit and farming countries in Canada. A country well suited for manufactures and a country that must prosper. But the industries along that road are hampered by the penny wise and pound foolish management.
I may say to my hon. friend (Mr. Black) that the time to which I allude was long prior to this company owning any steamer.
They only owned a piece of the road then.

As I remember they had some difficulties five or six years after they commenced to operate, and I think the company's road was opened about 39 years ago. The difficulties have not resulted since the steamships have been owned by the railroad. This Evangeline route affords a continuous line from Halifax to Boston and incidentally to St. John and to Montreal via St. John. It is absolutely necessary they should have lines ox steamships. It is operating very successfully several steamships from Yarmouth to Boston, one to New York, and one or two across the Bay of Fundy from Digby to St. John. It would be a great deprivation to the public if these steamships were not operated and it is not fair to charge up to the steamship lines any loss that may be made on the operation of the system. It would be very difficult to separate the steamships from the rest of the system. It is a through line partly by

steamship and partly by railway from Halifax to Boston on the one hand, and from Halifax to Montreal via St. John and the Bay of Fundy on the other. I have added these further remarks so that the situation of the line may be fairly understood.
Strengthening bridges, $70,000.
Last year we had a vote of $190,000 to do this work and we spent $120,000; this $70,000 is a revote.
Is this a renewal of the old bridges?

It is practically putting new bridges. These bridges were al old and we are putting in steel bridges m most of the places.
,,Mr- HAGGART. You are charging the whole cost to capital account?
Where a new work is constructed we deduct the value of the old work and charge to capital the difference between the old and the new.
What deduction has been made for the value of the old work ?

It would take quite a long while to get that information. Some ot the old bridges have been sold and we give credit for them.
. Mr. R. L. BORDEN. Perhaps the minister takes a short cut by valuing the old work at nothing?
on the Canada Eastern branch, is replaced with an iron bridge that is absolutely new work, and is chargeable to capital.
Are these all on the Canada Eastern?
Does the minister know that?	[DOT]

I am speaking from information given to my deputy. If it were an iron bridge of an ancient date which was being replaced with one of the modern style, they would sell the old bridge for what it would bring, and charge the difference between that and the cost of the new bridge to capital.
Oh, no.
He does not inter to make any deduction because he is char mg the whole vote to capital account.

I understand that theoretically that is so, but I am told that the practice more and more is to charge all betterments on an old line of railway to revenue; and I am not sure that under the rules of the commission that is not becoming to a certain extent a necessity.

Every year hundreds of millions of dollars are expended on capital aeount on old lines, for replacing bridges, improving grades and increasing rolling stock.
, Mr. FOSTER. My hon. friend is perfectly right in saying that these railroads spend millions on capital account, but he has not traced out the details. If he does that, I believe he will find that these betterments are in a great measure not charged to capital but to revenue account. Of course, if they built an extension, or increased the quantity of rolling stock, these expenditures would be charged to capital account; but I am informed that a great deal of the renewal of rolling stock, even though the new is of greater capacity than the old, is not charged to capital, but to revenue, and that is becoming more and more the case.

That is just what we do with a lot of our rolling stock. This year we have constructed a lot of rolling stock,

much heavier and larger than that which it replaces, out of revenue. The principle is that where you are putting in new rolling stock equal in carrying power to the old, you charge it to revenue; but where you are getting something new, that is charged to capital. The Pennsylvania Railroad has expended within a comparatively short time, between Philadelphia and New York, $200,000,000, all charged to capital acount; and that is not a new road, but an old road. By the returns I find that the railroad companies are sinners somewhat in this respect. When their revenues are buoyant, they stick to the line pretty closely; but when their revenue falls off, they charge to capital 'account what they formerly charged to (revenue.

I am not inclined to place implicit confidence in that. I want to show how easy it is to make an impression with 'nothing underlying it. My hon. friend has (stated that the Pennsylvania Railroad spent of late between New York and Philadelphia about $200,000,000. What has that been spent on? On the great New York terminals in the neighbourhood of 42nd street, on tunnels, and on electrifying the [DOT]system within fifty miles of New York city That $200,000,000 has almost entirely gone into that kind of improvement. That is not taking a bit of a bridge on the Mira-tnichi and replacing it and then putting that to capital account.
I made no reference to terminals or tunnels.

The hon. minister in his statement paraded the idea that they had bought rolling stock and charged it to capital. That is true of every road. Is it not true also that you have bought a mighty lot of rolling stock and charged it to capital?
Certainly.

And that you have lame engines and acres of rolling stock standing along your whole road from one end to the other, which you should have repaired and charged to revenue but which are lying idle, and you have kept your road going by a large expenditure on Tolling stock charged to capital account. Suppose you put an independent man on that Intercolonial Railway and have him take an inventory of every bit of damaged rolling stock and tote up what that would cost for repairs to be charged to revenue, you will have a different set of accounts from those brought down to us. Of course you have paid for rolling stock out of revenue, but I am inclined to think you have paid illegitimately for rolling stock out of capital rather than face the repairing of the old stock and deduct that from revenue. But with reference to the $200,000,000 expenditure on the Pennsylvania road charged to capital, you will find
that the largest part was sunk in legitimate capital expenditure, comprising the almost unrivalled terminal facilities which that road has procured in New York.

The amount I have stated would not cover the terminals or tunnels.
It has spent an enormous amount _ getting rid of grade crossings and making viaducts, over-head tracks and levelling the road._ It is the same old Toad and all these things have been charged to capital. Every, railway in the world has to spend a certain amount each year and charge it to capital account. As to disabled cars, last, year I had the matter looked up and got a percentage made which I gave to the House. According to that, the percentage of disabled rolling stock was slightly less on the Intercolonial Railway than on the Grand Trunk Railway. Every railway has a certain percentage of rolling stock disabled, and ours was a little less than the Grand Trunk Railway a year ago. To-day I state unreservedly that the Intercolonial Railway has not a greater percentage of disabled rolling stock than the Grand Trunk Railway or the Canadian Pacific Railway.

I shall not discuss again the question of charging to capital, because in my view there should be no capital account whatever on the road. Here is a road which had an excellent bridge at Miramichi, an iron bridge, which lasted 30 years. When it became nearly worn out, we took it down and transferred a portion to the Prince Edward Island Railway. And the new one we substituted is charged to capital account. Let me mention another thing. We took over the Canada Eastern read in New Brunswick at a cost of some $800,000. And we had the assurance from the minister of that day that the road was ir. perfect order and could be run a number of years without any expenditure on repairs. Yet within three years we have spent on that road the full amount of its .cost. And to-day the minister asks us for a large sum to replace two bridges upon that road. These bridges were perfectly good two years ago, when we were buying that road at a large price, but to-day they are useless and must be renewed. Such statements as that tend to throw discredit on all statements made with regard to that road. We paid some $800,000 for that Canada Eastern Railway. And then when we bought it, we had the report of the chief engineer that it was in excellent order and would not require repairs of any consequence for a number of years. Yet in a couple of years we have paid in repairs the entire cost of the road.
Improvements at Sackville, $10,000.

This is to complete a freight shed. The total expenditure at that station has been $84,515 on everything. In

1907 we expended $26,000; in 1907-8, $58,344; and last year $23,134, making a total of $107,649.
From what date do you count that expenditure?
The Intercolonial keeps a record of the money expended on capital account at any station since the beginning of the road.

It means the same shops on a very small scale. Such shops are at the end of every division of a railway to carry on what are known as light repairs. For heavier repairs, such as remodelling or remaking the locomotives are taken to the central shops at Moncton.

I think I announced to the House that we would go on with the work this year, but, owing to the conditions we have found we have decided that we will merely do as we are doing at Moncton-get the right of way as far as we can and not' proceed with a great deal of the work this year.

I think the surveys are ma'de.

Yes.

About $3,600, I think.

On engines used all the way from Sydney to Halifax?

Yes, we also do repairs for the Dominion Atlantic and the Halifax and South Western. Our larger shops are of course, at Moncton.
Mr. F06TER. Does this mean a duplication of your shops at Moncton?

$394,135. It is 8i miles.
