I would not like to make a statement as a member of the government
on that point. Every one who has discussed pro and con the financial position of the world will, I think, approve of the conclusion come to by the government that for this year it would be advisable not to proceed with these larger works or to undertake any new ones. This would involve a large expenditure of money.
Not more than the Moncton cut off.

The Moncton cut off calls for only $50,000 this year. We are treating them both in the same way. At Moncton we are asking for $50,000 only instead of $374,000, and in this case we are taking a vote to go on, as far as we can, with the right of way. I can asure my hon. friend there is no other consideration in view in connection with this.
Was not the necessity of this work impressed on the government to overcome some heavy grades there?
Yes.

Is there not a great deal
of heavy freight to be handled from that end of the island?

Yes, a great deal of
freight.
Is it not important that these grades should be overcome as soon as possible? Are they not more important than the cut off at Moncton?
We are treating this in the same way. They both cut off grades, and my hon. friend is mistaken if he thinks I am treating them differently.
I thought one more important than the other.
No, the one is not being held back on account of the other, and I am as much disappointed as my hon. friend that this is not going on this year.
Can the minister give any assurance that this will be done next year?

I would not like to say absolutely. I am not a good promiser, I like to do as I say. I assure my hon. friend that this is one of the first works that will be done as soon as the conditions will warrant such expenditures.

There is not much activity there now, but there was a lot last October. I happened to be down there and went out one beautiful afternoon to enjoy a drive, and we had to keep a look-out at the masthead for fear of running over these numerous stakes. We called at one store where there was one set of stakes in front and another at the back door ; the proprietor was staked before and behind. We were in dire peril of destroying government works and being taken up therefor.
You escaped pretty well.

This is not at all a new question and it is entirely wrong to suppose it was gotten up for election purposes last fall, although it happened to be prominently before the people, I suppose, at that time. Twenty-two years ago, when the road was located in Cape Breton the island was not as important as it is to-day, the traffic was not so large and the prospects not so bright as they are now. The road was laid out 22 years ago and the best grade and the best route were not selected. The Liberals of the county of Cape Breton and their leaders always contended that the route was wrong, particularly between George's river and Sydney. A short cut was taken between Leitches creek and George's river, over a mountain where there are high grades on both sides. It was always contended by those in opposition in 1887 that the road should have followed the shore as is proposed now, and come down to the town of Sydney Mines, which is an important town of 7,000 or 8,000, putting that town upon the main line, then continuing the line to North Sydney, where the hon. member was tumbling over the stakes, putting it also on the main line and then running on to Sydney. That would have been the proper

course and would have given the level line that you must now, at great expense, obtain in order to handle the traffic. Delegation after delegtion came to Ottawa during Conservative and Liberal rule to have this matter rectified. At last the present Minister of Railways and Canals was persuaded that the change was necessary and that in order to handle the traffic we must have a better route than we have had. It is now found necessary to make that diversion from George's river around by Sydney Mines and thence to North Sydney and to Sydney on the best available route. I think the item is not well worded, diversion of lines Sydney Mines and River George. I understand this to mean a diversion of the line from George's river to Sydney Mines thence using the present line to North Sydney and continuing to Leitches creek to make the proper connection with the Intercolonial which is the intention and is a longer distance than was mentioned by the minister in answering the member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Maddin?. The distance from George's river to Sydney Mines would be 81 miles, and there is the further distance from North Sydney to Leitches creek which would be two or three or four miles, more. I must express my own particular desire that this work should be proceeded with as rapidly as possible. It will be of great advantage to the two towns and to the road itself. I think the deputy minister and the minister know that the train load that can be hauled over this heavy grade from Leitches creek across this high hill to George'-s river now is not more than one half the train load that could be carried all the way from Sydney to Point Tup-per if this diversion was completed. I trust therefore that every effort will be put forth at as early a date as possible to have this road completed and this advantage given to the people of North Sydney and Sydney Mines, as well as to the management of the road. Talking of freight, the smaller of the two great companies down there paid to this road last year the handsome sum of $250,000 in cash for freights. Therefore it will be understood that to give proper accommodation to such a customer as the Nova Scotia Steel Company is itself important if there were no other important customer at that particular place. What applies to it I would say, although I have not the figures, would apply with equal force to the Dominion Steel and the Dominion Coal Companies. There are customers of the road that will all be accommodated by the completion of this diversion of the line. I am disappointed that the work is not being proceeded with this year. Of course, I must accept the explanation of the minister that he is not in a position to go on with it now. I hope that my im-Mr. D. D. McKENZIE.
pression and belief are true that the matter will be taken up and that steps will be taken this year to obtain the right of way and to fix the line where it should be and where it is going to be and that as soon as possible the road will be constructed along the line that will be agreed upon.
They will keep it for the next election.

My hon. friend says something about the next election. It is a long time away and the hon. whip, who is getting to be an old man, should be thinking more about the world beyond than about the next election. I am sorry that such frivolous things should bother him so much and that' he should forget better things.
You must be qualifying for a divinity student.
There is so little divinity on the opposition benches that I think it would be well for them to borrow some from this side.
You look a good deal like a bishop.

There are a great many things that I would like to point out in reference to this matter, but T think the minister understands the necessity of carrying out this work, having taken the very important step that he did take, and I hope it will be followed up to completion as speedily as possible.

My hon. friend from Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) has pointed out that this question of diverting the line has been agitated by members of his party in that part of the country for the past twenty years and that it is a mistake to imagine that it was to meet any political exigency that an item was put in the estimates last year to provide for this work. I would like to point out that it was very significant that, although members of the hon. gentleman's party had been sending delegations and praying this government to divert the line, as it is proposed to divert is at the present time, during the years_ of boasted progress, prosperity and overflowing treasury that this country is alleged to have enjoyed, the government did not undertake to make this diversion until on the eve of the election last fall when their resources were very much inferior to what they are to-day. I think the fact that the government now say that they are unable to carry on this undertaking would indicate that there is something to found the suspicion upon that the sum of $25,000 which was put in the estimates last year for this proposed line was to meet some political exigency. The fact that the hon. member is satisfied

with the explanation and that he believes that the work will be completed is not a very satisfactory guarantee looking towards the future. I may say to the committee that the surveyed lines of railway have intersected that county to such an extent that a plan of the county looks like a cobweb. One particular line of railway has served, within my recollection, no less than seven elections. I do not know how many this one is calculated to serve. I think it was not asking the minister too much to say that he would undertake to have this much-needed railway constructed during the next fiscal year. With regard to the friends of the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria having always held that this road was built on the wrong line, that was certainly a matter of opinion and the election was run in that county on the question of two certain routes. The railway was built, as the result of the election issue, by way of the route that it follows at the present time. The route which is in operation now was quite competent to carry the freight at that time. The town of Sydney Mines, as the hon. gentleman points out, has a population of perhaps 7,000 or 8,000. It has grown from a small mining village with a population of only 2,000 or 2,400. The works of the Dominion Coal Company were not then in existence, although some of the older pits were in operation under previous owners. The road, when built, was built to suit conditions as they existed, but it is a well known fact that in the last nine years conditions have arisen there that have called for an alteration of its route and, when the hon .gentleman says that his party have always urged upon the government the alteration of the route, it has to be borne in mind that the opinion in regard to the alteration of the route is shared by all parties in that country regardless of political affiliations.

I am sorry that the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Mad-din) thinks it necessary to import severe party politics into this question. If he wants to go into the history of the building of that road in Cape Breton county and if he wants to know something about whether it was ever known politically or not, I would say to him that if he had lived in Cape Breton county at the time this road was surveyed he would know that men were up to their waists in snow banks cutting the trees out of the right of way on the verge of the election of 1887. He would know that a few of our strong Liberals in Cape Breton county had been switched over from Liberalism to Toryism by giving them large contracts for clearing away the woods in the midst of the election of 1887. No influences of this kind have been used in our day and nothing was
said about the building of this road last summer to influence any individual or any set of individuals. The hon. gentleman is too young a man to know much about the political history of the county of Cape Breton, but if he knows anything about conflicting routes in that county he ought to know better than to suppose that there was any conflict between the George's river and Sydney Mines route, and that across the hill from George's river to Leitches creek. The two routes were the southern route via St. Peter's and the central route.
I did not say that the route proposed to be diverted and the present route were in dispute at that time.
I understood the hon. gentleman to say that the election of 1887 settled the difficulty.
Not as between these two proposed routes-certainly not.
My hon. friend gave me a wrong impression then when he said that the election of 1887 settled the question as between the route from Georges river to Leitches creek and the proposed one.
It did not.

They were canvassing this change for election purposes. My hon. friend is quite aware that in 1895-1 think it was-when the right hon. Sir Charles Tupper was running an election in our county, he made it a part of his platform and he laid it down as the policy of his government to build this road from Georges river to Sydney Mines. It has been continuously agitated ever since that time in the county. It so happens that the hon. gentleman who is now occupying the position of Minister of Railways and Canals was the first Liberal Minister of Railways who had the courage and enterprise to declare the expediency of this work being undertaken and completed. But the hon. gentleman for Cape Breton must not say the Liberal party did not do anything towards accomplishing this purpose. The hon. member well knows, if he wishes to give the present government the credit for it, that this government extended the line from North Sydney to Sydney Mines; that it has given Sydney Mines the benefit of railway connection, that it has given North Sydney the benefit of that continuous connection. I can tell the hon. member (Mr. Mad/din) that his predecessors in the representation of the county of Cape Breton sat quietly in this House and supported the Conservative government in a proposal to build a road in the county of Gape Breton that clean shut off the two important towns of Sydney Mines and North Sydney. My hon. friend (Mr. Maddin) speaks of Sydney Mines in these days as an insignificant

little village by the wayside. Well, it was just as important as the town of Sydney. The town of Sydney Mines and North Sydney were much upon a par. North Sydney was larger at that time than Sydney, and without saying anything disparaging to the town of Sydney which was the capital, Sydney Mines was just as important as either of the other two. North Sydney and the town of Sydney were incorporated about the same time, and the fact that Sydney Mines was not incorporated did not make it any smaller or any less important. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maddin) wishes to discuss the history of both political parties in respect to railways in the county of Cape Breton, what he has to confront is that the members who then supported the Tory government in this House were perfectly satisfied to get this road any way at all before the Dominion elections' of 1887, when they were trembling in the balance, and if it were not for this road and the impetus given their canvass they never would have been returned. They cared not where the road went once it passed the Grand Narrows. Once it came to the door of the man who was then supporting the government, once it brought grist to his mill they cared not how it got to Sydney. And the hon. member who sat with this gentleman at that time agreed that it did not make very much difference whether North Sydney or Sydney Mines were left out in the cold or not. They had no railway accommodation; we got a section of the road built into North Sydney for which we undertook to pay for all the right of way ourselves. That is the history of his friends in regard to getting railway accommodation to North Sydney and Sydney Mines. But as soon as the Liberal government came in we got better treatment. Up to the time the Liberal government came to power the railway was left out in the woods with no communication with the shore or with tidal waters at all. The Liberal government extended it to the shore, gave us a first-class wharf, gave us communication with Newfoundland, and we have now a steamer running between North Sydney and Newfoundland which is a great feeder to this railroad and which is of course a benefit to the people of Newfoundland and to the people of North Sydney and the country generally. This government gave us further an extension of the railway to Sydney Mines which of course is veTy beneficial to that town. The road from North Sydney to Sydney Mines was built with a view of its extension to George's River and ultimately with a view to the completion of that road in the place where it was intended from the first and where it should have been. Now, Sir, that piece that is built between North Sydney and Sydney Mines will not be lost because it is part of the main line and will link on to it.
Mr. d. d. McKenzie.
My hon. friend (Mr. Maddin) has said that the Liberal government has done nothing during the last twelve years to establish this line of railway. Well, we have done that much, that we have built into North Sydney and Sydney Mines, and that part is completed and the right of way and everything belonging to it is the property of the government. The Liberal government and the supporters of the Liberal government have nothing to be afraid of in comparing their history with the history of the Conservatives, and of my hon. friend's predecessors with regard to this matter. I had no desire to. introduce any politics into the question; I had no desire to treat it in any other way but as a question affecting the whole of the people and which is of great importance to them, but if my hon. friend wishes to launch into political criticism, or if he wants to make any political capital out of it, then, if the hon. gentleman chooses upon the floor of this House to cross swords with me as to the political history of the two parties in this matter he shall always find me ready to meet him.

I do not know that it is very good taste on the part of the hon. member (Mr. McKenzie) to throw down the gauntlet and then take it up m Committee of Supply. I do not think it is a thing upon which he can compliment himself very much when he says that I have not lived long enough in the county of Cape Breton to be as familiar with its railroad history as he is. I can tell the hon. gentleman I have lived long enough in that county to be as familiar with the best railway routes as he is, and I am prepared to enter into a competitive examination at any time before the Minister of Justice in order to satisfy him that I am just as familiar with the railway history of the county of Cape Breton as he is. The hon. gentleman refers to the great things that have been done by the Liberal party for railway development in the county of Cape Breton, and in enumerating all these great things he points to the extension of the railway from Sydney to Sydney Mines. Why Sir, do you know that in the county of Cape Breton _ every mile of railway in that county owes its existence to the Conservative government with the exception of this two and a half miles from North Sydney to Sydney Mines? If the hon. member (Mr. McKenzie) wants to boast about the records of the Liberal government in connection with that insignificant piece of railway it will redound very little to his credit or to the credit of the Liberal party. And further, when the House learns that it took five years from the time it was undertaken until its completion, and that it cost the people_of this country no less than $58,000 per mile, running as it does parallel with the Nova Scotia Coal and Steel Company's Toad and partly on the same roadbed, the House will see

that the hon. gentleman (Mr. McKenzie) has not much room for boasting. When the hon. gentleman talks about the great benefits the people of Cape Breton county have derived from this government in the matter of railway facilities, I wish to say that they have had to be content with what was handed to them on the eve of the last election. There has never been even an election for municipal councillors that the Liberal party in that county have not proposed some railway scheme or another. It was not an unusual thing in connection with the last election to find a man and a boy bailing water out of a post hole four or five feet deep at high water mark and having to go back into the Bras d'Or lake.
And charging it up to capital?
That looks like watering stock.

Surely that would compare with the condition of affairs in 1887 when men stood to their waists in snow chopping down trees, as depicted by the hon. member (Mr. McKenzie). However, I submit that two wrongs do not make a right, and if the hon. member wants to point out that in 1887 the Conservative party engaged men in midwinter to make a survey of a line; if that was wrong it should not be a justification in the year 1908 for the Liberal government putting in the estimates a sum of money which they did not intend to spend .and did not spend, and having a survey made and stakes put down at every other man's front door or back door for a proposed line of railway, all of which took place between the time intervening after the prorogation of parliament in July and the elections on the 26th of October, and all of which is too significant to require any comment. The hon. member (Mr. McKenzie) may be quite content with the hope that now that the survey is made this railway will be completed, but the industries of the county are not content that it should rest in that manner. This extension is so absolutely essential to move the heavy trains from the Nova Stfotia Steel and Coal Company, from the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, and from the Dominion Coal Company, that it is important the work should be undertaken at once. I have no doubt that the hon. member will be quite content that a sum be put in the estimates and that the scheme will be delayed from time to time, so as to help Mr. Murray in the local elections in the course of a couple of years, and may be to help the hon. gentleman himself when he comes before his constituents at the next general election. But that method of carrying on public works does not meet with the approval of the people of the country. It is not calculated to serve the industrial centres in 93

that part of the country, and I would urge upon the minister the desirability of having this grade changed at as early a date as possible.
Diversion of line at Chatham and branch to wharf, $36,000.
What is this?

This is an item which we had in the estimates last year. I expected this year to proceed actively with the work, but the conditions were not favourable. I am asking for a revote for the purpose of getting the right of way as far as possible. That is what I had in mind in asking Mr. Henry Reid to go down and negotiate for the land; but he would not accept the position, and we shall have to get some one else.
Locomotive and car shops with equipment and new freight yard at Moncton, $400,000.

The total cost of these, With the line, is estimated at about $2,000,000. The total amount expended has been $1,351,446.76. In addition to this vote, we are asking for another amount, which will make for machinery about $500,000.
How are they off for machinery there now?
I think about $100,000 will finish the machinery.
Where does the minister bay that?
We buy it in practically all cases by tender, and nearly all from Canadian manufacturers.
Who has charge of ma chinery.
Mr. J. R. Joughins is our superintendent of motive power.
Is a certain amount of it bought in the United States?
Necessarily and occasionally, some machinery which we cannot get in Canada. But we make it a point to buy everything practicable in Canada.
Does the minister give bona fide public notice in these matters?
Yes. We send specifications to every manufacturer of these goods in Canada.
Open competition and tender?
Absolutely.
Is all this paid for out of capital?
Yes.
Suppose you have a station house at Sussex which is sufficient
for the business and some night it burns down and you build a new station house in the place of it, do you charge the new station to capital?

It would depend on cir cumstances. It would depend somewhat on the question of the new style of station we put up. The Canadian Pacific Railway built their Angus shops at Montreal and equipped them out of capital. Conditions vary so much that the railway companies do not stick to one absolute line. These shops at Moncton are absolutely new. The old shops are still there, except the portion that was burned. We had an offer to lease them, but it was so small that I would not accept it.
I understand that the answer the minister would have given is that the new station at Sussex would be charged to revenue?
Several of the smaller stations have been replaced out of capital.
When you replace the old shops with new ones, which are a great deal better than the old, would it not be fair to charge some portion of the cost to revenue?

The old shops were repaired out of revenue. We spent on them about $56,000 out of revenue. Even if a fire had not occurred, these buildings would have had to be reconstructed. During the last year or two we have been working there under great disadvantages. We hope to cheapen the cost of our productions by having the new shops.
To increase water supply, $74,700.
We are endeavouring t0_ improve our water supply at many points along the line, in some cases making a new supply. I have a long list of the places.
Is there a special contractor who gets the most of these?

No. Take the water supply at Little Metis, tenders were asked by posters and four were received and the contract given to the lowest, Mr. McManus. At St. Charles Junction, also four tenders were received, and Mr. McManus was again the lowest.
To increase accommodation and facilities along the line, $133,000.

This is for a large number of expenditures. Altogether we have expended at different times, since the Intercolonial Railway was constructed, along the line, $539,809. These expenses comprise new Windsor Freight Office, $82,000; tipper Dorchester Sidings, Marieville Freight Sheds and additional sidings, ad-Mr. FOSTER.
ditional sidings at Boiestown, electric semaphore at Petit Rocher, station and platform at Little Metis, and other items of like character.
Was there no station at Little Metis before ?

The old building was worth but $1,200 or $1,300 and was practically no station at all, and the tourist traffic demands a decent station. Then there is $7,000 at Princess Pier for additional siding accommodation and track scale; $6,000 for a crossing siding at St. Pacome, and 35 miles of track fencing, not previously fenced, $23,500.
Any buckets or tin pails?
No, none in this list.

I would like to call
attention to a specific case in North Cape Breton, that at Christmas Island. That i3 a very important country centre at which some very important people live, and it has no station at all. We had a small building there, but it was burnt down a year or a year and a half ago, and I would not care to describe the condition to-day. I hope that out of this general vote provision will be made for a station house, properly equipped and commensurate with the amount of business transacted. It is one of the most important country districts in North Cape Breton. We do not look for anything very expensive, but ought to have a presentable wooden structure which will meet the requirement.

I will consider that matter very fully.
Improvements at Ste. Rosalie, $55,000.

This is entirely a revote. It is a junction of the Grand Trunk Railway east of Montreal. We are putting up a round house and making an accumulating yard where we have to gather our freight and our trains.
How far from Montreal?
Thirty-six miles.
Is that on the leased line?
At the junction of the leased line and our own.
The lease provides that we are to participate in their terminals and improvements, I understand ?
At Montreal, but they have none at Ste. Rosalie.
Could not this assembling be done at Montreal?

On the Grand Trunk branch from Ste. Rosalie into Montreal we carry big trains. One engine from/ Ste. Rosalie hauls nearly equal to two trains. We have all these cars to re-arrange. We interchange with the Canadian Pacific Railway as well. Therefore, we must have large yards to handle the cars. The Grand Trunk are not under obligation to give us terminal accommodation there.
Do they give us in Montreal all that we expected to get?

We use their terminals in Montreal. They think we utilize them too much, but we think we do only what we have a right to.
Improvements at Drummondville, $5,000.
This is to provide additional yard' accommodation. The whole amount is a revote; we did not get that extended last year. I am surprised that, in the face of an election, we were so moderate.

It was hung up there all the time.
Engine-house, machine shops, &c., at Rivi-fere du Loup, $158,500.
This is for the machine shop at Riviere du Loup that I spoke of a little while ago. It is something along the line of the Halifax shops, designed to carry on light repairs.	*
Are these shops at all equal to those at Halifax?
Not so large as at Halifax. This is more for locomotives; the car repairs are made more in the Halifax shops.
How much has been expended there?
Altogether, since there was a railway, $329,580.81.
How many men have you there?
About 150 employed there now.
How many at Halifax, when you were in full swing, but with no election on ?

I don't think it would vary much-about the same number as at Riviere du Loup.
At six o'clock Mr. Speaker took the Chair.
What is to be taken up after eight o'clock?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Of course, there will be Private Bills for the first hour, and then 931
my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) will continue, to be followed, should he finish, by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley).

We shall not be able to go on-with the item with reference to the Intercolonial, collection of revenue. We shall have to have our discussion on that. Could we take some part of it, or is it in one lump sum.
In a lump sum.

We want a discussion on going into supply on that. We could finish the capital votes to-night, I suppose. Before Mr. Speaker leaves the Chair, I desire to say just a word with regard to the proposed work of Tuesday. Certain information was asked for by the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden), and the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) has said that it would be supplied. But the Finance Minister will see that we ought to have it printed, and in time so that we may have an opportunity to study it. Does the hon. minister think he can have that information printed for us in good time for Tuesday?

We can talk it over on Monday. But the minister had better keep it in mind. This is a very important question, and we should be placed in a position to discuss it intelligently.

Yes. As soon as mention was made of the matter, I put it in hand and an officer was sent to Montreal to expedite, as much as possible, getting the information concerning the company's affairs.

House in Committee of Supply.
Improvements at Campbellton, $64,500.

['This is rather an old story. Mr. Buell has been engaged for some time investigating express matters for the commission. I do not know just what this particular work is but he is not a counsel engaged to present the general complaints of the people against the railway companies. This is rather an investigation into the methods of the express companies which has been going on for a year and a half or two years.']
Will the minister please explain this?

This is for continuing the improvements that we have been carrying on at Campbellton. This is for the extension of the water supply, additional accommodation for baggage and express, oil house, six stall section of new engine house, turn table, enlarging station, ice house, &c. There was an expenditure last year of $8,887.78. Tenders were asked for by posters.
As the vote is very much larger this year than last, are some of these new works that you are undertaking?

This is a continuation of works that were undertaken last year. They are not new.
Improvements at Point Tupper, $4,000.

This is for a brick building, for transfer bridge, engine house, to raise reservoir and a few other minor things.
To provide a subway crossing at Eastville, berts, about two miles north of Londonderry station, $5,000.

This is to remove a level crossing.
To provide a subway crossing at Eastville, about one mile south of Londonderry station, $10,000.
This is a dangerous crossing in a very deep cut. There have been some accidents ana we have decided to remove the crossing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Rolling stock, $170,550.

This is to provide a commissary car, to equip 500 platform cars with racks for carrying pulpwood, to increase the size of steam heating pipes in passenger cars, to equip cars with new gas light apparatus and several other contingencies.
New machinery for locomotive and car shops, $95,800.

This was explained pretty well before we adjourned for dinner in connection with the several works at the Moncton shops.
Prince Edward Island Railway-branch line, Harmony to Elmira, $50,000.

I wish to ask the minister if it is the intention of the government to build that railway the present year. I had some questions on the Order Paper some time ago, and I regret to say that the answers were not quite clear. One question was this:
Is it the intention of the government to begin the construction of the road during the present year?
The answer is as follows:
It is the intention to begin the work.
Does that mean that the government is going to start the construction of the road this present year?

We have asked for tenders and to assure my hon. friend that we mean to go right on with it we have asked the people submitting the lowest tender whether, if we accept their tender, they will agree to proceed as far as this appropriation will allow them this year, on the understanding that we will provide for some more expenditure during the following year. We are awaiting their reply. We expect to let the contract shortly. We intend to proceed with the work just as soon as the conditions will allow us to.
The contract has not been let then?

It is just in the condition I have described. We have the tenders and the lowest tender will be accepted if they will agree, as I have suggested, to be content with this expenditure this year, in the hope that we may be able to proceed more rapidly with the work next year. I am asking them to accept the contract on that understanding.
The minister is well aware that this is only a very short piece of road and it seems like making two bites of a cherry to extend the construction over two years. The road is only ten miles in length.
It is estimated to cost $380,000.
The lowest tender is not quite as high as that, I understand.
I have not the lowest tender with me. I would not care to make it public until it is accepted.
Is it the intention to build the road on the line surveyed? This road has been used as a political football.
I would not think that.
It is very hard to be responsible for what the minister may think on these matters. I would not like to hold myself responsible for his thoughts.
It would be a dangerous experiment.

The first survey that I remember was started in 1904, just as the elections were going on, and it ran from Souris in a different' direction from the route according to the last survey. The survey in 1904 was run in the direction of Souris, and although that survey cost three or four thousand dollars, when the elections were over no effort was made to build the line and the whole thing was hung up until the general elections were approaching last year. Then, they ran a survey out to Harmony six miles within the previous survey, and just before the elections tenders were called to be opened on the 31st of October, five days after the elections. Why, the woods were full of people running surveys.
It did not seem to do any good in your county.

Well, you can fool all the people some of the time and some of the people all the time, but you cannot fool all the people all the time, and as you could not fool them they elected me. The people were tired and sick of this surveying business. In my county during the last two elections there were surveys made for five or six branch lines of railways and no wonder there is a deficit on the Prince Edward Railway when you are wasting thousands of dollars in fruitless surveys like this. In one of the leading Liberal papers in my constituency published on the 16th of March I find this statement:
The contract for building the Elmira branch will shortly he let and the work is expected to start on the 1st of June.
I ask the Minister of Railways is there any foundation for that report?
I am not responsible for what every newspaper publishes, but I have stated clearly and distinctly what is to be done, and I cannot make it clearer if I should repeat my statement.
Then, if the tenderers are not satisfied to take the contract with the conditions stated the contract will not be let. Is that your answer?

The hon. gentleman will not get me to make any statement along the lines he suggests. We are going to spend the amount of this appropriation on that branch this year, but not any more, owing to conditions which I have explained to the House, and which I think the financial world will say are justified under the circumstances. We intend to build this road from Elmira to Harmony and the fact that my hon. friend was elected will not change our intention one iota. We expect to build a good road there with all possible speed, but owing to present conditions we will not spend more than $50,000 on the work this year.
I am pleased to hear the minister say that the road will be built.
Don't stop the estimates then, and let us get a start.
The minister says the estimate for this 10 miles is $300,000?
My memory is that it was stated it would cost about $200,000.

$380,000 is the estimate, and I think the hon. gentleman will find it will cost that before we are done with it. I do not think a railway can be built for less than $38,000 a mile through that country.
Is it the intention of the government to delay this until there is another election coming on.
My hon. friend is not serious in asking that. By the way, there possibly may be a by-election;, has my hon. friend any fears about that?

No one on either side of the House can say when these by-elections may come. We have heard complaints in this House about deficits on the Prince Edward Island Railway, but the minister knows very well that part of the waste takes place during election years, and that the deficit in an election year is always larger than in any other year.
This year is an exception. I am happy to say the Prince Edward Island has done better this year.

That may be, but the history of that railway is that for a month or two before the elections there are spare hands and extra hands employed along the railroad until they are almost as thick as potato bugs. I have a map here which

*shows that there were five or six branch lines from Montague under survey last Summer previous to the election, but not one mile of railroad has been built and there is not one dollar in the estimates to build it. Is it right to use the people's money in this way, sending a number of people out picknicking and chasing rabbits and partridges through the woods in the fall of the year, when you are pretending to make surveys.
What about the tun nel?

We will come to the tunnel later on and I hope you will not oppose it. I can tell the minister that if the government is going to build the road from Elmira to Harmony according to the last survey it is going to inconvenience the people from Elmira a great deal because they will have to travel by rail about five or six miles further than if the government had built the railway according to the survey of 1904 which came in on the old line and went through the village of Souris. That is the proper route on which to build the railway if ever it is built. Last year however, they changed the survey and took it out to the old line and you have to travel out to the old line about six miles before you come to the branch, and the people from Souris and east of Souris who will use this railway will have to pay extra freight and passenger rates on this additional six miles which they would not have to pay if the line was built as at first surveyed through the village of Souris and out east. This is one of the things that leads the people to believe that the government is not serious ibout building that road. Can the minister tell us why he changed the route, and instead of starting the railway from Souris, he started it from Harmony?

This matter was left to the engineer to give us the most direct route, and I understand that he did. My hon. friend may be speaking for a particular section, but I understand from himself that this road runs through a section of country which it would not run through if it took the route he suggests, through a section which has already railway facilities.

I do not think the minister understands the matter clearly. The old route runs almost east and west, but at Harmony it turns and runs almost directly south for a distance of five miles to the village of Souris. Then it runs in a northeasterly direction to Elmira. This route was surveyed in 1904, and it is the proper location. This time, instead of turning into the village of Souris the route stops at Harmony, and runs in an easterly direction to Elmira. The railway will not begin at Souris, but at a side station called Harmony. The people of all parts know that Mr. FRASER.
the proper location is the one surveyed in 1904, to give accommodation to the people of Souris and the public generally. I would ask the minister why he changed the location since?

The minister made no change at all. He asked the engineer to survey the most direct route, and he did so. My hon. friend is speaking for Souris, of course, but Souris has already railway accommodation, and to run that line to Souris would be to give it a second line. This line is not continued to Souris, but when it reaches Harmony it goes straight on. I do not blame my hon. friend for urging the claims of Souris; that is natural; but we want to accommodate the most people, and from the railway standpoint, we regard the present route as the best.
Mr. FRASER Why was the survey made in 1904?
M. GRAHAM. I cannot speak as to that. I am speaking of what was done last year. I may say that the chief engineer is going to visit the ground before the road is constructed, and will report upon it himself.

I know a good deal of this section of country, having spent a good many summers there, and I think the route chosen will be found to be the most direct. Personally I would like the road to go to Souris, but that would probably lengthen it. By bringing it to Harmony, and continuing it from there to Elmira, as is proposed, you get a direct and straight road; whereas if you turned to the south at Harmony to carry it to Souris, you would of course reach the harbour, but you would then run northward again and skip a certain portion of country in the centre. The northern shore, near the east point of Elmira, is a very fine part of the country. If you deflected the line to the south, you would neglect the northern and central portions of Kings county. The centre of Kings county is a very fine section, but it has not been very much developed. The woods are excellent and the soil exceedingly good. If it were made fairly accessible, it would be one of the most fertile sections of Prince Edward Island, which is saying a great deal. The line as proposed will be a very direct line to Elmira or East Point. The hon. member for Kings (Mr. Fraser) in criticising the surveys made last year on Prince Edward Island, spoke of some seven lines having been surveyed. I may say that that is a rather unfortunate number for Conservative members to refer to; because I remember that in 1896 the then leader of the Conservative government came to Prince Edward Island, and he used this mystical number of seven in promising branch railways to the people; but it happened that they did not place much confidence in his promises. Among the lines he promised

was this Elmira branch. Every time there was to be an election it was brought up. It was like the robins coming in spring; whenever you heard of the Elmira branch, you knew that an election was coming on. It became a proverb in Prince Edward Island. The same thing happened in Kings county with regard to the Murray Harbour branch, which used to be surveyed whenever an election was coming on; but as soon as the election was over the surveyors were called oft'. It became such a humbug that in 1896, the last time the Conservative government's surveyors came, the farmers pulled up their stakes and drove them off their places . I am glad to say that that road has been since built by the present government. Last year surveys were made where several short spurs were required. Our Conservative friends thought, or sai,d they thought, that every one of these tidal surveys meant a railway which the present government was offering to the people in order to get their votes. One of these surveys was made in my own county, and I hope to see a railway built there before long. It is needed. I have been inquiring, and find that the surveys were completed. The plans and reports are not yet in, hut I hope they soon will be. These surveys were made, the people were told at every public meeting, for the purpose of persuading them that they would all have a railway at their own doors. That was not the case. They were made for the purpose of ascertaining what would be the best route, and the best route would be selected, as will be done in the case of the Elmira branch. No doubt that is the reasou so many trial surveys are made, but my hon. friend seems to think they were done for the purpose of influencing the election. Several of the branches are much needed, and no branch will be built. The Elmira branch will no doubt be constructed. It was proposed by the Conservatives some thirty years ago, but the only hope the people have of getting it is from the present government.
Have the engineers who were on these surveys made their reports ?
Yes, but I have not got them here. I will give them to my hon. friend.

I want to read a quotation from a letter I received from a friend of mine a few days ago. In that letter he says:
The great engine in their hands was however railway surveys. Survey parties were at work over nearly the half of Queens county. The place were dotted over with white tents, where so-called engineers with crews of 12 to 14 men were driving stakes through farmers' fields. The railway was of course g-'i".-through their farms and liberal payments were to be made for the rights of way, and
there would be abundance of work and good pay for everybody. Those were called trial surveys, and went to French River, New London, Stanley Bridge, Wheatley river, North and South Rustico, Stanhope, Bedford, Suffolk Covehead, Bedford. Also Valleyfield, Hac-kendale, Murray Harbour Road, Bellevue, Iona, Grand View, Lyndale, Fairville, &c.
The minister has the reports on all these routes and will, no doubt, as he promised, lay them on the table.
The Minister of Railways in the last of the session placed $10,000 in the supplementary estimates, and it was used solely to defeat us. The accompanying map may give some idea of the work. The reports of these engineers should be asked for.
Did the minister put $10,000 in the supplementary estimates of last year, and was that spent paying these tenting parties, which came out just a week or two before the elections and drove stakes and made surveys. My correspondent sends me maps of the lines of survey, and there are red lines in all directions covering every farm on the island.
I will bring down the reports and a statement of the whole thing.
How much of last year's estimate of $30,000 was spent?
What was that $3,000 for?
It was paid for the survey.
Did that cover it? *
It covered the amount spent on this particular branch.
How much was spent on the island?
I will give a statement of that.
Has the hon. gentleman the expenditure in connection with the Prince Edward Island survey ?
No, I have not.
A great many of those surveys were done since the election.
No, they were called off the next week.

Some time ago I put a question on the Order Paper asking how much had been spent out of this $31,000 for construction and I received an answer that $3,077 had been spent for construction on the Elmira branch. I was very much pleased to hear the minister say that before this branch was finally located, an engineer would go down and locate it "where it will do the most good to the greatest number of people. When the engineers do so, no doubt the branch will be located where the survey was run in 1904.

and that is through the village of Souris East. Souris is the only shipping port in that part of the country for many miles, and all the freight would have to be carried there from East Point and Elmira. If the road is put where the last survey ran, or six miles farther than they would over where the 1904 line was located, because the branch running from Souris to Elmira will be very little if any longer than the branch running from Harmony to Elmira. But when they get to Harmony, they will have to go in five or six miles over the bid road and will have to pay passenger and freight rates on the six miles, which will be a considerable expense and not give accommodation to the people through Souris as if the branch were built through Souris as outlined in the survey of 1904. If the minister will say that before this branch is finally located, an engineer will be sent, that will give assurance to the people because the people want to have the line into Souris East.

The chief engineer will go down himself.
To increase accommodation at Charlottetown, $184,000.

This is for a wharf and freight shed, $53,000, extension of the east side of wharf $11,000, engine house $11,000, additional freight accommodation $10,000 There was expended last year $138,000.
There has been expended at Charlottetown [DOT]all told something like half a million dollars. Tenders were asked for the wharf [DOT]and Messrs. Reid and Archibald got the [DOT]contract. Mr. Clark got it for the freight [DOT]shed.

Has the minister received any complaints concerning the new station built at Charlottetown about a year ago? I have a letter, lately received, saying that the roof is leaking badly, that the plastering is falling down and the workmen are. engaged already making repairs, and also' that there are several large cracks in the stonework and in the concrete around the building. Has the hon. gentleman any information as to the defective work that seems to have been done there?

I think the defects cannot be very serious, for we have not heard anything of them in the department. I have had the misfortune to do some building myself, and I imagine that there is no building in the world, if looked at twelve months after construction by a person who wishes to find fault, but some defects will appear. I am informed hat this building in Charlottetown is a first-class building.
_ Mr. FRASER. I am only furnishing the information I have, and if it is true there Mr. FRASER.
must have been some very defective work there.
We will make inquiries.

I had the privilege of going through there two weeks ago. There were a couple of places where the roof leaked, but not seriously. I did not hear about any cracks, and if they had been there I think I should have heard about them. Some people are apt to make mountains out of molehills, and you cannot always rely on what you hear.
I must ask the minister to let the next two items stand- the Transcontinental and the Hudson Bay Railway.
Does the hon. member want the Hudson Bay item to stand also?
Yes; the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) cannot be present to-night, and he has some inquiries to make.

The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) asked me not to go on with the working expenses item to-night, and if these others are not to be taken up, I have no more estimates to go on with. I would not have agreed not to go on with the revenue item if I had known that exception would be taken to going on with any of these expenditures on capital.
There are only two items here.
I think it not unreasonable to ask that the Transcontinental item should stand, but I think the Hudson Bay item should go through.

The minister might give some information as to the Hudson Bay vote, and that might be sufficient to allow it to pass later on. We would like to hear as to the surveys, and also as to the future policy of the government in this matter.
U Mr. GRAHAM. Somd days ago, I laid on the table all the information with regard to the surveys up to a couple of weeks ago. The gist of that information is the raising of the question as to whether Fort Nelson is not a more favourable harbour than Churchill. As we wish to get the best possible harbour, I am asking for an appropriation to make a further survey of Nelson as well as Churchill. If I remember well, the engineer figures, that the route to Nelson will be sixty miles shorter than to Churchill. If that be the case, and if we can do as well or better by going tot Nelson, it would be foolish for us to build these sixty miles of road. The country toward Nelson, I believe, is equally as good as the other. That question having been raised by the engineers, my idea was that
2962

we ought to spend a little more money and learn just where is the best port. The road will stand in just the same position as before so far as construction is concerned. We have no idea of abandoning the project, and will proceed at the earliest possible moment that the conditions will warrant, but I am asking for $65,000, part of it a revote, to learn the best route and the best harbour,-but, of course, not to proceed with actual construction.
No survey of Churchill has been made?
Yes, they have made a survey of Churchill.
But not of Nelson?
No.
Do we understand that this money is simply for the examination of the harbours and nothing beyond that?
It is absolutely for survey work; it is to be spent to gain information. Of course, with this amount, we could not do anything in construction.
There will be an examination of the harbours, I suppose ?

Yes, we are asking our engineers to get all possible information as to the harbours also. The hon. member (Mr. Lake) threw out the suggestions as to the possibility of making ocean navigation as far as Winnipeg. That does not enter into our calculation in asking this amount; that is a question for the future. Our present object is to make sure of the port to which we should build the road.
It was understood by this House, I think, that the money to be expended on the construction of the Hudson Bay Railway was to come from a special fund to be created by the sale of pre-emptions.
Yes.

L understand that a certain amount of that fund has already been provided. Does the minister know how much that fund is at present, and can he estimate how much will be available twelve months from now, when, as I understand, he expects the actual work of construction to go on?

This is not in my department, but in the Department of the Interior, but I think little or none of that money can be available yet. If my memory serves me well, the purchasers of these lands have a certain time in which to make payments, and so there will not be any money in the treasury from the sale of these lands at present. An hon. friend near me informs me that there is a small amount on hand.. But, of course, it must go into the Consoli-
19, 1909
dated Fund and be voted out just as though it were not the proceeds of the sale of these lands. There is no intention of abandoning the work, but it is in the same position as other large works and at present we do not feel like proceeding with it. Construction will be proceeded with as soon as conditions prevail that will allow us to undertake it. We want in the meantime to ascertain the b'est available route with the best available port, as between Fort Nelson and Fort Churchill. Perhaps the Minister of the Interior could give the infromation as to the money obtained from the pre-emptions.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I had the figures here a few days ago but I have forgotten exactly what they are. The payments on pre-emp-tibns do not become due for three years so that no money has yet been received, but about two millions acres of land have been taken as pre-emptions. Whatever has been paid in on account of purchased homesteads, upon which the first payments are made with the entry, will be in the treasury and could be considered as available for construction purposes, but what the amount is I cannot at the moment say.

Will the government wait until they derive sufficient money from pre-emptions before commencing work or will they place the money from the preemptions in a special fund and pay for the construction of the railway from that fund, providing the money for construction immediately and recouping themselves from the fund afterwards?

I think that the question of the amount of money received from the pre-emptions would not control the beginning of the road and as proof of that, if conditions had not arisen which have impelled us to cease for a time from undertaking these large works the construction would have been started perhaps this season, but that condition having arisen and there being also the other question which the hon. gentleman has raised as to the comparative merits of the two ports, I think it would be advisable even if we had the money on hand and were otherwise ready to start, to wait until we made a full and complete survey of the other route.

I agree as to the advisability of waiting to ascertain which is the best port, but that will not occupy the whole of the next year and the money might now be taken for the commencement of construction. However, the government have decided not to take that money and the opposition have no power to move an amendment in that direction; we have to accept the position as it exists. Is it the policy of the government to construct the road as a government work or to place it in the hands of a private corporation?

The question of how the road shall be constructed is a large one. I think that last session it was left in this way, that the government proposed to construct or to have constructed a line from The Pas to a port on Hudson bay. The Premier during his tour stated that the government proposed to construct it as a government road. I do not pretend to be quoting him literally but I think that was the meaning of his utterance at Niagara.

I do not think it was as definite as that; I understood at that time he had not made up his mind. He may have made up his mind since, but at Niagara I think he said it was still an open subject as to whether it should be dealt with by the government or handed over , to a private corporation.
I would not care to go any further than the Premier's statement at Niagara, and I have given what I construed to be the meaning of that statement.

The minister stated that the government was prepared to construct a line to the Hudson bay from The Pas on the Saskatchewan river. What is the condition of the line now running to The fas? Are trains running over it and do the government propose to make it j)art of their system or will they construct abroad quite independently of the present line to I he Pas.

The government's idea was to construct from The Pas Mission to a poTt on Hudson bay and not to duplicate a line already constructed. The idea of the construction of the government road was to give railway connection from the nearest line to a Hudson bay port. I think I had some complaint a few weeks ago that trains had not been running regularly on this line. I communicated with the railway company and was informed that the trains were starting on a certain date and since that time I have not had any complaint.

The line as I understand was reported completed to a considerable distance last year and the land grant of 12,800 acres a mile was granted to the Canadian Northern Railway. Were trains running over the line so reported as completed during last summer? I Understand that trains can run over the line in winter when the ground is frozen. But I have had information given to me from a credible source that it is practically impossible to run trains over that line during the summer season when the frost is out of the ground. Could the minister give the committee some information in regard to that particular matter? It would be very interesting to me to hear what the condition is and whether the government is propos-
ing to take any steps to have that line put into a condition that trains can be run regularly over it during the present season?

If I had any information concerning it I would be delighted to give it to the committee. The only complaints concerning this line, as far as I can remember, except my hon. friend's observations last session in the committee, were the ones to which I have referred and no further communication having been made on the subject for a certain length of time-
How long?

I cannot just say. It was for some time, but I am not prepared to ,say because my memory does not serve me. But, on communication with the railway company they said that they were starting a train. I conveyed this communication to the gentleman who made the complaint. Since then I have not heard. They may be running a train or they may not be. But I should think that a question of that kind would be the subject matter of a complaint to the Board of Railway Commissioners.

The minister has stated that it is the intention of the government to run this line simply as far as The Pas from the Hudson bay. I hope he will reconsider that decision. It appears to me that if this line is to be run as a government undertaking, as I understand from the minister that is his general idea of the matter at the present time, it would be very inexpedient to run it simply as a feeder to the Canadian Northern Railway. I have always held the opinion that the Hudson Bay Railway should be a government undertaking and that it should be run so that it could make connection with the three great railways of that country, the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern Railway, so that the shippers on these lines of railway will be able to get the full benefit from its construction and operation. I hope the minister will come to see that that view of the case is the correct one, and that he will not start out with the idea that his railway is simply to stop at The Pas.
I would like to ask the minister if I am correct in understanding him to say that no work will be done on the construction of the work this year?
No.

I would like to ask the gov-erment whether the inspector has passed the whole of the road from Etiomami to The Pas? I think the latest information which was given to this House was that a considerable portion of the road had been accepted and passed by the government inspector. Has it all been passed and has the land grant been given upon the whole of the railway up to the present time?
My present information is that it has not been altogether, but I would not say that for sure. I can get that information and give it to my hon. friend to-morrow.
From what point is this new survey going to start?
It will start from The Pas Mission or from a point on the survey already made to Nelson. It will go along the Nelson river probably.
I understand the minister has agreed to give me this information the next time his estimates are up?
I will send it to my hon. friend.

I find in the Votes and Proceedings of last session, No. 39, that the following subsidy was given to the Canadian Pacific Railway:
To the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, for a line of railway from Winnipeg beach northerly to Gimli, not exceeding 9J miles; and a line from Gimli to Riverton, not exceeding 25 miles; not exceeding in all 3i% miles.
Under what conditions was that subsidy granted and how long have the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to build that line? This is a very important line to the settlers in that district, and I would like to know if this is just to remain a subsidy or whether the road is to be actually built. The people have been promised this road for years. Before the elections this subsidy was used in that part of the constituency as an inducement to the electorate to vote for the government candidate. I want to know if the government are going to ask the Canadian Pacific Railway to build that line?

Of course, this is in the statute now and so long as they comply with the statute the government have no power. They are given the regular time in their charter to begin and to complete the railway. The House need not renew that charter and when their charter lapses their subsidy also lapses. The Subsidy Act itself fixes the time for starting and completing the work. If they do not comply with the statute and if they ask for a renewal of the subsidy, parliament, in its wisdom, may not renew it.
How long will it be before they will have to ask for a renewal?
I would not like to speak from memory. If my hon. friend will look up last year's statute he will find it stated there.

There is another matter I want to draw the minister's attention to and that is the condition of the Komarno branch through to Icelandic river.
They have built that road to a point on Russell lake. The work was stopped last September and the contractors were taken off, but just on the eve of the election, my opponent, Mr. Jackson, went out and engaged 150 Galicians and put them to work on the dump. As soon as the elections were over these men were taken off. I would ask it the Canadian Pacific Railway will be required to complete that road at once. It is a great hardship to the people of Icelandic river that the road should not be completed. I do not know whether the government or the Canadian Pacific Railway were responsible, but somebody was responsible for putting these men on.

These roads are all being constructed under the same condition. I am surprised, to put it mildly, that the Canadian Pacific Railway would do anything to assist the present government'. I did not suspect them, but if my hon. friend assures me that it is so I would take his word absolutely, even although I were not obliged to, because I believe it would be correct if he said so, but it inspires a new feeling within me to think the Canadian Pacific Railway did that.
I want to assure the minister that it is an absolute fact that 150 men were put on the road and that immediately after the election the men were taken off the work.
They were paid out of the election fund.

I do not know how they were paid. They got their money I presume.
Public Works, Ont.-Blanche river-improvements on main stream and south branch, $6,500.

This is to remove snags and cut channels through shoals obstructing navigation at low water on the Blanche river which empties into Lake Temiskam-ing. There is quite a settlement on that river. The work was commenced in 1904-05.
Is there navigation?

Yes, for small vessels; there are four boats now on the river.
Burlington channel piers-reconstruction, $50,000.
This is contract work. It is for reconstructing the piers destroyed by storm.
When were they destroyed?
In the spring of last year.
Will the piers be of concrete?
Yes. This forms the entrance to Hamilton harbour. We are building piers both on the lake side and on the bay side.
Will this vote complete the work?
No; the total probable cost will be $110,000.
Why is the work not included in one contract?
The head blocks are by contract, but much of the other work is repair work and the engineers say that it can be more economically done by day's labour.
Who is the contractor?
Joseph Battle.

The work on this channel has been going on continuously year after year for a long time. It is the duty of the government to keep that channel open and it is absolutely necessary to do this work because this forms the outlet from Lake Ontario to the city of Hamilton. I remember that at one time I suggested that instead of spending $50,000 a year the government had much better ask a sufficient amount to complete the whole job at once.
Since confederation $200,000 have been spent there and before confederation, $400,000.
It would be much better to complete the work at once and give the people of Hamilton the benefit of it rather than to make this vote a kind of hardy annual.
Repairs have been necessary from year to year, but last spring there was a large amount of damage done.
When will the work be finished?
In about two years.
What is the length of these piers?

The wooden superstructure to be replaced by concrete on the south pier is 1,500 feet by 20 feet and there is a further reconstruction in concrete 420 feet by 30 feet. I presume the north pier is about the same length.
Cobourg-Extension of breakwater, dredging, &c., $60,000.
This is contract work and the total probable cost to complete the improvements will be $154,000 outside of the dredging.
Who has the contract?
The Randolph Macdonald Co., Limited, has the contract for the breakwater; W. E. Phin has the dredging.

What do you pay for the
dredging?

For rock $3 a yard; all other materials, such as sand and clay, 18 bents a yard, scow measurement.
Goderich harbour, repairs to piers, &c., $5,350.
This is for renewals of the walings on the piers, and general repairs, estimated at $1,000; and for 290 feet lineal of protection work on the inner harbour. This work is done by day's work.
Why not put it under contract?

These repairs can hardly be put up to tender.
Harbours, rivers and bridges, general repairs and improvements, $25,000.

I think the minister said that the piers of Burlington channel were destroyed or badly damaged a year br so ago by a heavy storm. I may say that at that part of the lake there appears to be a good deal of washing away of the banks. The village of Burlington is within 'about half a mile of the Burlington channel, and there is a continual washing away bf the shore in front of the village, and also two or three miles eastward; and the people there have an impression that it is the duty of this government to construct a breakwater to prevent this continual washing away, otherwise the village may rbe gradually wiped out. It is already encroaching very closely on the leading street of the village. The village has a population of only 1,700 or 1,800, and could not afford the expense of constructing a breakwater, and the people are looking to this government to do something of the kind.
Why to this government ?

I will tell the hon. gentleman why, and I have a very good reason. The gentleman who opposed me in the last election promised the people that if he were elected he would secure a breakwater. I assume that he did not make that promise off his own bat, but that he must have had some instruction from the Minister of Public Works that a breakwater would be constructed there, and he held that out as a reason why the people should vote for him instead of for me.
What did the hon. gentleman promise?
I promised nothing. I simply promised that I would call the minister's attention to it.
I suppose that is all the promise he made.

No, he promised a great deal more than that. I have been informed that he promised the breakwater. The Minister of Agriculture went into that county to speak on behalf of this gentleman, which gave him a standing, and the people had the right to expect that any pledge given by him would be carried out by the government for which he was seeking their support. If the promise was made in good faith by the government or through the government candidate, I think the minister ought to do something about it. I think it is a proper thing to do, and I believe the government is spending money in a great many instances where possibly it would not be doing as good service. I may say that while there is a considerable amount of shipping from that port, it has never to my knowledge had a dollar of government money expended there, either in dredging or in building a dock. Any docks there are private docks, and the government could well afford a do something of this kind for the people. I think it is the duty of the government to protect the village, and not allow a portion of it to be practically washed away. Since the promise was made by the government candidate, I hope the hon. minister will send an engineer to look into the matter and see if something can be done. The matter will have to be dealt with some dav, either by the municipality or by the government. I do not see that the provincial government can be called on to do it.
Why not? Is it not purely local in its character?
There are a great many local things done by the government. The building of the Burlington piers is local.
That is for the advantage of navigation.
And the other is for the protection of the village.
Is not that the distinction?
I do not know that the distinction is sufficient. The inland waters are, I think, under the care of this government.
Only navigation.

And it is the inland waters that are practically washing away the people's farms and highways. It seems to me that this is the government that will have to do that work by and by, and the sooner it is undertaken the better. If this washing away is allowed to go on for a few years longer, a great deal of harm
will be done, and it will certainly cost more to_ prevent it five years after this than it will now. I would suggest to the minister that while his engineers are engaged in examining the Burlington canal, which is within two and a-half or three miles away from the places I speak of, it would be well to send one to look into this matter.

Do I understand my hon. friend to say that he knows personally that the Liberal candidate promised that a breakwater would be built and that he had the authority of the government for making that statement.

I did not hear him make that statement, but I have it on authority perfectly reliable, and I have no doubt he promised those people that he would apply to the government for the construction of a breakwater there to prevent the shore from washing away.
That is a different statement? He said he would apply to the government.

But he did not get
elected.
That is not his fault.

The people, I presume, did not put much confidence in him and had the good sense to believe that the Minister of Public Works would not be so corrupt as to build a breakwater only on condition that a supporter of the government would be elected. If it is a proper and -wise thing to build that breakwater, I have no doubt the minister would do it just as well as if the other gentlemen were elected. I was not present at any of the meetings and did not hear the gentleman make that statement, but that was the current report, and I have not the slightest doubt as to its accuracy. But apart from that, the claim is a propeT one. That important village and shore has never received any government consideration whatever. It is a place of considerable importance. There is a large amount of grain and apples shipped from there, and they have never received a dollar foT the construction of a pier or the dredging of their harbour. I am happy to say that they have a sufficient depth of water without dredging, but as for the docks, they are private and belong to the men who do the shipping business. If the minister will promise to send an engineer to look into the matter and see what can be done, he will be taking a step in the right direction.

The reason I asked my hon. friend if he ever heard the statement made by the Liberal candidate that this breakwater would be built, was because I have heard a good many rumours as tc

alleged statements made by Liberal candidates and have found, on inquiry, that they were absolutely without foundation.
No doubt the hon. minister will find that this one is correct.
If my hon. friend had heard the statement he would be sure.
I did not hear it myself, but have it on the best authority.

What I would rather assume is that probably the Liberal candidate, being impressed by the necessity for this work, promised that if he were elected, he would urge it on the favourable consideration of the government, and I would rather infer, from the last version which my hon. friend gave, that that was all the candidate said. This matter had not been very strongly brought to my attention, and I certainly gave no assurance that a breakwater would be built there and did not authorize any one to give that assurance. But as the matter is brought to my attention, I shall have it looked into.
That is all I can expect the hon. minister to say at present.

With regard to many improvements of this character a question of great importance is arising and will no doubt be pressed home upon us very strongly in the future, and that is how far the federal government should go in the carrying on of protection works which are not for the purposes of navigation, but to protect towns and villages situated as Burlington is. I have during the past year been asked to join in the cost of building protection works on the Fraser river; and as towns and villages grow up on that very extensive river, there will be very large demands of a similar nature from them in the future. If I would undertake these works on behalf of this government, the federal exchequer would have very heavy burdens imposed on it. In the past we have done works of this character. On the Fraser river we have borne one half the cost, sharing the cost jointly with the provincial government. We have been asked to do that on the Saskatchewan river near Edmonton and at other localities where there is equal danger. Only the other day my hon. friend from Chicoutimi and Saguenay (Mr. Girard) wrote a very strong letter inclosing petitions setting foTth, the very serious condition of affairs at a place some distance below the Saguenay where there is a large village located on the banks of the St. Lawrence, and where the banks are very high and there is considerable danger of their sliding into the St. Lawrence, causing great destruction of property and loss of life. I did not feel that this was a federal work for which I could pledge the government to ask parlia-Mr. PUGSLEY.
ment for an appropriation. The work has nothing to do with navigation, it is purely local in its character, and hon. gentlemen will see how difficult it is to draw the line. It requires great consideration, because if we undertake in a general way works of this character, it is difficult to estimate where we shall be able to stop.

The village of Burlington, on the shores of Lake Ontario, has been a very prosperous place for a great many years and a large shipping point, yet not a dollar of public money has ever been spent on the wharfs. Look at the millions we are voting to other provinces for similar works. But you may begin at Burlington and go down all the way as far as the province of Ontario extends and all along the shores of the St. Lawrence and Lake Ontario, and you will find that all the wharfs there have been erected by private individuals. In other provinces however the government not only builds the wharfs but will come down with an estimate for a wharf and turn it into a bridge.
