Here at Burlington, on the shores of Lake Ontario, the people built their own wharf, and not only the wharf, but the town is likelv to be undermined from the lake, yet the government will pay no attention to it although their candidate promised that they would give relief if he were elected. I have drawn attention on several occasions to the township of Wolfe Island. The people on that island have no means of getting off except by boat, and they have to put their hands into their own pockets and build their own wharfs. Wolfe Island is at the foot of Lake Ontario. The only way to get there is by steamer. Steamers ply on both sides and the government have never contributed a dollar. If it were a little creek in some of the other provinces, the government would build the wharfs themselves, and construct docks _ where there is no navigation. Application has been made on behalf of Burlington, and that application should be recognized by the government without delay. Last night we discussed a work carried on by this government-building a concrete pier for the municipality to set a bridge upon-
That was four years ago

We had it before the committee last night. It was shown that it was built inshore from the current where it would not prevent the silt from coming down as was said to be the purpose. Why should not: the provincial government or the municipality be called upon to do that work? It would seem that the municipalities in constituencies that return sup porters of the government are treated differently from those that return members of the opposition. I think it is time that the government should come to some definite

understanding as to the kind of works it is their duty to erect and as to those which should be left to the province or municipality.
Little Current-improvement of Northern channel in Georgian bay, $28,000.
This is to complete the dredging work of the year. It is very important work.
At what portion of the channel ?

Right at the town of Little Current. We are widening the channel and straightening it. There is a very swift current there, and this work will make what is known as 'the inside route' for steamers. That is, it will pass inside Manitoulin Island.
Is this vote of $28 -000 for work that has been done or for work that is to be done ?
Work to be done during the coming season.
I notice that in the supplementary estimates there is a vote of $82,000 for the same work.
That is to close up for work done during the current year.
Does the minister intend to deepen the channel beside Picnic Island out of this $28,000?
No, there would not be enough for that purpose.
How much of the channel is to be completed? I think there is about 1,200 feet already dredged.
There was about 1,800 feet in which work had to be done, and this is to complete the work.
I suppose that, under this item, the minister could give no information as to the work done on Honora wharf?	j] ;;
No appropriation is being asked for that wharf, and therefore I have no information before me with regard to it. If he desires it, I will get the information.
The minister is aware that a wharf was built there just before the elections. I shall have something to say about it later on.
I do not know when it was done. The House did not rise until about the first of August.
To what depth has this northern channel been dredged?
Twenty-two feet.
And what is the present depth of the part that is being dredged?
Twenty-two feet.
And what is the present depth of the part that is being redredged?
When we began the work, the depth was about 14 feet. It will be noted that this is rock drilling and blasting.
And there is no appropriation for widening the channel towards Picnic Island?
No. To widen it would be very expensive. It is a needed work, but it cannot be done at present.

I presented a petition to the minister from the vesselmen showing the necessity of widening the channel at this point. Does he purpose doing anything about it?
Mr. PUGSLEY'. We have a report on it, and I recognize the necessity for it. But it is one of those works not imperatively necessary at the moment, and I regret to say that we shall be obliged to let it stand over for a short time.
Last session, $125,000 was voted. Did the minister expend that and $82,000 besides on that work ?
Some money was due from the previous year. I could get the full details if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Geo. Taylor) would like them.
Where did the money come from for the work which has been referred to as having been built just before the elections?
That has nothing to do with this appropriation.
Was there an appropriation for it?
I think there was. But we have a general vote of money for repairs.
How much was spent out of the general vote, or out of any vote on this work?
I have no memorandum of it here.
Will the hon. gentleman get it?

I shall be glad to do so.
McGregor's creek-renewal of bank protee-tion work at Chatham, $7,100.
This is protection work on a bank.

This is to complete the renewal of sheet piling protection on the south bank of McGregor's creek, reported by the engineer in charge to be needed to prevent the bank sliding into the creek. Since this estimate was made, a further break has occurred endangering the houses, in fact, some of the houses have actually fallen in. I think a distinction can be made between this work and the work at Burlington, because, in the opinion of the engineer, this has followed dredging operations carried on by the federal government, and therefore we have thought it our duty to build protection works. When I speak of dredging by the federal government, I do not mean the present government, because this was done before the present administration came into power.
Is this work to be done in the city of Chatham?

Yes.
Montreal river-improvements above Latch-ford, $25,000.
Is this in connection with the dam to be built there?

This is to construct a dam just above Latchford for the purpose, as the expression is, of drowning out the Pork rapids, and so affording navigation for the conveyance of the large number of people who are going up that river to engage, in mining operations and to settle on the land.
Have negotiations gone on between this government and the Temiskaming^ and Northern Ontario Commission relating to the land about to be drowned?

Negotiations have gone on for a very considerable time, and it is largely in consequence of these not having been brought to a successful issue that the work of building this dam has not already been undertaken. I desire to say, and I say it with regret, that the commissioners of the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway have not shown the disposition which I should have expected them to show to facilitate this work. We have endeavoured to get them either to make a reasonable settlement as to land damages or to waive any claim for damages because the building of this work will be of great benefit to the interests of the province of Ontario, but so far we have not been successful in coming to an arrangement.
Are any further improvements contemplated in the Montreal river?
There is another rapid at which we have been urged to build a lock but we have not decided upon that.
Has the matter been brought to the attention of the Minister of Lands, Forests and Mines of Ontario?
Yes.
I understood him to say he was disposed to make any arrangement to get that improvement.

We went to the trouble and expense of appointing Mr. Davis of Latchford to get the land damages settled. He reported that he had interviews with the Commissioners and also with the Ontario minister to whom my hon. friend refers, but he was not successful in coming to an arrangement. I hope that now the, matter has been brought more forcibly to the attention of the Ontario government we will be able to come to a satisfactory arrangement soon. The work is important and I regret that we have not felt it was desirable or safe to enter into the contract because of the possibility of having these claims outstanding. The moment I can see daylight, so far as land damages are concerned, I am prepared to go ahead with the work and let the contract, but I do not want to enter on the work with an uncertainty as to the amount of claims to be brought against the government for flooding the lands.
Is it not within the power of the government to expropriate the right to flood these lands ?

Possibly it is, but I do not think that when the federal government is prepared to engage upon a large expenditure for the purpose of improving the navigation of a river like the Montreal river, which would give accommodation to people going in there to settle upon the lands of the Ontario government, to develop their mining properties, that the Ontario government which owns the townsite upon the shores of Temiskaming lake should make any claim against us for damages that might occur through the flooding of unoccupied lands and particularly of town lots unsold, and not built upon. I do think they should join with us to that extent in having these improvements made and give freely and without compensation the lands which would be affected by the building of the dam.

Of course I appreciate that the hon. gentleman thinks that the chairman and other members of the Commission and the Minister of Forests, Lands and Mines are not acting in a reasonable way, but it is not impossible that these gentlemen have the same view in regard to himself. I know the chair-* man of the Commission and some of the members and also have the privilege of 'knowing the Minister of Mines, and I be-

lieve him to be not only a very capable but a very reasonable gentleman who would be sincerely desirous of doing everything possible to facilitate the improvement _ of navigation for the benefit of people using that river. Perhaps the minister would bring down any correspondence he may have in reference to the matter, which is of some importance, as the river in the summer should be a very excellent highway, affording access to a country lacking in other communication.
I shall be glad to bring down the correspondence.

Did the minister give directions to his department at Toronto to look after this matter ? It would seem to be of sufficient importance not to leave it to an irresponsible gentleman in that northern country.

I do not accept the suggestion that the matter was left to an irresponsible gentleman. We appointed a gentleman of high standing in Latchford to endeavour to make a settlement with the owners of land which we thought would be flooded by building the dam. Among the owners were the Commissioners of the Ontario and Temiskaming Railway, representing the Ontario government. We instructed Mr. Davis to confer with the Commissioners and also with the Ontario government and he reported that he had several interviews with the Minister of Lands and Mines of Ontario as well as with the Commissioners, and that he was not able to make a satisfactory arrangement.
What is his profession?
A lawyer.

He knows nothing, of course, about the value of lands.
Port Stanley-groynes on east side of harbour entrance, $7,100.

This is protection work for the protection of new Orchard Beach 'from further erosion. The groynes are to be built on the east side of Port Stanley entrance. The claim is made upon us- and this also differentiates this from the case to which some hon. gentleman referred to-night-that by reason of the breakwater built there the waters of the bay weTe given a certain direction and caused erosion of the soil. The department recognized the strength of that claim, and the work of building these groynes for the protection of the land was entered upon.
I think the minister is justified in spending that money just as he says. I know the location and it is necessary work. Will the work be done by day's labour or by contract?
It is to be done by contract and the contract has been let to John H. Smaill, of Port Burwell. The contract price was $6,535.
Who is the overseer? The gentleman in charge now is named Smith.
I do not think an overseer has been appointed; Mr. Smith may have been appointed recently but I have no memorandum of it.

This expenditure is very necessary. Port Stanley is an important harbour where there is a large revenue from the coal traffic. The amount is not too large. I find nothing for Port Bruce. Is it the intention of the minister to spend any money in improving that harbour this summer?
It has not been decided to spend anything at Port Bruce during the coming season. ,

I hope the minister will spend some money there. It is an old harbour gone down. It is now used as a fishing port. There are men engaged in fishing there who have their homes, boats and nets and everything invested in their plant, and unless the harbour is kept open it will be useless. Unless the harbour is improved it will be useless. I hope the minister will set aside something, not a very large amount, to keep the harbour in such a condition that fishermen can go in and out.

I will make a note of it and have it looked into.
Richard's Landing-St. Joseph's island-repairs to pier, $1,700.
What is the explanation of this? Is not that the wharf that was built up there where the summer hotel was erected?
No, this is away up in the district of West Algoma not far from Sudbury.

Will this complete it?
Mr. PUGSLEY This will complete the repairs.
Were any of those repairs done last season?

We will require $1,700 for repairs during the coming season. We have spent, up to the 30th November, $1,398.46. Repairs have been going on during the winter, so that we will have spent about $1,600 by the 31st of this month.
In addition to the $3,000 voted last year?

Yea, the total estimated cost is $4,700; $3,000 was voted last year and we are asking for $1,700 this year.
River St. Lawrence-improvement of Canadian channel between Kingston and Brock-ville, $75,000.

This is to improve, by blasting and dredging out what will probably be all rock, the Canadian channel between Kingston and Brockville, so that vessels navigating the St. Lawrence can go through the Canadian channel instead of being obliged to use the American channel. The work is being done under contract. The total estimated cost is $125,000.
Who has the contract?

Frank Gilbert, of Montreal. Tenders were called and in response to a public advertisement these tenders were received ranging from $3.95 per cubic yard of rock to $4.98. The contract was awarded to Frank Gilbert, his being the lowest tender, at $3,95 per cubic yard of rock.
I understand that most of this is removing an island at Fiddler's Elbow?
There is quite a large number of points at which material has to be removed.
That work will be proceeded with this summer?

Yes, it is being proceeded with this winter.
Rondeau harbour-improvements, $25,000.
What is being done at Rondeau?
There are breakwaters to be built.
I was there a short time ago and I thought the piers were very good.
This is to extend the breakwaters to afford protection to the harbour. There is a contract let for the construction of breakwaters and dredging.
This is to further improve the harbour?
This is to extend the breakwaters to a thousand feet.

This is to extend the piers outward? The piers were very good as far as they went. This has become a very important harbour, there is a very large coal business being done and large steamers come there. I think this is a de-sirable,work. Port Stanley and Rondeau are two of the most important harbours on the lake. Besides doing a large coal busi-Mr. G. TAYLOR.
ness I do not know but that they are good harbours of refuge in case of a storm.
Sault Ste. Marie wharf - dredging an-proaches, $55,000.
This is to complete the work.
That is under contract?

Yes.
Southampton-extension of and repairs to town dock, $6,000.

This is under contract also.
Toronto harbour-improvements, $375,000.
This is the western channel with which the committee is familiar.
This is under contract?
Yes.

Before leaving the Ontario items, I want to draw the minister's attention to the fact that last year a vote was put through for a wharf at Graven-hurst. I also want to draw the minister's attention to the fact that it was not built and that nothing has been done there. It was kept before the electors all summer and when the election time came it was a very important issue whether the people would get their wharf or not. A communication was sent to the minister right in the midst of the election and a telegram was apparently received from him which was published and put in the hands of every elector in the town, stating that it was owing to the persuasive qualities of the Reform candidate that the minister had come to the conclusion that a wharf was necessary.
Was that a telegram from me?

From you. I would draw the attention of the minister to the fact that from time to time representations have been made from the town council of Gravenhurst, and strong deputations have waited upon the government urging this public work. I suppose the government came to the conclusion that they would put a little vote in the estimates for that wharf and apparently the Reform candidate was sent for and came down here so that he might get credit for this appropriation. As I have said, the telegram of the minister was used to that effect in the riding of Muskoka and in the town of Gravenhurst, and the people were led to believe they would get the wharf at once. This was used with very telling effect against myself in the campaign and it lost me a considerable number of votes, and had it been that the minister had twenty-five or thirty wharfs to build in the riding, I

might have lost my election. However, I simply want to express the hope that the persuasive eloquence of my opponent which had such an effect on the minister will not have ceased to exercise its power, and that he will not forget that the town of Gravenhurst needs a wharf very badly. If there are supplementary estimates brought down I hope the minister will include in them an appropriation for this work and that at the very earliest possible moment he will have a decent wharf constructed in the town of Gravenhurst. I have drawn the attention of the minister and of his predecessor to the fact that there is a great deal of shipping in these northern waters and that this accommodation is badly needed. I can tell him that if the wharf is built the people will appreciate it very much.
Did the hon. gentleman issue a circular during the campaign in regard to his own action in reference to that wharf?
I issued no circular with regard to the matter.

My informatfon was that during the campaign the hon. gentleman either had issued a circular or made a statement that he had succeeded in getting the item in the estimates for the Gravenhurst wharf and repudiating the fact that our friends had anything to do with it. I was asked whether that statement was true and I did either write or telegraph giving credit to the gentleman who had come to Ottawa upon at least one occasion and urged very strongly the necessity for a wharf at Gravenhurst. I placed the credit where it was due so far as obtaining the apnropriation for the wharf was concerned, and to correct any misapprehension which I had been informed my hon. friend was endeavouring to spread among the electors. With regard to the wharf itself, I was impressed with the necessity for it. There is a good deal of shipping at Gravenhurst and the amount was put in the estimates in good faith last session, but unfortunately owing to the condition of the revenues this wharf must stand over for a short time as many other necessary public works.
Will the minister give us a copy of the telegram?
I have not a copy; I think it was a personal telegram sent from St. John.
Would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Arthurs) say whether in his opinion both these works are necessary public works and works which should be carried on in the public interest?
I think the minister will agree with me that the woTk at Parry Sound is most necessary and that the wharf accommodation there is very small considering the importance of the port.
What about Maganatawan?
That is exactly in the same position. There are 20 or 25 steamers plying there and there is not room at the wharf purchased by the government for more than one steamer at a time.

I am very glad that my hon. friend conforms to the opinion I entertained last session that these works were necessary, and I regret that I have been obliged not to include in the estimates an appropriation for them for the coming year; they have to stand over the same as many other public works throughout Canada.

Am I right in assuming that the minister has stated in the House that those works which had been commenced would be carried on to completion and that the works which had been left aside were those which had not been commenced or for which tenders had not been called?

I stated to the committee that in drawing the line in reference to works which were to stand over we had provided that where contracts had been let

or where the work had been undertaken by day's labour they should be carried to completion. If any work has been done on the Maganatawan wharf which would be of no value to the public unless there were further work done, or if the work were likely to be damaged if it were not completed then I think it ought to be completed. But if a further extension is only needed to get increased accommodation I think it might stand over without detriment to the public interest the same as many other works in different parts of the country.
The timber is bought and lying there rotting.
So far as the wharf at Parry Sound is concerned I think that is being done by day's work, and if the timber is there-
Rotting.
It cannot be rotting because it is only there a short time and we will see it does not rot. I will make inquiries of the engineering department and see what can be done.

I draw the attention of the Minister of Public Works to Meaford harbour situated on the Georgian bay. I understand that recently a petition has been sent to the Minister of Public Works with reference to that harbour. I quite rerecognize his policy of cutting down the estimates for Public Works, but at the same time I think that in the case of Meaford there should be an exception made. As I understand, the government adopted some plan or scheme for the improvement of the harbour, and in accordance with it have already spent $70,000 or $80,000, for which the town is grateful. But a storm of last fall proved beyond doubt that that plan will have to be radically changed, because it is not such as to prevent the devastation of the harbour. A number of boats lying in the harbour were tossed abortt arid some of their upper parts destroyed 'and some had to be removed to Owen Sound.' I would therefore ask the minister if he can put something in the estimates of the present year to preserve the harbour. This is one of those cases in which, if nothing is done, what has already been done by the government may be permanently destroyed. I understand that a deputation from Meaford is about to come to Ottawa to interview the government and to present a memorial on this subject. The harbour of Meaford is not a small harbour. It has many manufactures, a large elevator and a great deal of the grain from the west passes through that harbour on its way to the sea-board; so that it is more or less a national port. I would ask the minister in all earnestness to see if something cannot be done during the present year, either

by a vote in the supplementary estimates or otherwise, for the purpose of preventing the destruction of that harbour and whether he cannot have an inquiry made as to whether some change should not be made in the plan or scheme adopted.
I may say to my hon. friend that I have received the memorial to which he refers and I intend to look into the matter very carefully. But as to making provision during the present session-
You have a general vote.

But out of that we can only provide for small works; we cannot build wharfs or breakwaters. As to putting an amount in the supplementary estimates, I regret that I am not able to give my hon. friend any assurance at the present moment that there will be any supplementary estimates and there is nothing in the present estimates that would warrant me in proceeding with the work in the present year. If there should be supplementary estimates, I will give the matter consideration.
Would the minister send a competent engineer there for the purpose of making an examination?
I have already referred the memorial to the chief engineer of my department.	' -
Would the Minister of Public Works tell us why the objects for which moneys were voted in the supplemen-tarv estimates of last session are not being carried out by revotes this session?

Because our revenues will not warrant us in doing so. During the past year there has been a falling 1 off of about $12,000,000 in the revenues, and, as I have already explained several times in the committee, we had to cut down the estimates in my department by some $7,000,000 or $8,000,000. It became necessary therefore to postpone the construction of a large number of very necessary public works which were provided for in the estimates of last year.

Is it not a fact that the country is better off financially at the present time than it was when the supplementary estimates were brought down in July last? Is not the fiancial condition of the country as good now as it was when he sent that telegram to the province of Ontario to which the hon. member for Muskoka has referred?
That telegram was only to correct what I thought was a wrong impression that was sought to be conveyed.
But there was an amount in the estimates?
Of course there was, and I was only speaking of that, not making any promises for the future.
Is not the financial condition of the country now better than it was when that amount was put in the estimates?
I am satisfied that the outlook now is exceedingly good.
Is not that a reason why the hon. minister should live up to his preelection promises in respect to public works?
What pre-election promises?

They were contained in the estimates.
Manitoba-harbours and rivers and bridges -general repairs and improvements, $6,000.
This is a general vote to do work which is not specially provided for.
At what places are you going to have it expended?

I have no special places in mind at present. Last year the expen diture up to the 31st of December was $3,667, leaving a balance of a little over $2,000 unexpended. There are always repairs and small works to be done in different sections of the country.

Some little time ago I interrogated the minister regarding the bridge at Lac du Bonnet. The bridge is too low. I understood that the matter was referred to the resident engineer. It is a very serious matter. I have had several letters in the last few days asking if the government has taken any action.
Who constructed this bridge?
The city of Winnipeg.
That would not be a matter for my department specially to interfere in.
The bridge is across a navigable stream, and I think the government owns it. I do not think the government would allow it to be constructed without its approval.
The plans would have to be approved.

I am informed that at high water there is less than four feet between the water and the girders of the bridge, and as the current is very rapid, it is a menace to life and property. Something ought to be done, and done at once.

My hon. friend can easily understand that if a bridge was not built according to the plans, it would be quite open to any one to file information and compel the city of Winnipeg to remove the bridge. I do not think it would be the duty of my department to do that; it would rather rest with the Attorney General of the province. He is the man in whose name any information for that purpose would have to be laid. However, I have given instruction to have a report made, and shall be glad to lay it before the House as soon as it is revised.
If the plans were approved by the Department of Public Works, in what position would the government be?
I would not like to say what would be done in that case. That would show that somebody had blundered in case the plans were defective.
If the city of Winnipeg had not carried out the plan submitted to the government the city was responsible.
Yes.
On the other hand, if it had built according to the plan submitted to your engineer, surely the government is responsible.
It would be the fault of our department, but as to whether there would be any legal responsibility, I am not at the moment prepared to say. It might be an error of judgment. I have sent for a report.

This is a serious matter and I hope the minister will take it up seriously. ' There is another matter to which I wish to call his attention. There was placed in the estimates of last year, just previous to the general elections, an amount of $7,500, for the purpose of commencing what was termed a protecting nier at Winnipeg beach. This amount is conspicuous by its absence in the estimates of this session, does that mean the work has been abandoned?
The fact of its not appearing in the votes ought to be convincing proof to my hon. friend that it will not be possible for me to go on with the work during the present season.

I want to recall to the hon. gentleman that on the 1st of_ February I asked him the following question across the floor, as will be seen in 'Hansard,' page 352:
What has the government done regarding protection pier at Winnipeg Beach? Is it the intention of the government to proce<d with the construction of this pier at once? If not, when?

The minister replied as follows:
Plans and specifications have been prepared contingent upon certain work being performed by the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Boundary Park Realty Company. It has not yet been decided to go on with the work, but a decision will be come to before very long after we hear what the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Boundary Park Realty Company are prepared to do.
This reply conveyed the impression that the Boundary Park Realty Company and the Canadian Pacific Railway had not carried out their part of the understanding which must have existed between the government and these companies. The reply which the minister gave me at that time was published in one of the Winnipeg papers, and in that way came under the notice of the Boundary Park Realty Company, and the secretary of that company wrote me a letter which I think I should read to the committee for the information of the Minister of Public Works:
Winnipeg, Peb. 3, 1909. G. H. Bradbury, Esq.,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir,-In a despatch from Ottawa it is stated that the building of the protection pier at Winnipeg Beach was being held up by the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Boundary Park Realty Company.
Speaking for the Boundary Park Realty Company, I may say that we completed our part some months ago by giving a clear title, free of cost, to the Canadian Pacific Railway to about seven (7) acres of land fronting on the proposed harbour.
They in turn gave us a written agreement to the effect that they would do the necessary work inside within a certain time after the Dominion government built the pier. We have done our part and the Canadian Pacific Railway cannot do anything until the outside work is completed by the government. I understand that the railway are willing and anxious to go on with the work at the earliest date possible.
Any further information you might want from us would be gladly given. We are very anxious, as are all the other Winnipeg Beach residents to see the matter go through without delay as we have waited 'for over a year for a safe anchorage for our boats. Thanking you in advance for the trouble you are taking in this matter,
I remain, yours truly,
I submit that the inference which the minister wished me to draw from his reply was that these companies had not carried out their part of the understanding.
My answer does not say that. It says that we were waiting to hear from them and then will decide what we will do.
I think the fair inference is that these companies had not done what they agreed to do.
I did not say that.
I think that is the fair inference. When the despatch was published in the Winnipeg papers, that was the inference which the Realty Company drew from the reply.

The telegram apparently was a misstatement. The telegram said it was alleged that the work was hung up by these companies. I used no such expression in the House. Therefore the company must have been misinformed by the telegram.

The minister said that the plans and specifications had been prepared contingent on certain work being performed by the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Boundary Park Realty Company. The government therefore were to go on with the work if these companies did what they had agreed to do. Well, the realty company, on the strength of the appropriation voted last year, did dispossess itself of seven acres of valuable land fronting on this proposed pier, and the Canadian Pacific Railway gave them an undertaking that as soon as the government carried out its part of the work, the Canadian Pacific Railway would proceed and do their part.

Do you not think my department ought to have some word from the Canadian Pacific Railway ? Do you think we are bound by a private arrangement between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Realty Company of which we were not informed?

I cannot help but feel that the reply of the minister was hardly ingenuous. I think the inference he wished to convey was that these companies had not implemented their pledges; and in view of what has taken place in this committee from time to time, it is evident that when the money was voted last year, previous to the election, there was no real intention on the part of the government to proceed with the work. The minister said to-night that the reason why the government did not proceed with some public works was because of the falling off in revenue. That would be a good reason, were it not for the fact that in the lower provinces the government are providing in the estimates for the expenditure of hundreds of thousands of dollars for works not really as necessary as this one at Winnipeg Beach. At that place it is really necessary, in the interests of life and property, that a harbour should be built. The building of that pier, if I understand the purpose of the government, is required for a harbour. There is no harbour within 25 or 30 miles

along the lake front, so that a very dangerous condition exists. I would strongly urge upon the government to make that expenditure this year. In view of what I know, it strikes me that this was simply a pre-election promise.
A promise to build an unnecessary work.

If the minister thinks it an unnecessary work why did he put a vote in the estimates for it last session? Either he must have known then that it was necessary or he was deceived by the then member for that constituency in this House, because when the late member, Mr. Jackson, came before the electors, he referred to that in his address. In that address he said :
$7,500 has been voted for a pier at Winnipeg Beach. This pier is to cost $16,000. The contract will be let this fall.
In addition to that statement in his published address, we had men coming down from Winnipeg and Selkirk, purporting to be contractors and going over the work and measuring it, and giving out all through the district that they were going to proceed with the work as soon as the bay was frozen over. In addition to that, we had the government tug lying there, with its engineer and staff of helpers, during the time of the regatta held there late in September. With four or five thousand people there, this government tug was pointed out by the friends and admirers of Mr. Jackson as proof of how the government was taking care of the people and was so prompt in responding to the request for the building of_a pier. They were told that the pier would be proceeded with and that before spring they would have the pier completed and would have a first-class harbour. This work was dangled before the eyes of the electors during the whole campaign. The same is true of the Elmwood post office. A vote of $10,000 was put in the estimates for . this work. And, further up the lake, $4,000 or $5,000 was to be spent at Gimli. This last-named work was proceeded with, and it was the only one that was proceeded with. It was gone on with during the campaign; men were hired by the day, and the whole dredging outfit that had cost this country a large sum of money was moved, at great risk, from the mouth of the Winnipeg river to the Icelandic river, where it was kept going for several weeks, and $4,000 or so was spent in dredging. I hold that this principle of making appropriations on the eve of a campaign, even if the government is serious and intends to spend the money, is a bad one. But how much worse is it when large appropriations are made running up into tens of millions of money, only to be dropped the following year. Of many of these appropriations made' last year, not a
dollar is to be found in the present estimate. It looks like making pledges to the people that the government never intend carrying out. I am satisfied there were thousands of voters fooled and tricked by these appropriations into voting for the government. It is a deplorable thing that the government of a big country like Canada should be guilty of such conduct as I believe this government stands guilty of. If there were words that I could use that would be strong enough to induce the minister to reconsider his decision in this matter and to implement the pledge that was made
I must say the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bradbury) has not a very coaxing way about it.
I grant you, Mr. Chairman, that I have not the same smooth way that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) has.
It sounds as if you were declaring war.

I wish to point out to the minister that we are not blind to what the minister and the government did previous to and during the last campaign. The mere fact that, when I asked that question in the beginning of the session, and received the answer I did from the Minister of Public Works, the Boundary Park Realty Company and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company had fully discharged a# they had undertaken to do, convinced me that the minister and the government had no intention, when that money was put into the estimates, of ever expending it. But this is not a political question so far as I am concerned. While this work will be in my constituency, the building of that pier would not go to accommodate my constituents. It would be built at a summer resort and would mainly benefit the people of the city of Winnipeg. I want to to say that this is a very serious matter. Several lives have been lost on that beach, because there was no harbour in which boats could seek shelter from the storms. There is no doubt that the promise was made to build that pier, and the appropriation put in fooled quite a number to vote for the government candidate last election. I have not any great hope, I confess frankly, of inducing the minister to reconsider his decision, because I have noticed his attitude in the House in regard to several of these things, and, no doubt, the government will take the position taken by the minister, that on account of the falling revenue, it is not wise to proceed with this work. I have already pointed out that if this be a good reason now, it was much stronger when this vote was put in the estimates. for everybody who knew anything about the country's finances knew that the revenue was falling and that this condition

would continue. But this did not stop these gentlemen making the appropriation. They were on the eve of an election, and they opened the flood-gates and voted, not merely millions but tens of millions, and, as I have said, fooled thousands of the electors from the Atlantic to the Pacific, into giving votes that they would not otherwise have given.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bradbury) has certainly presented an argument against engaging in this work in Lake Winnipeg. I had supposed, from the arguments presented to me last session by the gentleman who then represented the constituency that while Winnipeg Beach was resorted to in summer by many people, yet this work was necessary in the interest of navigation as .well, and would be an advantage to the commerce of the lake. But the hon. gentleman, says that it is used only as a summer resort for the people of Winnipeg. He presents an argument which makes it very important to consider whether or not this work should be postponed, pending the completion of works that are essential for the commercial and navigation interests of the country. It is a question, and always will be a question, how far the federal government is justified in spending money simply to afford summer resorts for the people of large cities. However, that is a matter that has not been brought to my attention as it has been by the hon. gentleman this evening. But,fcthough he has presented that view of the case, while I do not say that the work will be abandoned, I do say that it will have to stand over the same as many other public works of greater necessity than this would appear to be from the hon. gentleman's statement. I do not think, if he is sincerely desirous of accomplishing anything for his constituency, that he has gone about the matter in a way which one would expect. He acts as if he were seeking to provoke some quarrel-not personal, but political-with myself in respect of this work. I repeat what I have said, that, when this item was put in the estimates last session, it was put there in good faith upon the urgent representation of Mr. Jackson, who then represented the constituency.
And just on the eve of an election.

It was put there at the only time when it could be put there. Parliament had to be asked for the appropriation, and parliament did not rise and the Supply Bill was not passed until about July 20. After that we had to consider how rapidly we could go ahead with the works parliament had authorized. The hon. gentleman speaks of Elmwood public building. He does not do himself justice or seek to do me justice in that because Mr BRADPHRY.
we proceeded with that as far as we could reasonably go, we purchased a site, we showed our good faith in that way and we now have the site vested in the Crown and will be in a position to go ahead with the work whenever parliament puts me in a position to do so. All the items were put in the estimates in good faith and not with a view to dangling them before the electors or misleading the electors. The best evidence that we have acted in good faith is that in many constituencies, I would almost say scores of constituencies, which have returned our freinds to parliament we have deferred going on with many of these public works. We have not shown any discrimination and intend to treat the various works in good faith, and with a desire to carry out, as far as possible, the wishes of the people in respect of works which are really necessary and to meet the public convenience as far as we reasonably can. My hon. friend has referred to an answer I gave in this House and he has followed the example of one or two hon. gentlemen opposite, an example which I do not thinkjie. should follow. He says he does not think I was ingenuous in making this answer. Let me see if he was justified in that statement. First, let me say that the answers in my department are not prepared by me, nor are they prepared by the ministers in other departments. We send them to the proper official who prepares the answer in accordance with the facts, and I rarely see the answers until they are completed and ready to submit to the House. His insinuation that I was not ingenuous is not justified. The question was:
1.	What has the government done regarding protection pier at Winnipeg Beach?
2.	Is it the intention of the government to proceed with the construction of the pier at once? If not, when?
My answer was:
Plans and specifications have been prepared contingent upon certain work being performed by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and Boundary Park Realty Company. It has not yet been decided to go on with the work, but a decision will be come to before very long after we hear what the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Boundary Park Realty Company are prepared to do.
My hon. friend says the Boundary Park Realty Company has made an arrangement with the Canadian Pacific Railway ; but my department has not been informed of that. We wete to undertake this work if the Canadian Pacific Railway did a certain amount of work towards the completion of these harbour works. We have had no communication, as far as I am aware, from the Canadian Pacific Railway, and no information as to the arrangement between that company and the Realty Company. When we get word from the Canadian Pacific Railway as to what they are prepared to do,

then I am prepared to bring the matter before my colleagues and the decision as to when the work shall proceed will rest with the government.

I do not feel like allowing the minister to place_ a false construction on what I have said and I feel he has done that. In the first place, regarding what was said about the pier being of no use to the navigation of Lake Winnipeg, I stated distinctly that lives and property were lost last year because there was no harbour there.
Did he not say it was purely a summer resort for the people of Winnipeg?

I did not say it was purely a summer resort. I said it was a summer resort and was largely used by the people of Winnipeg, and not so much by residents of the county of Selkirk. If the pier were converted into a harbour, as it ought to be, it would be of very great value to the navigation of Lake Winnipeg; but according to the hon. gentleman it is to be simply a pier and he says it is contingent upon the Canadian Pacific Railway doing certain work. The fact is that the Canadian Pacific Railway could not do any work until the government had built the pier; their work came in after the pier was built.
Surely they could enter into an agreement to do the work?

There must have been some understanding between the government and the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Boundary Park Realty Company before the hon. gentleman authorized an appropriation of $7,500 to start this work. On the face of it it is evident there was, because the Boundary Park Realty Company, on the strength of that agreement, dispossessed itself of seven acres of valuable frontage to the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway gave an agreement to the Realty Company that as soon as the government would carry out their part of the work, the Canadian Pacific Railway would complete their part. It must be plain to the committee that the fault lies with the Department of Public Works and not with the two companies. The government have failed to implement the promise they gave to the people 'and the understanding must exist some place between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Boundary Park Realty Company and the government. The hon. gentlemen say there is no agreement, and that they have had no communication from the Canadian Pacific Railway.

I did not say that we had had no communication. I said we have had no communication as to the com pletion of the agreement, and no agreement has yet been entered into. There was some time ago a proposed agreement, but we had not been informed of the completion of the agreement with the Realty Company and no agreement has been entered into.

I do not know how the minister can justify the appropriation of last session if there was no arrangement between the companies interested. There is no question that the two companies had carried out their part of the agreement and the government had failed to carry out theirs. The minister accused me of being unfair in saying he was not ingenuous in his replies and he stated that he had nothing to do with the making up of the replies handed to him. I am not supposed to know that, I am simply taking the reply given by the gentleman across the floor of the House. I cannot hold the deputy responsible for his replies; I must hold the minister who made the replies.
And the reply happens to be according to the actual facts.

If the reply is according to the facts, I was quite right in saying that the minister was hardly ingenuous in making the reply, because if he knew the facts, his statement that it was contingent upon the Realty Company and the Canadian Pacific Railway doing something was not accurate. Consequently I think my statement that the minister was not perfectly ingenuous is in accordance with the facts. I do not wish to antagonize the minister ; but I am here a new member and I have a duty to my constituency to perform. This work should have been carried out to protect life and property. If the intention of the government is to create a harbour at that place there is no question that one is needed, that would be open to the lake boats. I understood from the minister that it was simply a pier, and when I made the statement that I had thought it was used principally by people from Winnipeg I stated what was accurate and at the same time if a harbour was created there it would be a great benefit to the lake traffic. I do not intend to take up any more time upon this question, but I am sorry that the minister has seen fit to make the statement across the floor of the House that I have been guilty of conduct that an hon. member should not be guilty of.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: A statement by an hon. member that another hon. member had been guilty of conduct unbecoming to a member of the House would have been checked by the chairman.
I did not use that expression.

I do not think I am misquoting the hon. gentleman. I think he made the statement that when I said he was not ingenuous I had done what no hon. gentleman should do in this House. I hold that when I made that statement I was stating simply what the facts warranted me in stating and I think the hon. gentleman ought to withdraw his statement.
I did not make it; therefore I could not withdraw it.
Is this vote for the repair of bridges built by this government?
This is a general expression. It says Dominion bridges. There would only be one at Shellmouth.

Is that the only Dominion bridge that has been constructed in Manitoba?
was expended upon that bridge, it was built higher by several feet than there was any necessity for and the result was that it imposed an unnecessary expenditure upon the municipality to build the approaches to the -bridge. There have been other bridges across that river constructed by municipalities in Manitoba at a cost of less than $10,000. This has been a very expensive bridge and the government could easily have constructed three bridges with that amount of money and thus have given accommodation to a greater number of people. I would ask the minister if he does not think that this bridge, is just as much entitled to a grant from the Dominion government because it is as much an interprovincial bridge as the bridge at Shell-mouth ?
It would be pretty difficult to justify the building of this bridge. We were criticised a good deal by reason of having built the Shellmouth bridge.
I think so. I am not aware of any other.

The minister will remember that a short time ago I had some communication with him in reference to a bridge across the Assiniboine river not far from the town of Roblin. The minister's reply was not favourable stating that this bridge could not be looked upon as a Dominion work and explaining that in the province of New Brunswick all interior bridges were constructed by the pro vincial government. That was not very useful information to me inasmuch as each province probably has its own particular system. The province of Manitoba grants fifty per cent of the cost of the construction of bridges and the municipalities contribute the other fifty per cent. In this case the bridge I asked for is very much in the same position as the Shellmouth bridge inasmuch as it is across the same river, close to the boundary line between Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and the people of Saskatchewan make the town of Roblin on the Manitoba side their market town.
I might draw the minister's attention to the fact that the people there have been very hard hit for a couple of years past, they have been visited by frost, their crops have been injured, they are not wealthy people and they are not in a position to construct this bridge. Inasmuch as it is really, in effect, an interprovincial bridge I thought I was justified in asking the government to give a grant as they did in the case of the Shellmouth bridge. I would like to ask the minister to reconsider his decision in that regard. There is this to say about the Shellmouth bridge, that it is a splendid bridge, but far more money was expended on that bridge than there was any necessity for. Upwards of $43,000 1

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: Adversely criticised ?
Yes.
By whom?

I do not know by whom; probably by hon. gentlemen on that side of the House. If the hon. gentleman had been here last night he would have heard a very severe criticism of my department because, two or three years ago, permission had been given to a municipality in the province of Quebec to rest one end of its bridge upon a wharf which had been constructed by this government. Suppose the constituency which my hon. friend so worthily represents had been represented by a Liberal and he had found an item for building a bridge in that constituency how the hon. member from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) the lieutenant of the leader of the opposition, would have railed against us for engaging in the construction of what should have been a local work. The ground upon which the Shellmouth bridge was justified was that the territory adjoining the province of Manitoba was not a province but was part of the Northwest Territories and all public works at that time in the territories were carried on at the expense of the federal government. It was also justified on the ground that the Dominion government owned a large area of land to which this bridge would give access. It was somewhat difficult to justify it, quite a point was strained, but I am afraid that if we were to build another bridge wholly within a province it would be difficult to justify it. At all events I was obliged to give to my hon. friend the answer that I did give, that I did not feel that I could ask my colleagues for an appropriation for constructing what would be entirely a provincial bridge.

I think the minister is quite incorrect when he says that the grant was adversely criticised in this House. The only criticism called forth by the item was by myself, and it was not adverse criticism, but rather because of the fact that the vote appeared year after year in the estimates and very little progress was made with the construction of the bridge. The item first appeared in the estimates in 1904 prior to the election at the instigation of the then Liberal candidate who made the construction of that bridge his principal drawing card in the contest. This is the first occasion upon which I have heard the reasons assigned by the minister to-night. One was the fact that the government had a certain amount of land in that vicinity and the other was that the province of Saskatchewan had not been formed at that time. I feel convinced that the bridge, the construction of which I am urging upon the government, is just as necessary and just as much entitled to a grant from the Dominion government as was the Shell-mouth bridge. The minister told us' that he had some difficulty in persuading his colleagues around the council board and in justifying the grant to the Shellmouth bridge. I thought that most strange because the bridge was nearly completed before he came into the cabinet at all.
I had to call for a large additional vote to go on with the work.

$43,000 was too much to expend on that bridge and there is no necessity for any such expenditure.
Lake Dauphin-lowering lake by removing obstructions from bed of Mossy river, $5,000.
The government are doing this with their own plant.
$10,000 was spent last year.
Yes. Carried.
You would not carry that? I would like to know how that expenditure of $10,000 was made last year.
Cost of material purchased $1,025; day's labour, chiefly the building of the dredge, $8,263.77.
What was the material that cost $1,025?
It would be lumber for the dredge and machinery as well.
Where is this dredge being built?
Right at the site of the work.
Where is the site of the work?
At the Mossy river.
Which end of the Mossy river?
I cannot tell which end; I think it is about the middle of the river.
Was this material bought by tender ?
No, bought at the lowest price in the usual way. We got prices.
From whom ?
I cannot tell you, a great deal of it would be lumber.
Has that dredge been built?
Not completed.
Is it even partially built?
Yes.
Well, 1 was at that place and there is no sign of a new dredge being built although there is a pile of lumber there which I was told was for the purpose of building a dredge.
When was the hon. gentleman there?
In November. When were these expenditures made?
I have not the dates of the expenditure. We have not^had a report recently from the resident engineer.
Who is the resident engineer?
Mr. Dufresne, at Winnipeg. He thought he would complete it in three months.

In the case of a large expenditure like this I am perfectly justified in asking from whom the material was bought and why it was not bought by tender." My late opponent was in the lumber business and I want to know how much he has profited, if at all?

The department would have to communicate with the resident engineer and I would be glad to get the information and lay it on the table or hand it to my hon. friend. I will undertake to wire to Winnipeg.
If it was bought from the source I suspect, it came very near be a violation of the Independence of Parliament Act. Will you please take that into consideration?
I will get the information.
Where is the work to be done with this expenditure of $5,000?
On the Mossy river.
Where on the Mossy river?
Between Lake Dauphin and Lake Winnipeg. There are about 3,500 feet of river to be improved and of course the work will be done where there are most obstructions.
The purpose is to lower Lake Dauphin?
To clear the bed of the river, remove boulders and straighten the course.

I am anxious for information about this because the government dredge has been working at the mouth of the Mossy river for the past iive or six years and if this new dredge is going to be operated as the old one was it will not be of miich use. The old dredge was equipped with a crane and the sand and mud taken out on one side of the dredge were dumped again into the creek at the other side of the dredge, to be washed back into the channel with every northeast wind.
How many years ago is that ?
As late as the time of the general elections last year.
Will you allow me to say
Excuse me first, because I don t want you to put words,in my mouth, as I notice you are very fond of doing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The chairman should be addressed, and if reference is made to any other hon. member he must be referred to in the third person.
I submit of course to the ruling of the chair. Does that rule apply both ways?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes.
Then I would ask the chairman to notice that the Minister of Public Works has been addressing me as you. What is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The remark T made is applicable to both hon. members who used the expression.

The people living on Lake Dauphin are very anxious that this work should be done, and I trust that the money will be properly expended and not absolutely wasted as it has been at the mouth of the river for the past five or six years. They have succeeded in removing in six or seven years one boulder down at the mouth of the river, and as there are some Mr. CAMPBELL.
thousands of them to be removed at the source of the river it will apparently take a considerable time to complete the work. How you are going to remove the boulders with a dredge is beyond my understanding. That dredge has been nothing more or less than a political dredge and the money expended there has been wasted. The government tell us that these are hard times, and so I want the money used and not wasted.
Hear, hear, that is right; that is the way we try to use it.

Mr. Chairman. Is it permissible to look a little lower down in the estimates and to ask if money which is going to be expended in other places should be expended in my riding where it is more necessary?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is not in order to move that the money in one item should be used for another purpose.

If it were in order, I
would have very much liked that some of the useless expenditure which I see is going to be made in Saskatchewan, for instance, should be made in Lake Manitoba.

A few evenings ago I directed the attention of the minister to the condition the bridge is going to be left in across the St. Andrews rapids, and I now want to renew my statement that it is the duty of the government to complete that bridge. There is no question that the bridge has cost a great deal of money. The provision for the bridge is made, and I presume that it will be completed and planked, and that it will then be left standing in the middle of the Red River, with no connection at either side. I contend that the large expenditure that has been made on it is entirely unjustifiable if the government does not complete it. The bridge will remain and the planks put on it will rot, and it will stand as a monument that will be no credit to the Minister of Public Works. The reply I got from the hon. minister was that the local government or the municipalities ought to make these connections. Every one from Manitoba knows that the municipalities are utterly unable to provide the money that will be necessary to make those connections. I am told by competent men that it will take from $75,000 to $100,000 to complete the bridge so that a vehicle could drive across it, and it is of course utterly impossible to expect that the municipalities can supply that money. The government have expended nearly $1,250,000 in providing the dam across the river and putting the bridge there, as far as they have gone.

Building locks as well, so that there would be a bridge under any circumstances.

Mr, BRADBURY. There would be a working bridge; but if provision had not been made for a passenger bridge I am satisfied that it would have cost the country at least $100,000 less than it has cost. My argument is that the government having seen fit to make provision for a passenger bridge, which I think was wise, the intention was to give the residents on both sides of the river a first-class bridge, but if the bridge is allowed to remain as it is, it will simply be useless as a passenger bridge, and the municipalities are not in a position to provide the connections. I again urge the government strongly to complete the work in its own interest.
I want to correct one statement of the hon. gentleman. He speaks of the planking on the bridge rotting. I may say there is no planking on the bridge. It is to be steel and concrete entirely.
Before the item passes, I would like some assurance from the minister that he will see that this money is expended in a proper way, and not in the ways that moneys have been expended in the past.
That assumes something of which I have no evidence-that there has been any improper expenditure in the past. He would not expect me to admit that.
I would like an assurance from the hon. minister that he will see that this money is properly expended for the purposes stated here.

I think the hon. gentleman can rest assured that the same prudent and economical management will take place in connection with this expenditure as we endeavour to have in all matters connected with my department.
River Assiniboine-improvements near Portage la Prairie, $1,000.
Is this for the same work that was carried on there last fall?

The same work. This is to settle land damages. The work has been completed.
Some resolutions reported.

Monday, March 22, 1909. The SPEAKER took the Chair at Three o'clock.
Report of the Department of Trade and Commerce for the year ending March 31 1908, part III.-Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
On the orders of the day being called:

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) to a despatch which appeared in the ' Mail and Empire ' of March 14, with respect to the Railway Commission. It says that Mr. Buell, of Brockville, representing the government, is presenting the complaints against the express company. I would like to ask the Minister of Railways and Canals if this is a permanent counsel appointed in connection with the Railway Commission and, if so, why is there this discrimination in favour of the western shippers as against the eastern shippers? Why are not the farmers of North Ontario provided with counsel the same as the shippers of the west are ?

speakeroldname: Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext: This is rather an old story. Mr. Buell has been engaged for some time investigating express matters for the commission. I do not know just what this particular work is but he is not a counsel engaged to present the general complaints of the people against the railway companies. This is rather an investigation into the methods of the express companies which has been going on for a year and a half or two years.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege or explanation. Bill (No. 69) has been on the Order Paper for a considerable length of time. I was expecting that it would be reached and when it was reached I intended to make an explanation which was due to the House with regard to something I said when the Bill was introduced. It was a Bill to amend the Land Act and I made the statement based on a memorandum handed to me containing the minutes and proceedings of the Senate, which showed that the Bill as it had passed the Senate had contained an amendment. I stated that the amendment made by the Senate had been dropped and that the Bill had passed this House and received the assent of His Excellency without the amendment. I also referred to section 42 of the Bill, but I do not purpose saying anything in reference to that now as at some future time I may have an opportunity of dealing with it. I simply want to say that I made a verv careful inquiry into the whole matter and I found that a misapprehension had been created owing to a mistake made with respect to the matter in the Minutes and Proceedings and the ' Hansard ' of the Senate. I have a copy of the minutes which gives the facts exactly as I gave them to the House, but I

find that the minutes are entirely wrong. The clerk of the Senate turned up the record and showed me that the Bill had passed the House without this amendment being in it, although the minutes stated that it had been carried in the affirmative. It came to this House and was passed. I was quite satisfied that I had done a grave injustice to some person, myself and the House by basing my remarks on a statement that was not justified by the_ facts. speechtext:
I understand that some members of the committee have expressed a wish that I should pronounce some sort of opinion with reference to this legislation. I scarcely know upon what point that opinion is desired. Upon any legal question that arises with regard to this or any other legislation which may be under consideration I am at any time ready to. express any opinion that I may entertain, but my difficulty is in seeing what legal question arises upon the legislation now before the committee. It may be that the question is as to the necessity for this legislation, and I can quite understand that there may be different opinions in that respect; it may be that there is no need for it. On the other hand it may be that under the true construction of the statute of 1879, which this legislation proposes to amend or to interpret, a result has been reached which
was not the intention of parliament in 1879 when the previous legislation was passed. Now, with respect to what the true construction of the statute of 1879 may be, the whole question is no doubt one of law as to the interpretation of the language then used. Upon that subject I formed an opinion some months ago when the question was raised before the Department of Justice upon a reference to that department by the superintendent of insurance, and the opinion which I then expressed and which for my part I still entertain as a matter of law is, that under the wording of the Act of 1879, and giving to the language there used its strict legal interpretation, the company or the shareholders of the company cannot deduct from the general earnings of the company a percentage by way of interest upon the amount of their capital stock before calculating 90 per cent of the profits for distribution among the policy-holders.
I presume that the legal advisers of the company are of the same opinion, or this legislation would not be presented. So much for the opinion which as a matter of law I entertain as to the meaning and effect of the legislation of 1879. I do not know any ground upon which the competence and power of this parliament to pass the legislation which is now under consideration could properly be questioned. The matter is, so far as I can see, entirely within the jurisdiction of this parliament. I do not know any other question of law that arises. If it is a question of the propriety or wisdom of passing the legislation which is now before the committee, I respectfully take the position that every hon. member of this House is as well qualified as I am to come to a conclusion on the subject. That is not any matter of law. That is merely a matter of the propriety and advisability of passing or refusing to pass this legislation. But if any hon. gentleman desires to know what course I propose, as an individual member of this House, to take with regard to this legislation, I have no objection to stating it, whatever it is worth. So far as I am concerned, I intend to support the legislation, and I rest myself in doing so upon the action of the committee to which it has been referred. I think, in the matter of any private Bill, it is 'not usual for this House, or this Committee u whole House, to decline to accept the considered action of any special committee which has taken the legislation into consideration and has passed an opinion with regard to it; and certainly I am prepared to credit the special committee in this case with having had established before it, before its report was presented to the House, such considerations as in its view justified it in the report which it made

favouring the proposed legislation. It seems to me peculiarly a question for consideration before a committee. The second section of this Bill, which is I suppose the only one about which any special amount of controversy would be likely to arise, is a declaratory section, stating what was the intention with which the legislation of 1879 was passed. That I take it is a pure question of fact in regard to which the committee which investigated this question is in a better position certainly than I am, and probably than any member of the House can be, to come to a correct conclusion. In the everyday experience of a practising lawyer, it is not an infrequent thing to find, in any legal document, that the true intention of the parties to that document may not have been correctly expressed. Every lawyer is familiar with an action brought by one of the parties to a contract, before a court of equity, to have the language in which that contract, if it has been reduced to writing, has been expressed, rectified by the court-to have the language of the document made to express what was the true intention of the contracting parties. In any such action, if it is resisted, we always have of necessity the opposing litigant declaring that the document as drawn expresses the true intention, that he so understood the bargain; and perhaps he will contend that he has altered his position upon the faith of his understanding of the language used in the document which expresses the contract. To determine what is the truth, in such a controversy, is the function of the court, and the court if it reaches the conclusion that the complainant is right, and that the written document does not truly express what was at the time of the contract the intention of the parties, does not hesitate to correct the writing and to express what it finds to have been the true intention with which the writing was signed. I take it that is exactly the position here. No court could correct this error in the language used by the parties thirty years ago; no court of equity could interfere in a matter of this sort. The only tribunal which could correct the mistake, if there has been one, is this tribunal, the high court of parliament; and in coming to a conclusion whether or not that correction should be made, this high court of parliament, I take it, ought to act not only cautiously and judiciously, but also judicially and on judicial principles. The first thing to be satisfied is that there was a mistake. It was, I take it, the function of the committee which considered this legislation to be satisfied of that; and in the view that before reporting this Bill the committee must have been satisfied that such a mistake did occur, it seems to me there is no difficulty on the part of members of the House who rely

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: INVESTIGATION INTO DEPARTMENT , OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.
speechtext:
upon the work of the committee in accepting its conclusions. If it is the fact that there was a mistake in the language used in the legislation of thirty years ago, then that mistake ought to be now corrected. If the conduct of the parties interested, through all the years since 1879, demonstrates that there was such a mistake, and that that mistake was common to both parties interested, I presume that there would be no difficulty in coming to the conclusion that parliament to-day ought to say in clear terms what it would have said in 1879, if the danger of misunderstanding or erroneous interpretation had been then present to the mind of parliament. This legislation proposes to enact that in the language used in the Act of 1879, what was intended was that before arriving at the amount, annually or quinquennially, as the case might be, of the profits of this company, which were to be distributed to the policy-holders, the interest upon the amount of paid up capital might be deducted.
If that was the intention in 1879, and if that intention had then been clearly expressed, of course there would be no need for this legislation. We are asked to-day to determine what was the true intention in 1879 and to give expression to it. I was not present in the Committee on Banking and Commerce and am not able to say what facts were brought before that committee to satisfy it that this was the intention in 1879; but it has come to _ my knowledge in various ways that ever since 1879, the business of the company has been carried on under that impression. If we look at the conduct of the policy-holders, who received, under the statute of 1879, certain increased benefits, I would think that there was evidence in their conduct pointing to a like interpretation on their part. So far as I understand the situation, from that day to this, every policy-holder has acquiesced in this course of business. I have not heard that from 1879 up to the present time, any policy-holder has effectively objected, by bringing an action to have it declared that the course of business pursued by the directors in this respect was contrary to the true meaning of the statute of 1879. If any such action were before the courts, probably different considerations might arise. Probably, the question then for consideration by this committee would be whether or not such action could be interfered with by legislation. ^ But so long as no litigation is on foot in connection with this difficulty, it seems to me that what we have is at most a difference of opinion between the shareholders and the policy-holders as to the meaning of the old statute of 30 years ago. I do not know that there is such a thing as a vested right arising out of a mistake. I have never ' heard that any defendant, resisting ail

action brought before a court of equity _ to rectify the terms of a writing into which he had entered, could be heard to say that while the writing did not truly express the bargain, he had a vested right to hold his adversary to the consequences of the mistake. The whole question for the court to determine would be whether or not there was a mistake; and if the court came to the conclusion that there was, it would disregard any contention of the defendant that he had a vested right to hold his adversary to the consequences of a common mistake between the two. I speak with some deference. I have a personal interest in this matter. I am a policy-holder in the company to a considerable amount and am not a shareholder. If this legislation does wrong to the policy-holders, it injures me personally as much as any policy-holder whose policy is not greater than mine. But the whole question narrows itself down to the one question of fact, whether or not the Act of 1879 did really and accurately give expression to what then was the intention of parliament and of those who applied to parliament? If it did not, the mistake ought to be corrected, and no one has any right to claim that he is being injured because that mistake is now being made right.
