If it was the desire of hon. members to ascertain from the Minister of Justice what position the government took with respect to this Bill and the retroactive character of the legislation proposed, that desire has been disappointed. If on the other hand, it was the desire of hon. members to secure any light on the subject frpm the Minister of Justice himself, in his personal capacity as a member of this House, then that desire has also been disappointed. But if the members of this House expected to have an expression of opinion from the hon. minister, based on reasons that are utterly unfounded, that expectation has not been disappointed. The Minister of Justice takes first the ground that this legislation has reached a status by reason of its having passed the Committee on Banking and Commerce, where he is not as free to oppose it as he otherwise would be. Not being a member of long standing, I do not wish to discuss at any length that position; but I am not aware that the mere passing of a Bill of this char-95
acter through the Committee on Banking and Commerce places it in a position where is is beyond the. responsibility of the government and does not require any endorsation from the minister, within whose particular province it falls. But on the other hand,
I would draw the attention of the Minister of Justice to this feature of his own argument. He assures us that he holds a specific opinion, which he has entertained for some time, as to the legal effect of the amending Act of 1879, which opinion he believes the solicitors of the Canada Life Insurance Company also entertain. Let me point out to him that the very solicitor of the Canada Life who urged the passage of the Bill through the committee, did not make any such representation to that committee but the very opposite. Therefore if the position on that point taken by the Minister of Justice be correct, we should refer the Bill back to the committee, because the committee was absolutely misled regarding the position taken by the legal advisers of the Canada Life. The legal advisers of the Canada Life Assurance Company, or, at least, the adviser who was before the committee, distinctly stated to the committee that, in his view, the amending Act of 1879 meant what they now desire to have it declared to mean-meant that the profits there referred to did not include interest on capital stock. He stated that a contrary opinion had been given, and it was to remove the utmost possibility of doubt that this Bill was before the House. That is very different, and very materially different, from the position taken by the Minister of Justice, which position, he assures the House, is the legal stand taken by the solicitors of the Canada Life. Therefore, the Bill was put through the committee in such a way that it should not receive further sanction or higher status in the eyes of either of the Minister of Justice or of any member of this House. Now, the Minister of Justice goes on to further argue that only a pure question of fact was before the committee, and that that committee was as competent to judge of the fact as he or any other member of the House. What are the facts? In 1849 the Canada Life Assurance Company took out a charter. By the terms of that charter they were required to distribute their profits to the policy-holders and shareholders on the basis of 75 per cent and 25 per cent respectively.

The point is immaterial. As the law stood at the time of the Act, and perhaps for some years before, the distribution had been on the basis of 75 per cent and 25 per cent, the company besides laying by a reserve of 4:67 per cent interest on their capital stock. By the amending Act of 1879, procured at the request of the company, a clause was inserted reciting that the company had been distributing during these years their entire profits and enact" ing that thereafter the distribution should take place in the proportions of 90 per cent and 10 per cent instead of 75 per cent and 25 per cent. Now, for some thirty years the Canada Life has proceeded upon the basis of the Act but has cpntinued to put by a reserve of 4-67 per cent for the .shareholders before arriving at the profits which they were to distribute in the proportion of 90 per cent and 10 per cent. The Minister of Justice takes the position that the question before us is simply a question of fact. He says the high court of parliament is in the position of an ordinary court of justice which has to deal, with two litigants who have entered into a contract, one claiming that the contract is a mistake and the other resisting the claim, and the one resisting the claim perhaps setting up that he has acquired rights under that contract on the basis of that alleged mistake. The minister says that the parties now come before the high court of parliament in an analogous position. That is the foundation of his case. Is that a correct statement of the position? I submit that it is not. Do the two parties who entered into that contract in 1879 appear before parliament? They do not. The only party to that arrangement of 1879 was the House of Commons of Canada. The parties to the contracts appeared later, and they were the Canada Life Assurance Company and the 35,000 policy-holders, who, since that date, have acquired rights by the Act of 1879. The two parties as they existed in 1879_ do not come before the high court of parliament. If there was any mistake, then it cannot be attributed either to the Canada Life Assurance Company or to the policy-holders, nor can it be attributed to the shareholders of that time. The mistake, if there were a mistake, is to be attributed to the parliament of Canada alone. Therefore, the legislation which the Minister of Justice now favours is not to correct the mistake of any of these other parties in 1879, but to correct a mistake of the parliament of Canada-that is, granting that it is a mistake. But who are the Mr. A. H. CLARKE.
parties who are interested in this matter at the present time? Even assuming that the Minister of Justice's statement as to the analogous position of the parties is right- that is, that the parties to this contract who erred were the shareholders and the policy-holders of 1879-are they the parties in any sense who come before this House now? They are not. The parties before this House are the shareholders and policyholders of 1909-different parties altogether. Thirty-five thousand policy-holders have come in since 1879 who were not parties to the alleged mistake of 1879, who derived no rights from the parties to that mistake, but stand in an absolutely distinct position and on a higher level altogether, and it is from the point of view of these policyholders that this Bill should be .considered. Has the Minister of Justice discussed the case from the point of view of the 35,000 , policy-holders who have come in since 1879? Not a word has he uttered in his statement, which has been looked forward to for eight days in this House, with respect to the policy-holders; not for one moment .has he stood in the position of these policy-holders or argued the matter from their point of view. The innocent policy-holders are the first to be considered. They are greatest in number and their rights are the greatest, and we should discuss this matter, and the Minister of Justice should have discussed this matter, from their point of view.
The Minister of Justice goes on to argue that the policy-holders have acquiesced. I have yet to hear it argued in a court of justice-where some very strange things are sometimes argued-that the acquiescence in any position of any party who is not a party to the original contract is a reason why that party should be deprived of rights which he otherwise would have. These
35,000	policy-holders either have rights under their contract with the Canada Life Assurance Company, or they have no rights. The Minister of Justice was considering whether or not they had rights which this Bill affected, and he frankly comes before this House and tells us that he thinks they have rights and that this Bill affects those rights. But he says that they have had these rights for thirty years and have never come before a court of justice and asked for redress. Is he going to set it up as a precedent that because certain citizens of Canada have slept on rights for thirty years that that is justification for the House of Commons of Canada to pass an Act to cut under those rights and take awav the foundations on which they rest? If he does, where will his precedent carry him? If rights are not to be observed simply because no one has chosen to enforce them in courts of justice, then by what criterion does the Minister of Justice decide whether

he cuts into vested rights or not? This afternoon he comes forward and says there is no litigant. I regret that the rules of the House forbid me from referring to a discussion that took place about two weeks ago in reference to a similar principle. I will say, however, that the acquiescence of parliament has never in the past been held to have destroyed the rights of citizens in any way. Now they have the rights, but the Minister of Justice says they are not in litigation, therefore he says parliament is justified in cutting them out. Does the Minister of Justice lay it down as a principle that vested rights are not vested rights until they are in litigation? Have they no status in his mind until they reach the status of litigation? Are not vested rights just as sacred to him and to this House before they are the subject of a lawsuit as they become by virtue of a lawsuit? Will they by virtue of a lawsuit reach a position and a degree of sacredness that they did not possess before? Furthermore, has it ever been argued by the Justice Department of this country, has it ever been argued within three weeks of this date, that the outrage, that the violation of the 8th commandment consisted in taking away the position of a litigant, the footing of a litigant, after he got into court? Has it not rather been argued that the outrage and violation consisted in denying the right to litigate? It was the right to litigate that was before sacred in the eyes of the minister, it was access to the courts of justice that was sacred to them, and it was the taking away of that access that was an outrage. Why is it not an outrage to-day? Surely it is not the policy of the House of Commons to stand between a litigant and the court. Is it any more right and just to step in between the litigant and a court of justice, than to go to the court and throw the litigant out? I see no difference. It has always been, as I have understood, the doctrine propounded by the Minister of Justice himself, and by the hon. gentleman who proposed this Bill, that the cardinal outrage of legislation of this kind was in cutting out the right to litigate, and not in throwing the litigant out of court. Why is that position changed? Why do the promoters of the Bill now come to parliament and say that these people cannot be said to have vested rights because they have not yet asserted them? Surely, that position is unworthy the dignity of this House, and unworthy the dignity and high standing of the Minister of Justice.
Now, what position are we to take? One of three positions we must take. Either firstly, the Act of 1879 is clear in its terms, and means that the profits include the same profits that any other business would include as profits, and include the interest 951
on capital. If that is the case, then policy-holders who have come in since that time have absolutely vested rights, and this Bill is retroactive and takes away those vested rights. Surely the Minister of Justice, in receipt as he is and as he will not deny, and the Minister of Finance, in receipt as he is, and as he will not deny, and the Prime Minister, in receipt as he is, and as he will not deny, of specific statements of claims from policy-holders, from a policy-holder who has come in since that time, not only of a specific statement of his rights but of an absolute statement that he wishes to litigate those rights, surely these hon. gentlemen, in receipt of that very statement, and knowing his position as a responsible policy-holder of this company, will not say that they are not doing now exactly the same thing as taking away the rights of the litigant, and throwing him out of court as well. That is one case that may exist. Secondly, the Bill of 1879 may be absolutely clear in its provisions, and it may not mean that the profits include interest on the capital stock. If that is the case, then this legislation is null and void in so far as the second clause is concerned. Then the Canada Life Assurance Company would have no reason to come before this House and ask for an interpreting statute, because the legislation is now just in the position they want it. So that on the first two grounds they have no right to ask this parliament for legislation. But another state of affairs might exist. It might be that the Act of 1879 is doubtful in its meaning, that there is a latent or a patent ambiguity in it, and that it may mean that profits should include interest on capital stock, or it may not mean that. But if the third position is a correct statement of the case as it stands, then the courts of this country are established for the purpose of interpreting Acts of parliament; they are established for the purpose of saying what is the real meaning of this clause in the Act of 1879, that contains a latent or a patent ambiguity. Why should the House of Commons, in this case, step in and interpret this legislation, if it is doubtful, unless it proposes similarly to interpret legislation in every other case where it is doubtful, unless it proposes to usurp the functions of the court and act as interpreter as well as an author of legislation? Why does it step in in the interest of a large corporation against the interest of many poor policy-holders? If the meaning is doubtful, it is the province of the courts to interpret it; and I say that when this comes before the courts for determination, the considerations urged by the Canada Life Assurance Company and by the promotors of this legislation will be given such weight at the hands of the court as they ought to receive, as those considera-

tions should receive, no more and no less. Considerations of the intent of parliament, in certain cases, are entertained by the court; considerations of the intent of the promoters of the Bill in certain cases, are entertained by the court, and in every case where those considerations are entertained, they would be entertained in this case. Principles of equity and of justice in this country have determined to what extent and at what time such considerations as intent should apply. Why not leave it to the courts. The answer is that the Canada Life Assurance Company taking the ground that if this Act is doubtful in its meaning, want more consideration given to the intent on our part even as against innocent policy-holders, than they are entitled to have given it in a court of justice.
We want certain provisions to have certain definite meanings just as they would have if they were placed before the proper tribunal for interpretation. We want the rules of equity that apply in courts of justice to apply to this case in order to bring it to a definite conclusion and to achieve a definite result. I say that if this is a matter of doubtful interpretation as they themselves contend it is, it should go to the proper tribunal which will give every consideration its due and proportionate weight and no more. On whatever ground, on whatever principle we may apply with respect to the meaning of the Act of 1879, whether it be the first as outlined, that 'profits' have to be taken as meaning interest on capital, I say, it involves the principle of retroactive legislation and therefore this Bill is distinctly retroactive and unjustifiable on every ground of justice and equity. If it be the second, if the Act is clear and if the word 'profits' does not include interest on capital stock, then there is no need of the Bill at all. If it be the third, then it is clear, and the Minister of Justice will not deny, that it is the province of the courts of justice to interpret legislation. I think I have covered the ground as put forward by the Minister of Justice. Let me now call the attention of the committee to another consideration, which I frankly admit should not bear heavily with the members of this House, and which I do not think comes really to the kernel of discussion, because the kernel of the discussion is whether we are going to cut off these 35,000 policy-holders or not from any sound claims to which they are entitled and from which they will be cut off if this Bill should pass. The phase I desire, however, to refer to is that of an adequate return on invested captial. It is a well known fact that from the time the Act of 1879 was passed up to 1899 the capital stock of the Canada Life Assurance Company was $125,000. On that capital stock 4-67 peT cent was laid aside as inter Mr. MEIGHEN
est before the profits were arrived at. In 1899 that capital stock was increased and up to that time the reserve for interest amounted to the insignificant sum of some $5,800. The Minister of Justice might, in laying this matter before the House, have pointed out, I think very reasonably, that the policy-holders would not have benefited to any appreciable extent individually, by the compelling of their rights in a court as he says they should have done. It is only since 1899 that that might have been done and I think no one would contend that the results to the policy-holders would before 1899 have been at all commensurate with the outlay which would have been entailed in court. During these years from 1879 to 1899 the shareholders of the Canada Life Assurance Company were in receipt of very considerable premiums. They tell us now that unless this Bill passes we, who have put a million dollars into this company, will only get 3-6 per cent or 3-8 per cent and therefore at a very opportune time the Canada Life Assurance Company comes to this House and asks for this legislation. But, it was not always thus, nor would it be always thus? For twenty years, prior to 1899, their capital stock was receiving dividends and interest to the extent of 20,	30
and as high as 70 per cent. It would average, I believe, 30 per cent or probably more for the twenty years on the $125,000 of capital stock. Now they have increased the basis of their capital in order that they might get eight per cent on their money and they have come before us at the very time that the proportion of their capital stock, compared with the volume of their business, is large and when they are not able to extract the enormous dividends which they were enabled to extract in years gone by and which they will be able to extract in years to come. At a time when dividends are at the lowest they seize the opportunity to come before this parliament and ask for legislation. Is there any reasonable anticipation that the low dividends will continue? Just as in years gone by, before 1896, the volume of business as compared with the volume of their capital stock, was great and the dividends that they derived brought them thirty per cent, so, in years to come, as the volume of business of the Canada Life Assurance Company steadily increases, as the volume of business of all large life insurance companies is almost mathematically certain to increase, if this Bill fails to pass, it is practically a mathematical certainty that the rate of dividend which will accrue upon the million dollars of capital will be a great deal laTger than it is today. So, we need have no apprehension on behalf of the shareholders. It is practically certain, there can be no reasonable

doubt, that the condition that prevailed before 1899, when the volume of business held a large proportion to the volume of the capital stock, will recur in years to come and that the volume of business will attain to the same proportion of the capital stock as in days gone by. There is no reasonable apprehension that these people under the law as it stands will not receive an adequate return on their money. The shareholders got together in 1899 and added to their capital stock to the extent of $875,000. Were they compelled to do so by any legislation from this House? I think not. They did so voluntarily and if I am permitted to quote the Royal Insurance Commission, they unwarrantedly increased their capital stock to the detriment of the policyholders. I am quoting that statement from the report of the Royal Commission. The Act of 1879 meant the same in 1899 as it means to day and will always mean unless this retroactive legislation is passed. They added to their capital with their eyes open and if that he so why should we come to the assistance of these people and relieve them from the situation into which they voluntarily plunged and plunged for their own benefit? I do not propose to go on and discuss the action of the Canada Life Insurance Company in piling up systematically, hurriedly, precipitately, its reserve to some $2,500,000 instead of following the course outlined in the Insurance ytct except to say that by that very action the Canada Life Assurance Company have put between the shareholders and possible loss in time to come that fortification, and that absolved them, one would reasonably think, not being an insurance expert, from any necessity of adding to the volume of their capital stock, and it would certainly absolve them from any right to come to this parliament and say that by virtue of adding to their captial stock and of the results thereof they are entitled to an Act declaring the meaning of an Act thirty years old and interfering with vested rights that have grown up during those thirty years. Let me, before concluding, make one reference to a statement of the Minister of Justice. The Minister of Justice says that the policyholders have slept on their rights for thirty years, that they have for these years been in that position and that they could have gone to the courts. The same argument exactly applies to the shareholders. The shareholders, for thirty years, have let the legislation stand while they could have gone to the court or come to parliament to ask to have it changed. I do not think it is fair to state that the policy-holders have stood on their rights for that time.
The fact that I am a policy-holder in this company for one thousand dollars only will not I hope influence my position on the Bill, but it enables me to say that for the
eleven years I have been a policy-holder I do not recall ever receiving any statement from this company to show that interest had been cut off before the profits were determined. It is only reasonable to assume that very many policy-holders would be in the same position, and even if they took the trouble to scan this report and compare it with the Bill very few would even suspect that their rights were being infringed. We are here to preserve rights as they are and not to preserve rights after they are in litigation. I want to make an appeal to members of the House who perhaps up to this point have been led to support the Bill without knowing its real meaning. I believe there are many members in the House who supported the Bill in select committee without knowing it has a retroactive character as the Minister of Justice has frankly admitted it has. Therefore, the vote of these hon. gentlemen in the select committee in no way binds them to support the Bill in'this Committee of the Whole. Let hon. gentlemen who support this Bill, seriously consider what they will be able to say in years to come when people may come to them and state that undeT a misapprehension of the law they have invested money, and now want parliament to help them out of their difficulty. How can we ever deny to such people redress, even at the expense of innocent parties, if we set a precedent now which I submit will be fatal in years to come?

That would have given ample notice to every policy-holder throughout the_ country of what was intended. I do not understand that the rules of the House require that full particulars of a Bill should be given in the notice. The notice is to draw attention that a Bill is to be introduced on a particular subject, and I venture to say that in the notice referred to, there is as much information as is contained in any notice of the kind. There is certainly as much information regarding the division of profits as regarding the change of date and the acquisition of more real estate. We have an officer here whose business it is to deal with these matters. Rule 95 is very clear:-
There shall be an examiner of petitions for private Bills.

Petitions for private Bills, when received by the House, are to be taken into consideration by the examiner, who shall report to the House in each case the extent to which the requirements of the rules regarding notice have been complied with; and in every case where the notice is reported by the examiner to have been insufficient or otherwise defective, the petition shall be taken into consideration without special reference by the Committee on Standing Orders, who shall report to the House recommending the course to be taken in consequence of such insufficiency of notice or other defects therein.
Everything was conducted regularly. The petition came before the examiner and he examined whether the requirements regarding notice had been complied with. I suppose if the notice had been put in the Toronto ' Globe ' instead of the Toronto ' News,' my hon. friend would have seen it. but it would not have been seen by others equally interested who read the Toronto ' News' and do not read the ' Globe.' The examiner is an official of great experience. He has been in the employ of the House of Commons many years. He examined the notice in this case and reported that it was in every particular in accord with the requirements of the rules; and on his attention being again drawn to the matter, he still maintained the opinion that the notice was sufficient.

maintopic: INVESTIGATION INTO DEPARTMENT , OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.
speechtext:
As a policy-holder, I am exceedingly sorry this matter is being discussed here. This discussion will not do the Canada Life any good. Some gentlemen who have amassed wealth may become too aggressive. There is too much haste about this Bill and the way it is going through this House. Two classes of securities are concerned in it-those held by the stock-holders and those held by the policy-holders. The first represent $1,000,000, and the second $25,000,000. I am not saying whether this Bill is right or wrong. As a policy-holder, I do not want my heirs to draw one dollar which belongs to the stockholders, but I do not propose that the shareholders shall draw one dollar which belongs to my heirs. As a policy-holder, and I suppose as a citizen of average intelligence, I should have something to say about legislation affecting my rights, and I positively got no intimation from the Canada Life of what they contemplated. That company, as a business organization, should have notified the people it was doing business with, and for whom it acts as trustee. We have other corporations coming before this parliament for legislation, corporations which have bondholders as well as stockholders; and it is a principle, I understand of legislation, which this parliament insists upon, that the assent of the bondholders should be obtained, up to a certain percentage, before any legislation affecting their rights is passed. I am not asking that in this case, but I say that we
should insist that the people who are interested should be properly notified. I am personally strongly of the opinion that in the Insurance Bill before this House, there should be a clause providing that where insurance companies seek legislation affecting the interests of the policy-holders, they should be compelled to give each policy-holder two or three months' notice _ so that he may be in a position to protect himself. I say again, I do not know that this legislation is bad, I do not know that it is good, but I do know that the people who have a large amount of money in it have not been advised. And I say that it is no excuse to plead that these companies give notice in the papers. Other corporations who come for legislation likewise give notice in the papers, but this parliament insists that the stockholders shall have the assent of the bondholders before that legislation becomes effective. And I think that is a fair position to take. These gentlemen ought to be told to go back, and the policy-holders should be given an opportunity to consider their interest in this matter. It is true, there is a gentleman, Mr. Laidlaw, who has been sending around literature on this subject. I can say that Mr. Laidlaw does not represent me; he has never had authority from me as a policy-holder, to send out complaints to this House. I have not been consulted as a policy-holder. I think it is wrong that this legislation should pass under the circumstances.

maintopic: INVESTIGATION INTO DEPARTMENT , OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.
speechtext:
The motion before the committee, as I understand it, is that the committee rise and report progress. 1 think that every hon. member will admit that we are now in a very unusual position. I think that every hon. member will admit that the importance of this Bill and the gravity of the issues involved are such that it would be most regrettable if hon. members, in dealing with this unusual position, did not approach it with perfect calmness and impartiality, and with a sincere desire not only to do justice but to maintain the dignity of the House. I think that your ruling, Mr. Chairman, is, beyond question, correct. I think that no hon. member will dispute the soundness of your statement that the objection taken-that notice was not sufficient-while, in my judgment, a good objection, was not taken when effect could be given to it. But we are in this peculiar position:	Here is an important
point raised, yet it cannot be adjudicated on the merits. We are in a peculiar position also for this reason-and I think I may refer to it on this motion that the committee rise and report. This Bill came before the House a few days ago and the House thought the opinion of the Minister of Justice of such importance that it was

agreed unanimously to let the Bill stand until that opinion could be obtained. The Bill everybody recognizes as retroactive legislation. But the gentleman who promoted the Bill before the committee-I am not a member of the committee, but I am informed-denied that this Bill was retroactive legislation, but said that, inasmuch as the words of the Act of 1879 admitted of the possibility of a different construction, therefore to prevent the possibility of a construction which the House had not intended, it was desirable that this Bill should pass. Now, under the view of the Minister of Justice as laid down, it is perfectly clear that this clause, if it passes, will be retroactive legislation. if that be the case, and if the gentlemen before the committee distinctly repudiated that stand but asked to have this clause passed on entirely different grounds, I think we should not be casting any reflection upon the committee if the House, in its wisdom, should send the Bill back to the committee and ask them to consider this important legislation in the light of the opinion of the Minister of Justice which, for the first time, has been made public to-day. When it comes to the question of the word 'profits,' in the notice given in the 'Gazette,' it strikes me that the notice was really no notice at all, because this word 'profits,' as used in the notice, is a new word coined for the occasion. I am not aware of any case in the English language in which the word is used in the sense in which it is used here in section 2. If a person of ordinary English education finds the word 'profits' in a notice of application to parliament, he naturally takes it in the sense in which he has been accustomed to hear it used, and the sense in which any dictionary to which he might refer would authorize its use. It is a common word; we have banks, loan companies, other insurance companies in relation to which the word 'profits' is used. It cannot be a matter of great difficulty to find out what the word means, and I venture to say that the shareholders of any bank, the Bank of Montreal, for example, would be very much surprised to find that the 'profits' of the bank were only a certain small sum after the interest on the capital-and, I suppose, reserve also for that matter, for that is really part of the capital-had been deducted. Surely, the idea is so monstrous that the only way one can account for its being used in the sense in which it is used in this notice is that the individual and the company have become, as it were, synonymous, and so the gentlemen drawing the application for the Bill fail to distinguish between them. But, in law, they are very different indeed, even though these gentlemen may not be aware Mr. NORTHRUP.
of the fact. It is the company that makes profits, and it is not reasonable to speak of the company as making profits apart from its capital. The money is the money of the company; it is not the shareholders' money. When the shareholder pays in his money for his stock, it becomes the company's money. The company goes into business with the money, employs agents and does everything else required in the business, and makes certain profits, including interest on the money paid in, which is the money of the company, not Senator Cox's, or that of any other individual. It does seem to me, in view of the peculiar circumstances, in view of the fact that the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Samuel Sharpe) has pointed out, that there is a very grave doubt as to whether the notice has been sufficient, and in view of the fact that the Minister of Justice had laid down an opinion not before the committee, it is most important that every opportunity should be taken to consider this matter very carefully. Therefore, I have great pleasure in supporting the motion that the committee rise and report progress, and I do so with the hope that when the Bill again comes before the House it will be sent back to the committee to see that justice is done to all parties.

maintopic: INVESTIGATION INTO DEPARTMENT , OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.
speechtext:
May I ask the attention of the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) to the exact language of that portion of the notice which relates to this matter. The words are ' Define the provisions as to division of profits.' I am inclined to go further than when I first brought this to the attention of the committee and to say that that phrase seems to have been very carefully designed to withhold any information as to what was the real character of the legislation contemplated. It would be perfectly easy to give proper notice in a few words. Let us suppose that the gentleman, whoever he may have been, who drafted that notice, had inserted these words, ' providing that policy-holders are not entitled to profits accruing by way of interest earned on paid-up capital.' That would have given notice, with a minimum of language, to every policy-holder throughout Canada. They would have understood exactly what was contemplated by the legislation proposed. But when, instead of that, you have an expression of a very nebulous character in these words, 'defining the provisions as to the division of profits ' it seems to me a not unreasonable inference that there was no desire to give very useful information to the policy-holders throughout the country and in that way to prevent the organization of the policyholders in opposition to the proposal of these gentlemen. I am not discussing the merits of the Bill at present, but I am in-

sisting that reasonable notice to the persons interested ought to be given. And I would point out to the Prime Minister a reason which has been already hinted at, but, perhaps, it has not been emphasized, as to why a notice of this kind in a case such as this ought to be very explicit indeed. The shareholders and directors of life insurance companies, under the conditions which attend the carrying on of that business in this country and in all English speaking countries, are such that the directors and share holders stand in a position of trust towards the policy-holders. They have charge of enormous funds, which they are bound to administer in a certain fiduciary capacity. Now they are entitled to make a profit out of the business; they are bound on the other hand, to do justice to those who have insured their lives and made provision for their families by means of the business so carried on. When the directors of such a company come before the parliament of Canada asking that the business conditions as between themselves and the persons for whom they are trustees, shall be altered-for that is the effect of this Bill-then I say that they ought to be held to the very strictest observance of the rules of this House, and every committee of this House ought to see that the notice given by the persons acting in that fiduciary capacity, is such that there can be no possibility of any misunderstanding. I think that is a reasonable proposition, which ought to commend itself, and will commend itself to the Prime Minister. It is very different from the conditions which meet us in respect of ordinary Bills coming before this House. Here we have the directors of the Canada Life Assurance Comoany, both as share holders in their own interest, and acting as trustees of the interest of 35,000 policy-holders, coming to parliament and asking that the provisions of legislation passed 30 years ago shall be altered in their advantage, and to the detriment of the 35,000 policy-holders; and it seems to me that, without, discussing the provisions of the Bill at all, it is a firm foundation to stand upon that we should insist that the notice of that intention shall be expressed in the plainest possible way.

maintopic: INVESTIGATION INTO DEPARTMENT , OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

I do not feel disposed to quarrel with your decision, Mr. Deputy Speaker. As to the first point taken by the hon. member for North Ontario, taken as a technical objection, I can realize that you are probably right in saying that you could not entertain it. The second point, probably in the same way, though I was not present. But that throws upon us, the members of this committee, the duty of saying whether, under the circumstances as displayed by that notice, we are going on to legislate against the interests of the
policy-holders. Now it is perfectly clear to me that that notice could not convey to the policy-holders an intimation of what it is now proposed we should do. No person reading that notice could possibly gather from it that we proposed to enact retroactive legislation affecting the rights of policy-holders; and because you, Sir, as chairman, have the right to rule it out as a matter of order, does not take away the fact that it goes to the very merits of the matter we are dealing with; and that we, as a committee, and the right hon. gentleman who leads this House, especially, and the Minister of Finance likewise, who is our guide in matters of this kind, should see to it that this legislation should not progress until it is made perfectly clear that everything has been done to bring to the knowledge of the policyholders that their rights are being attacked. I am not prepared to say at this moment what attitude I should ultimately take as to what legislation should be enacted in this ease. I have a strong feeling against this legislation as it is presented to us, yet I am prepared to consider whether it should be ultimately enacted. But I am firm upon this point, that we should one and all unite to say that until every reasonable facility has been afforded the policy-holders of knowing just what these people are asking, we should not, as a high court of parliament, enact this legislation, or proceed further with the Bill.

maintopic: INVESTIGATION INTO DEPARTMENT , OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.
speechtext:
I have just one word to say with reference to this, and it depends almost entirely for the present upon the matter of the notice. Until I heard the notice read by the hon. member for North Ontario the other day, I had not seen it, I had not paid any special attention to it. With reference to what had been the practice by this company, with reference to what had been the practice of other insurance companies in the distribution of their profits as between shareholders and policy-holders I knew pretty well what the general practice was. In that respect I had no great quarrel with this Bill. If it had always been the practice to divide the profits on the basis of a certain reservation, first, as remuneration for the shareholders, if that had been apparently agreed to by both parties, and sanctioned by a practice of twenty years, if that was the practice with other great insurance companies, and if there had been a mistake made at first, even although that practice in 1879 was contemplated, which was afterwards carried out, then I would not have been disposed to give much opposition to the Bill. But there was one thing that I should like to have known then, and one thing upon which I got very little light before the Committee on Bank-

ing and Commerce, that is, as to the views of the other party to the agreement in 1879, because the other party to the agreement was conspicuous by his absence-if you can apply the personal pronoun to the policy-holders. But when I heard the other day the notice that was given, and when I knew it was the essence of the law and the essence of the practice of parliament that the notice to be given should be full and explicit, no matter whether the matter is important or unimportant-although I agree that the matter is greater in proportion as the interests involved are more generally distributed and are of greater importance-I came to realize then that that notice would not have been to me, if I had been a policy-holder in this company, the least intimation in the wide world as to what was going to be done; the place that the notice occupies _ would seem to me to give it no prominence. What are the other things asked for? First, there is to be a change as to date of meeting, and notice as to this change of meeting. Then it goes on to mention a provision as to the division of profits. Then there is a third, extending the powers of the company so that they may hold real estate in Ontario, and for other purposes. I do not know what might be held as a sufficient notice under these words 'and for other purposes', but to me as a policyholder, they would not have any meaning at all, and to my mind they would be -no sufficient notice of a meeting.
However, I want to proceed with the second one, that defining the provisions as to a division of profits. Now do we not all know, those of us who were in the Committee of Banking and Commerce, as well as those of us who are here to-day, that the one important thing these gentlemen wanted in coming to this parliament, was to make a change in the division of profits? The important thing is not that they should change the date of their annual meeting, the important thing was not that they should regulate the form of notice which should be given of meetings, the important 'thing was not extending the power of the company as to the holding of a little real estate in Ontario, but the allimportant thing was as to this arrangement about the division of profits. I want to read the whole of the notice to the Prime Minister so that the relation will be seen.
Notice is hereby given that application will be made to the parliament of the Dominion of Canada at the next session thereof for an Act to amend the Acts relating to the Canada Life Assurance Company by changing the date of the annual meeting, and by making necessary changes as to the notices of meetings consequent thereon, and providing for any further changes in the date of such meeting, defining the provisions as to the division of profits, oxtending the powers of the company as to Mr. FOSTER.
the holding of real estate in Ontario and for other purposes.
That is placed there, not as the main object of this legislation, but it is tucked in quietly and comfortably between two other demands, one as to the dates of meetings and one as to the holding of real estate. It does not have the prominent position that it inevitably and certainly has in the Bill based upon this notice. Suppose I had looked at those words ' defining the provisions as to division of profits,'-what would I have said of it? It could have no other meaning than this :	Here is a company with policyholders and shareholders which is engaged in a business; it requires a certain amount of money to run the business and a certain amount is set aside for reserve and the rest is profits. This meeting is held to define as to how these profits shall be divided. Divided between whom? Between the earning corporation and those who have interests in the corporation. That would be the sole idea that would be brought to my apprehension by reading that notice. I would think of nothing else. But when we read the legislation, what is it? It is not as to the defining of the division of the profits, but it is as to discriminating after the profits have been made between the different parties to the corporation as to how much each should relatively get. That is the* whole gist of the legislation. If it had read 'defining the provisions as to division of profits between the policy-holder and the shareholder', then I wouid have felt that there was something in the provision, which, if I were a policy-holder I would like to know more about, and which, if I were a shareholder, I would like to know more about, and I would say to myself: I am going to see what this is going to be. The notice is altogether insufficient, it seems to me, to express, in the plain use of English words, its meaning, and it would, to me, reading it, and I think to almost every other man, simply imply that, after the year's operations were through, the expenses were paid and the necessary reserve was laid aside, there was a plan to be proposed as to how the resultant profits should be distributed as between the corporation and those who held a special or individual inteiest in the corporation. We should be very careful how we pass legislation of this kind. We should be especially careful that the spirit as well as the form of the law and the rules of the House are thoroughly carried out and that the notice is sufficient. I do not believe that the notice is a sufficient one in this case, and therefore I should rather see it go back to the committee so that they might go into that matter specially. I beg leave again to dissent absolutely from the position taken by the hon. the Minister of Justice that my conscience is

absolved, that my responsibility is done away with as a member of this House, because, forsooth a certain recommendation comes from any committee of this House. Even if I were a member of a committee myself and the committee came to a certain understanding and so reported I would have a perfect right in this House, and my duty is not done as a member of this House unless I exercise that responsibility, to dissent and not hide myself behind the supposition that all has been done that has been necessary and that you must not question the result if, forsooth, the Committee of this House have recommended it by a majority vote. I appeal against any proposition of that kind, and I refuse absolutely to be bound by it. It is our right, as it is our duty to discuss the report of any committee and to feel ourselves absolutely free to dissent from it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: INVESTIGATION INTO DEPARTMENT , OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.
speechtext: As far as I have understood the observations of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat I said altogether the contrary in regard to this committee. I said that I was prepared to rest upon the finding of fact, which I assumed this committee had made, that there was an error, or mistake in 1879.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: INVESTIGATION INTO DEPARTMENT , OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.
speechtext:
It is a well understood rule that where a member has not had an opportunity or when, for any reason, a member fails to make any very close investigation of a private Bill, he accepts the judgment of the committee, not necessarily as a finality, but because the committee has undertaken the work which he perhaps was not able to do. It is only in that sense, I am sure, that any member would urge the principle that the finding of a committee should be accepted. I hesitate not to say that if any member is willing to go to the trouble to look into a Bill for himself and to make a careful investigation of it he is not bound to pay the slightest attention to the judgment of the committee. But with regard to most of these private Bills, it happens that many members, either from disinclination, or occupation in other directions, do not attend the committees and do not give close attention to the details. It is therefore the practice! of the House in such cases to accept the findings of the committee, and I think that as a rule that practice has worked well. Let me say, that the point as to the insufficiency of the notice has perhaps considerable strength. In a matter of such grave importance, affecting the interests of a great financial institution and affecting the interests of a very large body of shareholders and stockholders, there is everything to be gained by proceeding cautiously and slowly. It should not be said that this House is disposed to pass any legislation of this character if the legislation will not bear careful investigation
and critical examination, just as any legislation that we pass should, and I would therefore say to my hon. friend in charge of the Bill that I hope he will accept the suggestion that the Bill be not proceeded with further to-day, but that progress be reported with the view of permitting the Standing Orders Committee to make further inquiry into the question as to the sufficiency of the notice. Speaking entirely for myself, as this is a private Bill which does	not call	for	any	declaration	ofpolicy on the part of the government, I am inclined to think that this Bill is a good one, that it is a Bill that is necessary in the interests of a great number of people. I did not take any part in the	discussion in	the	Committee	of
Banking and Commerce, but I listened very closely to the proceedings. I was particularly impressed by the powerful speech in support of this Bill made by the hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Barker) who, with a full knowledge of all the facts and of the history of the Canada Life Assurance Company, reviewed all the circumstances of the case and gave very powerful reasons why the Bill should pass, reasons which influenced his mind as well as mine. For 30 years it has been the practice of the Canada Life Assurance Company to apply this method of declaring their profits, first to charge interest on their capital and then to strike the balance and distribute the profits accordingly. We have therefore the practice of 30 years of the Canada Life Company which has never been called in question. There must be some statutory limitation in all these things. And, while one may hesitate to adopt legislation which is of a retroactive character, while one may hesitate to adopt legislation which would take away some man's private rights, I say there ought to be some statutory limitation and that if men have slept upon their rights for 30 years they ought not to complain very much if it becomes necessary to confirm a practice which they themselves have acquiesced in.

maintopic: INVESTIGATION INTO DEPARTMENT , OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.
speechtext: What about the policy holder of a year ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: INVESTIGATION INTO DEPARTMENT , OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.
speechtext:
Then there is the next point: that the practice of the Canada Life has been the practice, I am advised, of every other company issuing a participating policy in Canada; it certainly is the practice of the companies generally. I do not know that there are any exceptions, but as a rule the same practice which has been followed by the Canada Life for thirty years is followed by the other companies. That practice has been subject to the inquiry and investigation of the Insurance Department and no question has ever been raised as to the propriety of that method of computing the profits. The third point is that

it is, I am advised, the practice in England, where under precisely similar conditions interest on capital is charged before profits are declared. Now, all these are strong reasons I would say for confirming the practice which has existed for such a long time, and that practice is so well established in the minds of insurance men that in the preparation of the general Insurance Bill which is now before the House that practice has been imported into the Bill, and it is specifically declared that in the computation of profits you shall first charge interest upon capital. That provision in a general Bill will of course not be retroactive ; and of course this special Bill would be necessary to make the provision retroactive.
There is another view: that for many many years the capital of this company was $125,000 and the profits were distributed over that sum. After this practice wdiich has now been called in question had been continued for a very long time, the shareholders put in $875,000 of new capital. I submit that these shareholders in putting in that new capital had a right to expect the continuance of the practice as to the regulation of profits that had been in existence for so many years. And when, a few years ago, they put in $875,000 of new capital with the full expectation that they were to receive interest on that capital before profits were declared, that being the practice of the company from its beginning, then if we are to turn round now and tell them that practice is wrong, the shareholders who put in that new capital are the men who would have the right to be aggrieved. If it be declared that the interest is not to be allowed before profits are declared, then clearly they were induced to invest that $875,000 of new capital in that enterprise upon a misunderstanding, to put it in the mildest form. And if this modern contention, which is only now brought to the front, is to prevail, then surely these gentlemen have a perfect right to say to parliament : let us take back the $875,000 which we invested upon the faith of an understanding which it now appears is wrong, I will put it as strongly as possible and I will say that I think this is retroactive legislation. Taking the opinion of the eminent English counsel which has been published in one of the documents; taking the opinion of the Minister of Justice; taking such information as I can get upon the subject I am inclined to think that while there would be no absolute certainty in the matter-while it may very well admit of a legal dispute and I suppose you can get good lawyers on one side or the other to argue the case-I am rather inclined to think it is retroactive legislation. I am inclined to think *it interferes with rights which policy-holders may have. But, they are rights which the policy-holders neveT knew they possessed, rights which they Mr. FIELDING.
never expected to possess, rights which they are not entitled to possess in equity, and therefore I would say that notwithstanding the fact that it may be retroactive legislation ; nothwithstanding the fact that you will say some action has been raised in court-although I believe that while there is actually no suit in court there may be one at any moment-notwithstanding all that, if we were dealing with the merits of the 'question, I should say that for the prevention of confusion and disorder it would be wise for this parliament to pass this Bill. See what will happen if you do not. Thirty years ago a shareholder in the Canada Life received a larger measure of profits than he was entitled to receive; he is dead; hi3 estate has been closed up; if you want to get the money back how are you going to get it? Take the other side of the argument -thirty years ago a policy-holder received less profits than he was entitled to receive; hedid not get what he was entitled to ; he is dead and his estate is closed up; how are you going to adjust the matter now ; how are you going to get it from the shareholder who is dead; how are you going to find the policy-holder to give him what he should receive? There are possibilities of great disorder and of great trouble. I say there would be no wrong in giving legal effect to the understanding and practice which appear to have existed for thirty years and which every policy-holder of the Canada Life, so far as he knew anything about it at all, accepted. I say there would be no wrong in giving legal enactment to such measures as are necessary to carry out that understanding.

maintopic: INVESTIGATION INTO DEPARTMENT , OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.
speechtext:
In view of the statement of the Minister of Finance that the policy-holders have never raised objection I want to say a word from their point of view. The fact is they never knew they were being improperly dealt with. I have a very strong letter from one who has been with the company for many years and his statement is that the profits he supposed were properly divided until of late years, seemed to dwindle away and could not be accounted for, and he says : I did not object because I did not know but that what I was getting was all that the law entitled me to. I expect that would be the case with practically the 35,000 policy-holders of the company. If they did not raise a claim because they were not getting what was coming to them under the law it was because they were not in a position to know how the division of profits was made and they took it for granted that the division was made according to law by honest men. But now it is brought to their attention and they feel very keenly with regard to it. The next question is as to whether they were or were not deceived. Take

the preamble of the Bill of 1879 and what would any ordinary business man in this country think of this :
The profits allotted are divided amongst the persons assured upon the participation scale; 75 per^ cent of all the profits realized from the entire business.
Would not any business man say that included profits from any source? If the English language means .anything it means that, and if the policy-holder believed he was getting a fair division of all the profits realized from the entire business of the company, then he would naturally come to the conclusion he was getting all he was entitled to. _ The Prime Minister told us that the objection taken did not apply to the clause we are considering; but my answer is that the question of the sufficiency or insufficiency of the notice vitally affects the whole Bill and every clause in it. We would not be doing our duty in my opinion if we proceeded with the consideration of the Bill without knowing whether the notice was sufficient or insufficient, and I believe the only proper course for the committee to take is to report progress and let the House deal with the Bill.

maintopic: INVESTIGATION INTO DEPARTMENT , OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.
speechtext: Though I have charge of this Bill, I have no other interest in it other than that of a policy-holder; so that I am dealing with it in my own interest as such, and I believe that if the construction now sought to be put upon it should prevail, it would virtually ruin the company. It would reduce the dividends of the shareholders from 8 per cent to less than 4 per cent, while the corresponding benefit to the policy-holders would be insignificant. Based on a capital of $125,000 it would not amount to over five cents a year on a $1,000 policy. The interest of the policy-holders is wrapped up in the security of the company; it is of the utmost interest to every policy-holder that the permanency of the company be established. But if you reduce the stock to a basis of less than 4 per cent and compel the shareholders to contribute 90 per cent of their earnings on the stock of the $875,000 as well as the original capital of $125,000, they will get less than one half of one per cent on the capital they put into the company in 1900. It seems so unfair a proposition that I cannot imagine that any policy-holder would seek to put such a construction on the Act.

maintopic: INVESTIGATION INTO DEPARTMENT , OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.
speechtext: Was this an important question when there was only $125,000 of stock paid up? It only became important after the shareholders put in the additional stock?

maintopic: INVESTIGATION INTO DEPARTMENT , OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.
speechtext:
Quite so, because in the one case they would only pay on $125,000, while in the other case they would
pay on the whole $1,000,000. If the interpretation now sought to be put on the Act is right, the shareholders, in paying up the stock of $875,000 in full, were making the company a charitable institution. People may be charitable if they wish to be, but it is not the business of the legislature to compel them to be charitable. It might be that the policy-holders of to-day would get an immediate benefit; but in the ulti mate interest of the policy-holders it would be one of the worst things that could happen for the company to be placed in such a position that the shareholders would not get such a rate of interest on their investment as would induce them to carry on the company. I have no personal interest in this Bill. I told Mr. Bruce, the representative of the company, that I would take charge of it if it were a meritorious and reputable Bill, and he assured me that it was. Whatever hesitation I may have had about it, the more I have studied the question, the more convinced I am that the Act which this House is being called upon to confirm is not only doing justice to the shareholders and preventing a fraud being committed on them, but is in the interest of the policy-holders themselves. Having stated my position a week ago to-day, although it was said that the Minister of Justice had been asked to give an opinion upon the Bill, I understood that it was desired to leave it over in order that it might be further considered, and I immediately acquiesced. Far be it from me to try to force this or any other Bill through the House if it has not had proper consideration. What is the object of the notice ? Notice of a Bill must be given five weeks before it comes up. That is to inform the public that a Bill involving certain questions is to be brought before parliament. That notice, I suppose, is not seen by one out of a thousand of the insured. Very few people ever see the 'Canada Gazette,' and very few read the newspaper advertisements. But the matter becomes known when the Bill is introduced in parliament. Then all the newspapers put the facts, not in their advertising columns, but in their news columns, and the policy-holders and every other class of people find them out.
I have just come from the west, where everybody knows about this Bill, and is talking about it. Although I am not a member of the Committee on Banking and Commerce, I was there one day, and I do not think it is possible to advance any argument here that was not brought up there.
I think the notice was sufficient, and the opinion of a man like Mr. Panet, who has been in charge of that class of work for many years, that it was sufficient, leads me to feel that we are not very far astray in

accepting it as sufficient. However, if members want to further consider the Bill,
I am not going to stand in their way. Though I am a little suspicious that these tactics are obstructive, I am going to give the benefit of the doubt to those who say they want to have further light on the measure, and therefore I am willing that the Bill should stand until next Monday, as I cannot be here again before then. I will therefore move that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again.
Motion agreed to, and progress reported.
House in committee on Bill (No. 79) respecting the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.-Mr. W. McIntyre.

By subsection A of this Bill the Canadian Pacific Railway are asking for authority to build a branch line from Lannigan into Prince Albert, but our people think this branch line comes really under the charter for the Manitoba North Western Railway, which charter is also owned by the Canadian Pacific Railway. The people of Prince Albert are not satisfied to accept the mere promise of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and feel that they should be given some surety that the Canadian Pacific Railway will_ implement its promises. That company should be compelled to build a certain number of miles every year, under penalty of forfeiting its charter. The old Manitoba and North Western Railway was given a charter in 1883, and previous to that a charter was granted to the Portage and Western Road. In the former there was a building clause provided, under which a certain number of miles were to be built each year, and by 1890 the road was to be completed into the town of Yorktown. But this building clause was not carried out, and in 1893 the Canadian Pacific Railway acquired the Manitoba and North Western charter. That charter also carried a provision that at least 20 miles a year should be built until the line was completed into Prince Albert. But this was not done, and the Canadian Pacific Railway repeatedly came to parliament asking for an extension of time, until 1902, when the Canadian Northern were building their line from Dauphin north and west to Prince Albert. The Canadian Pacific then made two surveys over the old proposed line of the Manitoba and North Western, for the purpose of hampering the competing line, but they did not build a mile of that railway. They then came back to this parliament and applied for authority to divert their own line from Shebo west to Saskatoon. And on this occasion, the people of Prince Albert endeavoured to Mr. A. H. CLARKE.
have a clause inserted providing that for each mile of railway built west, there would be one built northwest. This was not accepted by the company, and parliament allowed them a charter to build west. There are people in that section who moved out some 60 or 75 miles expecting this railway to be built because the charter carried a clause requiring so many miles to be built, each year. Many hon. members here will know that Prince Albert district was settled as early as Regina on the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and therefore had the Tight to expect some consideration from the granting of the charter to this Manitoba and North Western Railway.
It was not until the Canadian Northern had purchased the line from Regina to Prince Albert that the Canadian Pacific Railway asked for a charter to build from Lannigan to Prince Albert. This charter was granted, and it was thought by the people of that section that the Canadian Pacific Railway would fulfil this promise because they had been cut off from their connection with the city of Prince Albert, but we find to-dav that they are not prepared to go ahead and build although they have had their charter two years. Instead of doing so, they are again asking for an extension of time. As they have been promising to build the Manitoba and North Western over 16 years, the people of Prince Albert are justified in questioning the sincerity of the company, and are asking that they' should be compelled to give some evidence of good faith by building a certain amount of road each year. The Canadian Pacific Railway have another Bill asking for an extension of time to build the Mam-toba and North Western to Prince Albert I do not think it is possible that they intend building two lines into Prince Albert. It would Tather seem to me as if they wanted to hold the two charters and blanket the two passes available from the south and southeast into Prince Albert through the Birch Hills in ordeT that no competing company may get a charter through those passes. Evidently in 1902 and for some years later, when the Canadian Northern was building branches through the west, they and the Canadian Pacific Railway twere common enemies, but apparently there is to-day an understanding between them to try and cut out the Grand Trunk Pacific and other lines from getting charters to build through these routes. The people out there are compelled to haul their grain long distances and they feel that they should not be asked to take the mere promises of this railway any longeT without insisting on some guarantee. I therefore beg to move as a subsection to clause one that the company-, build 30 miles in 1909 and 30 miles each year until the road is completed.
