I do not know that I could do better at this stage than give to the House statements from individuals and reports showing the benefits that are possible from accurate topographical surveys. I desire to give to the House first a statement made by President Van Hise, of the University of Michigan, and which is, I think, a very practical illustration. He says:
A railroad company owned two lines in northern Michigan and Wisconsin which they wished to connect by a branch some forty miles in length. The country was unknown between the two lines. Under my direction topographical, geological and timber maps were made of about twelve hundred square miles, at a cost of about $35,000. After these maps were made the line was laid down in the office with a beautiful grade, and with the best location possible with reference to iron ore and timber. One of the features of the line was that it crossed a bold trap range which was supposed to be impossible to cross except at great expense, by finding gaps through it. This line crossed the branch of another railroad about twelve miles long, which because it went around the end of this trap range, when the gap was directly in front of it, was at least two miles longer than was necessary. These two additional miles of road cost fully as much as the entire survey of the twelve hundred square miles.
It is my profound conviction if topographical surveys were made of broad zones where it is expected to project railroads through forested country, that many times the cost of the survey would he saved in the construction of the railroads, besides getting a better location both as to resources and to grade than is possible by the random methods employed at the present time for the locating of railroads in rough forested country.
In answer to a question asked by the member for Cumberland a few weeks ago the Minister of Railways stated as to a recent survey for a projected diversion of the Intercolonial Railway, completed only about two months ago, that the cost thereof was $9,914.05. The greater portion of this amount might doubtless have been saved had that section of an old province like Nova Scotia been properly surveyed in the past. The statement has been made by General Francis A. Walker that:
If the state of Massachusetts had had a good topographical map in 1863, some $20,000,000 would probably have been saved in its public railway expenditure.
The area of the state of Massachusetts being 8,315 square miles, this saving would amount to over $2,400 per square mile. The topographical survey of the state has cost $13 per square mile. Dr. Frank D. Adams in a recent paper read before the Canadian Mr. A. K. MACLEAN.
Institute quotes from a letter from Dr. C. D. Walcott, lately director of the United States Geological Survey, as follows:
Such maps
-those iof the the United States Geological Survey

-are as essential to the proper development of all the resources of a state. We have reached the point where officials of railroads, of trolley lines, those interested in highway improvements and in the development of city water supplies and sanitary measures as in general engineering work, do not think of spending one dollar on field surveys until they have first procured from this office the topographic maps and the records of levels run in connection therewith. We are in daily receipt of testimonials showing the sums of money and the time saved in connection with all preliminary and also of some location survevs for such enterprises. Above all, however, is the topographic map, an essential to the study, along modern lines and by best methods, of the mineral resources of a region. The old descriptive methods of discussing the geology of a district have long been abandoned in this country. It has been found that every dollar expended in preparing a mathematically correct base map upon which to map the geologic formations for strikes and dip and from which to oonstruot structural sections, is returned many-fold in the value and accuracy of the resulting studies of the geologic formations and their economic possibilities. A good topographical map is just as essential a frame work upon which is to reproduce a facsimile of the underlying geology, as is the steel frame which modern architects use for, and support a masonry building of modern design.
I might give to the House many other statements and reports upon the urgent necessity of a trigonometrical survey of the Dominion, but it appears to be unnecessary to extend those already given. Now, I think this is an important matter and I believe a geodetic survey should be commenced as early as possible and that some work, even though but little, be performed each year. I believe also that this work should be carried on by a new departmental branch to be established, and not by one of the existing departments. This branch might be officered by the deputy heads of the departments now carrying on survey _ work. However this is but a matter of detail, and after all, is secondary to the main idea of a geodetic survey. I trust the government will see fit to take this matter into consider ation and adopt at an early date a policy which will ensure the commencement of an accurate survey of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. FRANK OLIVER (Minister of the Interior).
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is no question as to the importance of the survey work carried on from time to time in this country, as any one may judge from a glance at the estimates or at the Auditor General's Report. It is a necessity in the development of our

country, and it is right that the fullest, attention should be given to the matter. I am glad that my hon. friend has brought this matter before the House. I can hardly allow the motion to pass, however, without giving some information, and the views I hold based upon that information, which views are not altogether in accord with those my hon. friend has expressed. There is no doubt that the great feature of a survey is that it should be accurate, and that the various surveys should be properly related to each other. If it were possible that there should be a geodetic survey of the Dominion of Canada in advance of all other surveys, it certainly would be in the end a measure of economy, and would undoubtedly secure an accuracy that is not at present possible. But I need hardly suggest to the House that when it costs so much money as it does to keep within measurable distance of the actual survey requirements of the country as it progresses, the task of keeping ahead of the requirements with a geodetic survey would cost a sum beyond which I think the country could afford, or that parliament would sanction. If it were possible to keep in advance of settlement, in advance of railway construction, in advance of geological investigation, by a geodetic survey, still I do not think it would be advisable for the government to enter upon the enterprise, unless we assume that the country is made for the surveys and not the surveys for the country. A railroad survey is necessary because, for one reason or another, it is in the public interest that a railroad should be built, although there may have been no other reason for survey in the locality traversed by that railroad. It is desirable that there should be geological exploration, which should only be limited by the extreme bounds of our country; it is desirable that there should be lands laid out for settlement, well in advance of settlement, so that pioneers may have security in their holdings. But it would not be well that all these enterprises should have to wait until an accurate survey had been made in that part of the country where it was required for these various purposes. The theory that my hon. friend has expressed is an excellent theory, and no doubt it would work well if Canada were an island or a small and fertile country. But Canada being so extensive, the conclusion to which I am forced to come is that the proposition is not a practicable one, is not a business proposition, is not within the resources of the country, and would be greatly to the disadvantage of the country if it were undertaken. I speak however of a geodetic survey made in advance of the actual requirements, which is the ideal condition that my
hon. friend has suggested. But a geodetic survey that will follow these requirements which I have mentioned, that would check up and bring into their proper relationship the surveys already made, is another matter. It is not as theoretically sound, but it is much more sound practically. It is within reach, it is possible and it is not only being undertaken but it has made very substantial progress. The representations which my hon. friend has mentioned were made to the government some years ago have been dealt with, have been acted on to a certain extent; and the astronomical surveys branch of the Department of the Interior, some two or three years ago, took up the subject of the making of a geodetic survey of Canada, beginning in those parts which were already settled, where surveys for settlement, or railways and roads had already been made. These surveys were not in themselves accurate and it was thought necessary and desirable that they should be established in their proper relationship to each other. In pursuance of that work parliament has voted, from year to year, a considerable amount of money and is being asked to vote $50,000 for it during the present session. The work of the geodetic survey has been in progress, has covered a very considerable portion of the better settled^portions of Ontario, and is also in progress in the St. Lawrence valley in the province of Quebec. A number of members of the House have, from time to time, inquired as to the purpose and meaning of certain wooden towers which they have seen in different parts of the country. These towers are in connection with the geodetic survey and it may relieve the minds of hon. members of the House to know that they are not for any more harmful purpose than merely to establish the proper relationship of different points on the different surveys to the parts of the country in which they are situated.
Are they all wooden towers or are some of them iron?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think they are wooden. They are for the purpose of observation. The work has been undertaken, has made good progress and so long as parliament is willing to pay for the work so long can it be continued. There is no difference of opinion between myself and my hon. friend as to the desirability of a geodetic survey, but what I want to place before the House i3 the difference between a theoretically desirable geodetic survey which shall be in advance of all other surveys and a practical geodetic survey which shall, as circumstances admit, follow upon the surveys already made for the various purposes for which surveys are necessary. It is true that there may be to some extent a duplica-

tion of work in the surveys which have been made. That is only to a very limited degree. The survey which is required in the western country for the allotment of settlers and the surveys which were required in this country in the early days for the allotment of settlers do not interfere with or duplicate the surveys necessarily made for the construction of railways or in geological investigations. There may be instances where the work overlaps but these instances are of very trifling moment. The main point is that the need of the country, as it is at the moment and in the places in which it exists, is met as at present without delay, or with) the least possible delay and that, I submit is the object and purpose of any system of surveys. The absolute accuracy that is secured by the geodetic survey is something we can wait for until we can afford it, but we cannot afford to wait for it in pushing settlement and enterprise throughout the vast extent of this stupendous country. A geodetic survey of Belgium, or the state of Massachusetts, or of Ireland even, is one thing; a geodetic survey of the Dominion of Canada is quite another thing. Even a geodetic survey of the United States with its population of eighty millions and its stupendous revenue is quite a different thing from a geodetic survey of the Dominion of Canada with its population and revenue.
What progress has been made in the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have no idea.

Mr. Speaker, this is a very important subject and one that the House should not dismiss hastily. I very heartily agree with the remarks made by the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Maclean). The hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) who has just sat down, unfortunately, does not seem to grasp the basic idea of, the remarks of the hon. member for Lunenburg. He seems to think that a geodetical or a topographical survey is a theoretical survey and that th? only practical survey is the method at present in vogue by his department in laying out town lots, farm lands and work of that character. Let me assure him that as far as practical work is concerned the most accurate method is that which conforms to the requirements of the triangulation and topographical survey, and that the theoretical and purely nebulous idea is the idea at present in vogue of having surveys made without having any fixed point and without showing any topographical features. It is well known that in every country in modern Europe and in the United States there is a topographical and geodetic survey. The hon. member for Lunenburg has explained very clearly the difference between the present system Mr. OLIVER.
of surveying and a geodetic survey. Let me point out here that a geodetic survey commences first with the measurement of a known base. This base is measured with very accurate instruments and the error in a mile would not amount to the thousandth part of an inch. Taking a point say at McGill university,-a mile would be measured and from that the whole country would be triangulated and measured within the thousandth part of an inch. This work should be done, if it is to be done by , us, with exceeding accuracy. The United States government undertook a survey of this description of the great lakes and I noticed by reference to some of the correspondence of the ' Waterways Commission, that the survey of the great lakes has proven to be false in many respects because there was a slight error, possibly when they began, which, of course, increased into a vast error when the large number of angles were triangulated and closed up. Of course, the triangulation of the country in connection writh a geodetic survey could be very rapidly done and could be completed from coast to coast possibly within three or four years. Following that comes the topographical survey which radiates from the points fixed by the triangulation. I know a little about the subject and I may therefore be excused if I deal with it briefly.
The Department of Militia and Defence has already had a number of these topographical surveys made and I must say they are admirable so far as they go. Now, suppose the surveyors of farm lands throughout Canada were compelled to insert the topographical features necessary for a military map, the added cost would not be 25 per cent over the present cost and the work would be done at once and finished for all time. We were told by the Minister of Militia that the great general staff system of England is to be adopted in Canada. In every country in Europe one of the functions of the great general staff is to carry out an accurate topographical survey of the whole country. Nobody can doubt that at present there is an enormous waste in the making of surveys under our system. Even in the older sections we have surveyors privately employed in every township and their work is never finished because if they require to draw a second line after having drawn a first, there is no map and the work has to be done over again. We have also, under one department of government, the surveying of land into sections and quarter-sections, and that survey could just as well be conducted on the lines of a topographical survey in the first place. To do this it would need only the addition of one or two extra men to the surveyor's staff, because experience has shown that one square mile per day can be done by two men with such

a degree of accuracy that in no place will the work be out more than a foot or two at any particular point. Compared with the geological maps of the United States, our geological maps are but a laughing stock and as the attempts of school children. The railroads of the country do a great deal of topographical work, but the government of the country does not benefit by that at all. Then, the provincial governments are constantly spending money in making surveys and the existing system does not enable these to be available to the general advantage of the people of the country. We should understand, however, that a great many of the old surveyors are entirely opposed to a topographical survey because their system compared with the system which obtains in the best and most modern surveys is as different as night from day. They work with a chain, a field book, and a theodolite, but the modern system adopted in other countries is to do this work by the plain table method. Not one out of five of the old surveyors, good men as they are, understand anything about topographical work, using what is known as clinometer and prismatic compass and running various section lines over a square mile of territory, sketching the under features on a small portable drawing board as they go along. That is the military system of surveying, and it is as far in advance of the old method as the modern trolley car is ahead of an oxcart. In the United States the engineering and surveying work is under the control of the war department, but in Canada almost every department of government has its engineering staff and at the present time we have the Public Works Department conducting a survey of the Niagara Peninsula to ascertain the best place to run the Welland canal, when at the same time we have an excellent map, prepared by the Militia Department, which would give the Public Works Department in fifteen minutes all the information required without going to extra expense. Here is an instance of duplication. If we are going to adopt the methods which have been found satisfactory in England and other countries we must group all our engineering staff under one department and that one department should be the Department of Militia and Defence. I say this with a good deal of diffidence, because of my being associated to some extent with the militia of Canada, but it is a fact that in the United States the geological survey and other surveys and all public works are carried out under the supervision of the war department, and with possibly one or two exceptions the records of the Uuited States for the last twenty years have shown nothing dishonourable in connection with contracts, and the contractors have had to live up to their agreements, because the men in charge of the engin-97
eering work were men of as high honour as could be found in any service in the world. We have in Canada the Royal Military College, which is educating the very men best fitted for this kind of work. The Minister of Militia will agree with me that every graduate of the Rcyal Military College must be a thorough topographical surveyor as well as an ordinary surveyor. If all the surveying and engineering work of the government were grouped into one bureau, then the various departments of the government could submit their proposals to that bureau, the engineering work could be done by it; and we would avoid the duplication of effort which we have at the present time, and I believe several millions of dollars per annum could be saved to the country. I submit that this board which has been referred to should be made a section of the general staff and we should in its initiation include among its members the very ablest engineers and surveyors in the country. Any one who looks at the German maps will see that they are done in two colours, black and white, and you can tell from a glance at them where every vineyard, every stable, every house, every elevation or under feature of the ground is located. As has been pointed out in the statement of Professor Van Hise, the cost of this work is trifling, and when once it is done it is final. If you want to find out anything about the topography of the country you will not have to send a band of surveyors to run lines or go on a voyage of discovery; any engineer can take a map of that kind and ascertain where a railway or a street car line or a canal should be located and all that remains to be done in any engineering scheme is to put down the posts in the places marked on that map.	.
This is a subject which I think this House should take into its very serious consideration, because it is not wise for us at enormous expense to commence adding additional boards or commissions or departments of work. Would it not be better to have more centralization of this work and to have it under a competent head ? I know I am advancing revolutionary sentiments, so far as the ministers in certain departments are concerned; but ministers in charge of departments carrying on public works must realize that this is the way work of this kind is done in the mother country, to whose experience we constantly anpeal for the best methods. The Minister of the Interior says that this system would tend to make the country for the surveyors rather than the surveys for the country. I claim that it would not. Any engineer who understands topographical surveying will testify that the additional cost, for instance of laying out a country in the northwest by a complete topographical survey



would not be more than 25 or 30 per cent. The only additional cost would be in having a department where the maps would be accurately defined on copper plates, and the plates would be kept in a safe place, so that if at any time additional maps were required, the plates could be taken and the maps printed from them. I understand that the Waterways and Boundary Commission are adopting that method for the lake surveys. A department has been established in Buffalo where all the work of their engineers is transferred to copper plates, so that it will form a permanent record. I think this House cannot do better than adopt the resolution, or at least the sentiments, of my hon. friend from Lunenburg. The hon. Minister of Militia is doing excellent work in this direction; and though his colleagues may think that he is throwing away good money in having topographical maps provided, I think that he who understands the matter will assure this House that for the defence of the country alone it is a wise expenditure of money. It is only within the last year that we have had any topographical maps of this country which would enable officers not acquainted locally with the country, even in the older sections, to find their way. An officer who understands the reading of such a map and knows its scale, can fix his position on the map in two minutes, and if ordered to march twenty or thirty miles to a given point, he could, by means of his compass, find the direction in which to go; and, even if he had to pass through forests and ravines, he could come within a few feet of the very spot to which he was required to go. I would like very much to hear from the Minister of Militia on this question, in view of the fact that we have now pledged ourselves as a country to accept the staff system adopted by England; and it should be our desire to carry out that svstem faithfully by establishing' a department for carrying out both topographical and geodetic surveys.

Mr. Speaker, being in an agreeable mood to-night I am disposed to agree to a great extent with the gentlemen who have preceded me. We had a scientific survey, topographical and geodetic, started in this country in 1876, in Mr. Mackenzie's time. That survey was carried on in the western country for three or four years, and was then abandoned; but provision was made in the Surveys Act under which men were to be qualified and known as Dominion topographical surveyors. I have devoted considerable study to that branch of my profession. There are two interests to be served in connection with surveys, the commercial and the scientific. While I agree with the mover of this resolution that it is very desirable to get a scientific survey started, I Mr. J. A. CUREIE.
must at the same time admit the position taken by the Minister of the Interior that our great work is to get the country settled and to make the necessary surveys for that purpose. One criticism which I have to offer in regard to the move made by the government in collecting information is this, that it placed the matter in the hands of the officials of the various branches. While I have nothing to say against those gentlemen, while they are very able men, I feel that there must always be a certain amount of jealousy between the different branches. Under these circumstances it is desirable, if you are going to appoint a commission to investigate the question of a scientific survey, to go outside of your own officials. For my part, I would like to see a commission appointed by the government to investigate the methods in use in the United States, in France and in other countries, and to prepare Canada to take up a geodetic survey on the very best and broadest lines. I see no harm in that; I think it is a good move. I want to draw the minister's attention to the fact that in our western country we have a treeless area of from 50,000,000 to 70,000,000 acres. We have streams there running from the mountains and discharging into Hudson bay at from 200 to 300 feet below the level of the prairie. We have a soil largely clay, through which there is practically no percolation, so that it is almost impossible for people to get water in springs; and I take the position that any country where that is the case must be pronounced largely semi-arid in its character. I am not going to mention any particular localities; but if you examine the meterological returns covering fifteen or sixteen years, you will find many settlements where there is not on the average more than nine or ten inches of rainfall in the year. In this district near the Ottawa river, the water is carried near the surface, and the character of the soil is such that the water percolates through it, and in addition there is a very heavy rainfall. If nine or ten or eleven inches of annual rainfall is sufficient for crops, and if we are going to put an immense population into that western country, we shall have to have some system of water distribution. We cannot depend on the rainfall to secure for a very large population sufficient water both for domestic purposes and to supply the necessary moisture for crops. That in my opinion is a serious question, one that concerns every member of this House; because if there is any ground for my fears, we want to get busy, and get busy very quickly to see what we can do to help the people of our western country in this matter.
The mover of this resolution referred to Dr. Walcott and the work of the geological survey of the United States. That work was taken up some 15 or 20 years ago. In addition to taking thorough measurement of the

various streams, they also established contour lines throughout the country. The work is done at very reasonable cost, but it takes a series of at least 15 years for any scientific investigation to get with any reasonable accuracy what that water service is going to amount to, and the sooner we start that work on good broad lines the better. Take the river that passes our door, that river has been changing the last ten years or more. If we had been measuring that stream during all those years, we would have been notified by those measurements of certain things transpiring within the drainage area of that stream, and the same remark applies throughout the whole country. Our waters are the most valuable asset our countrv possesses and the sooner we get to work to obtain better measurements of our various streams the better. This is a matter which I commend to the hon. the Minister of the Interior for his most serious consideration. T?i the estimates there is a sum of about $10,000 for that purpose, but that is not sufficient. I spoke of this to the former Minister of the Interior a few months before he retired (Mr. Sifton), and he told me he would endeavour to put $20,000 in the estimates for that kind of work.. We need a great deal more than that to do the work properly. The commercial end we must look after, and the scientific end will follow. Take the west, where we have these irrigation companies, we ought to have certain surveys made there. Let me mention one case for the benefit of the Minister of the Interior. We ought to have a survey made from the Old Man river to see if it is not possible to carry water from it into the district in between the Little Bow river and the Belly river, for the purpose of running small creeks through the country to supply domestic needs.
I had no idea this matter was coming up to-night, or I would have been prepared to go into it to a much greater extent, but I should think it would be only necessary to draw the attention of the Minister of the Interior to the work for him to see its necessity. I want to get from under the load if there ever should he a time in the prairies when the people will not find sufficient water for their necessities. The matter is one of most serious import to that country, and I most sincerely trust the hon. Minister of the Interior will take the same view of it.

We are very much indebted to the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Maclean) for having brought this matter up and also the	hon. member	for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) for the very able manner in which he seconded the motion. We are much indebted to these gentlemen for the very clear way in which the question 97 i
has been discussed and the very valuable information vouchsafed to the House. I did not intend saying anything but since the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) has appealed to me, I feel it would be only courteous that I did say a word or two, particularly as I have had something to do in a small way with certain surveys which he has been good enough to characterize as excellent and which, I am happy to know, have been appreciated throughout the country. I do not intend to enter upon a discussion of any controversial character. It is a matter of little consequence to me whether the surveys are carried out by the Militia Department or by the Department of the Interior, so long as an accurate survey is undertaken promptly, and I am glad to hear from my hon. colleague the Minister of the Interior that such a survey is actually being carried out. In the United States, as my hon. friends from North Simcoe and Lunenburg have observed, these surveys, and in fact all engineering work, are absolutely under the control of the war office, and after the experience of a century the system has been found to work amirably. As the hon. member for North Simcoe, (Mr. Currie) has said, in not more than one or two cases has the good faith of the engineers in the United States, connected with public works, ever been questioned in the slightest degree. It seems to me to be reasonable too that if in a peaceful country such as the United States has generally been, and in Canada such as we hope it will always be, it is necessary to maintain a military force and an engineering branch in connection with that force, it is very desirable that some important work should be given to that engineering staff. In the United States the engineering staff has been engaged in work of this kind. I think it would be desirable, in view of the class of men we have now in the engineering branch of the) Canadian militia, that some work of this kind should be given them, and we have undertaken to do mapping work and surveys for the defence purposes of those portions of the Dominion of which an accurate knowledge of the topography is absolutely necessary if we are to know anything about the means of defending the country in the event of an attack being made.
As to how quickly this work shall be done that is a question, as my hon. colleague has pointed out, very largely of money, and I did not understand him to say that he in any way objected to carrying on a geodetic survey or a triangulation of the whole Dominion except from the point of view of the very great expense, and his

view is that it should be done gradually and that the surveys already carried out should be co-related for future use, I should hope that the report moved for will be brought down and printed and that every hon. member will carefully read it, and that parliament will be ready to vote to my hon. colleague the necessary sum to enable this geodetic survey and triangulation to be carried out in the most rapid manner possible, which very likely would not take, at the most, more than ten years.
My hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. A. K. Maclean) has quoted the statement of a very prominent gentleman of Massachusetts, a statement which I have read myself, to the effect that if there had been a geodetic survey of the state of Massachusetts fifty or sixty years ago, millions upon millions of dollars would have been saved to the state in the construction of railways and other public works. The same thing would be true of this country. Fortunately for Canada, the country has only begun to be settled, and it will be possible, I hope, to have the advantage of a geodetic survey in many portions of the country before the construction of railways is extensively undertaken. The papers moved for, I believe, are under control of the Militia Department. I shall have pleasure in having them brought down, if this motion is carried, almost immediately.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the discussion on the motion of the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. A. K. Maclean). I think that surveys of this nature, so far as this country is concerned, have been perhaps too much a matter of secrecy; the public generally have not had the advantage of the information contained in those surveys. I think we differ somewhat from the Americans in that respect. There is not the slightest doubt about the benefit to the public in the United States from the topographical maps. For one thing, they have saved a great deal of expense to the agriculturists of that country in the carrying out of drainage works. The federal government has undertaken the reclamation of large areas of swamp land, and these surveys have been very valuable to the people interested in that matter. I think they estimate something like 73,000,000 acres of swamp lands to be reclaimed east of the Rocky mountains, and these maps which have been issued to the public have been used largely with a view to assisting the agriculturists .in that respect. It seems to me that, under whatever department these surveys may be made, they ought to first take up the country that is more thickly settled, and where the information would be of greater interest to the public than in the outlying district. I can quite understand the force of what the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) says in reference to Sir FREDERICK BORDEN.
the expense. In a new country like this, we have to do a good many things in the rough, so to speak, because we must keep in advance of the immediate requirements of the people and the development of the country. The relation that these surveys may have to commercial enterprises is manifest, and I think that if they were taken up with a view to assisting in these as well as in military work, it would be greatly to the advantage of the people in the more rapid development of the country.

I listened with a great deal of attention and interest to the very instructive speech of the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. A. K. Maclean) and I entirely agree that he is entitled to the thanks of the House for having brought a matter of so much importance to our attention. The subject was mentioned to me, I think about a year and a half ago, by Professor McLeod, of McGill, the professor in charge of this work in that great university. I was very muck impressed with the view which he then urged, and on that account I have listened to the debate this evening with all the greater interest. I appreciate what has been said by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver). We cannot expect settlement or mining development or any other of the great enterprises of this country, to wait until we have had a thoroughly scientific survey. That goes without saying; it is hardly necessary to urge it. I did not understand that the hon. member for Lunenburg did urge it. But he did urge the very great importance of having a thoroughly scientific and accurate survey undertaken and carried out as rapidly as might reasonably be expected, having regard to the undoubtedly very great cost of work of that kind. The minister tells us that the work had been undertaken and has already made considerable progress. I should have been very glad indeed if he could have given to us a little more information as to the progress made, but that, perhaps, will be disclosed in the documents moved for by the hon. member for Lunenburg. The Civil Service Commission of 1907 pointed out in their report, if my memory serves me correctly, that a good deal of work in surveying by the different departments was duplicated, or perhaps, done three or four times by different departments. My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior does not seem to attach very much importance to that. But, possibly, there is more waste of that kind than one would gather from the hon. gentleman's speech this evening. Of course, we should all think it highly desirable that duplication of work in that way should be avoided, that the departments should co-ordinate to work a little more. I suppose there is always a certain amount of red tape wherever there are departments.

I remember my surprise some years ago on being told by a certain minister of the Crown of that day that his department had been obliged to pay demurrage for, I think, about ten days, while another department of the government was making up its mind whether it could use the wharf of that department. In the meantime, the public money was being paid over to the owner of a steamship with certain commodities aboard designed for the use of one of the departments. This friction and red tape as between the departments, should be put on one side, and these surveys should be carried on, as much as possible, without duplication of work. I do not know how far this work has progressed in the United States. They have been at work for many years. I should have been glad of information from the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) or the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden) on that point and also on the question how much these may expect to accomplish in ten or fifteen years. We have not received much information on that point. Perhaps it also will be disclosed in the papers brought down. I understand that the military surveys which have been referred to by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. J. A. Currie) and the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden) are topographical and not geodetic. Passing from that for a moment, let me draw attention to the necessity of emphasizing the views put forward by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Ma-grath). I am not nearly so familiar with conditions in the west as is that hon. gentleman or the Minister of the Interior, but I have been through the west on three or four occasions and have every reason to believe that settlement there is being retarded at the present time by the lack, in certain portions of that country, of water necessary for domestic use. The hon. member for Medicine Hat has pointed out the necessity of an accurate survey, especially in the west, of our water supply, * 1 *1' is water supply not only for purposes oi irrigation, but for domestic use.
He intended to point out, as he has just now observed to me, the importance of some scheme by which the abundant supply of water flowing from the mountains through the great regions of the west which might be regarded as semi-arid, could be utilized to a greater extent than it has been utilized for domestic use, and he is under the impression that that could be done, by a series of creeks or channels which would forward settlement very much in some of the regions where settlement has hitherto, been difficult, and in that way give to the people of that western country a supply of water for domestic purposes which has been lacking to a great extent. When I was in the west about five years ago I was approached by the inhabitants of two or three different communities, who told me that they had
been sinking artesian wells in various places to a great depth, but had not been able to secure water, and that some intervention or assistance from the government was absolutely necessary if those communities were to continue. It may be that in the particular instances which I have now in mind some relief has since been found, but there is no doubt whatever that this is a very serious matter in some portions of the west, and that it deserves the consideration of the government and of this parliament. I would only say in conclusion that while I thoroughly appreciate the attitude of the Minister of the Interior as to the necessity that great enterprises of settlement should go on without waiting for a scientific survey, still I am of the opinion advocated by my hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Maclean) that an accurate scientific survey such as has been carried on, or is now in a very far advanced stage, in every civilized nation of the world, should be carried on in this country as well, and that a reasonable amount of the revenues of the country should be yearly diverted to this purpose in order that we may not be behind other great nations in this regard.
Motion agreed to.

subtopic: DIVERSION OF THE WATERS OF THE ALLEGASH RIVER.

speechtext:
Mr. PIUS MICHAUD' (Victoria, N.B.) moved for
Copy of all corespondence and reports between the United States and the Dominion governments respecting the diversion of the waters of the Allegash river, a tributary of the St. John river.
He said: I desire to submit to the House a few remarks in support of this motion. We see in volume 1 of the United States statutes, under the heading 'Constitution of the United States,' that the constitution and the laws of the United States made in pursuance hereto, and all treaties made and to be made with other countries, including those with respect to boundaries between Canada and the United States, are to be regarded as the supreme law of the United States, and every state in the union is bound thereby, notwithstanding any legislation it may pass. By the Ashburton treaty, the River St. John, which is 450 miles in length, taking its source in the state of Maine and in the province of Quebec, was made the international boundary between the United States and the province of New Brunswick, at a certain point where the said state borders opposite Madctwaska county. By this treaty it was provided that in order to encourage and promote industry of the inhabitants living in the state fo Maine, or the province of New Brunswick, the waters of the River St. John and its tributaries, be free for the transportation of the products of

the forest and of agriculture. Now, Mr. Speaker, I desire to state that by the provisions of that treaty all lumber cut at the head waters of the St. John river was to be free to float down to the mouth of said river at St. John, on the Bay of Fundy. The Allegash river is a tributary of the St. John river, and is entirely within the state of Maine. In 1841, a year previous to the Ashburton treaty, an application was made for the purpose of cutting a canal between Lake Chamberlin and one of the branches of the Penobscot river. We find that this application was refused, for several reasons. In 1846 a company known as the Lake Telos and Webster Pond Log and Sluiceway Company was chartered by the legislature of the state of Maine, and was authorized to cut a canal between Lake Churchill and one of the branches of the Penobscot river. I desire to explain that the River Allegash takes its source in Lake Churchill, Lake Chamberlin and Lake Heron and a few other lakes. In 1874, another application was made for authorization to build a dam at the foot of Lake Churchill in order to divert the waters of the Allegash river into a branch of the Penobscot river, and prevent the lumbermen on the River St. John from enjoying the benefit they had derived from the waters of that river. Under the authority expressed or implied in this Act, the lumbermen of the state of Maine cut the canal and diverted practically part of the waters of the Allegash river into a river of their own. In 1903 our American friends were not satisfied with having diverted the waters of that river to their own use, and they made another application to the legislature of the state of Maine for authorization to build the dam a litle. higher in order to secure still greater advantages. The people of the province of New Brunswick at that time were aware of what was going on, and they hired a lawyer and sent him over to Augusta, the capital of Maine, to oppose that legislation.
1 am sorry to say that the legislature granted the application and consequently further authority was given to build dams, to cut canals and to divert more water from these lakes and from the Allegash river. What is the result of diverting that water from the St. John river? The lumbermen in the northern part of the province of New Brunswick are suffering every year. The lumber is driven down in the early part of the season passing the point at which Allegash river falls into the St. John river. In the beginning of June the water of the St. John river is lowered and a large quantity of lumber driven down from the headquarters of St. John is held back and part of it remains along the shore of the St. John river all summer. We know as a matter of fact that when a log remains exposed to the weather and the heat of the Mr. MICHAUD.
sun all summer its value, when it is manufactured into deals and boards the following season, is found to have decreased by probably one third. This is a great loss to the lumbermen of St. John and along the St. John river. This is a matter that I think should be brought prominently before the parliament of this country. We have tolerated the course of our friends in the state of Maine for years but I think the time has arrived when we should take steps to put an end to this grievance. We have now to submit our grievance to a commission and I am glad to say that the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugs-ley) has seen fit to look into the matter very closely and that a commission has been appointed to deal with it. The commissioners, I understand are about to commence their investigation in connection with the troubles which now exist between the lumbermen in the state of Maine and those in the province of New Brunswick. The treaty lays it down most distinctly that the interests connected with the St. John river should be protected. It is a matter of surprise to know that on different occasions the state of Maine has passed a law authorizing people in that state to cut canals, build dams, and divert the water of the Allegash river into the Penobscot. The laws under which treaties are made are called the supreme laws of the land. I cannot understand how the government, the legislature and the senators of the state of Maine should have passed laws at direct variance with the provisions of this treaty. We cannot help feeling very deeply the injury done to our industries by not abiding by this treaty. We have felt the insult to our honour as Canadians and British subjects. The treaty has not been carried out to the letter as it should have been by our friends. Since they call every treaty made under their institutions the supreme law of the land they should be the first to observe it. I hope the commission already appointed will take this matter into their serious consideration. I hope they will not only inquire into the trouble which now exists between the two countries but that they will go farther and ascertain the damage which our people have suffered for forty or fifty years by the diversion of the water of the Allegash river into one of their own rivers.

speakeroldname: Hon. WM. PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).
subtopic: DIVERSION OF THE WATERS OF THE ALLEGASH RIVER.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question which my hon. friend (Mr. Michaud) has brought to the attention of the House is certainly one of verv great importance not only to the people of the province of New Brunswick who are engaged in lumbering operations upon the St. John river, but also to a considerable section of the inhabitants of the state of Maine, who are also carrying on lumbering and business

operations on the river and who are equally interested with the people of New Brunswick in seeing that the navigation of the river is preserved. This diversion of the waters of the Alleeash from the river St. John into the Penobscot took place a great many years ago and, as my hon. friend has so well stated, it has been the cause of a great deal of dissatisfaction on the part of the people living on the St. John river, and it has led to very serious difficulty on several occasions, and, I think, I am safe in saying that upon more than one occasion it has almost led to bloodshed. Our people have felt that those who have acted under the authority of the legislature of the state of Maine have acted in disregard of those national obligations which the people of that country ought to observe towards the people of a friendly nation. While I was a member of the government of the province of New Brunswick I was the medium through which his honour the Lieutenant Governor was recommended to have a communication sent to the British ambassador in the hope of inducing, the United States government to intervene and to prevent this diversion of which our people complain. The protests were sent forward by this government in the ordinary way and through the ordinary channels, but, unfortunately, they have not so far resulted in the grievancei being remedied.	Of course,	one difficulty under which our people have suffered is that we can have no redress in the courts, because, if we were to proceed in the courts of the state of Maine, our people would be met by the fact that there has	been	passed	a	statute	ofthe legislature of the state of Maine authorizing	the	company	to	which	myhon. friend	has	referred	to	divert	the
waters in the manner which has been complained of. Therefore, it would seem as if the only recourse we could have is through diplomatic correspondence in the hone of inducing the government of the United States to take such action as may bring about a discontinuance of the interference with the navigation of the St. John river. I am happy to say that I believe, that, as a result of the feeling to which expression has been given by the government of the United States in agreeing to the waterways treaty and also in agreeing to the commission to consider the obstruction to the St. John river, there is apparent a desire, a sincere desire that these difficulties shall be overcome and that . all the causes of friction shall be done away with. It is a very important fact that in the waterways treaty which has been submitted to parliament it is expressly provided that there is reserved to each country the rivht to insist upon the necessity of navigation being preserved, and that neither country shall have the right to divert any waters flowing into
boundary waters or boundary rivers which would in any way materially lower the level of the water or interfere with navigation. If this treaty should become law, we will have in it a recognition of that principle and that right, and the logical consequence which I hope will follow at no distant day will be, that the United States government will take steps to do away with the provisions which have been made for diverting the waters of this very important river into a river in the state of Maine, and allowing it to flow again in its natural channel, thus preserving to our people the navigation of the St. John river which, as the hon. gentleman has said, is of extreme importance to the Dominion. I can assure my hon. friend (Mr. Michaud) that the papers for which he has now moved will be brought down as soon as possible.

speakeroldname: Mr. JAMES CONMEE (Thunder Bay and Rainy River).
subtopic: DIVERSION OF THE WATERS OF THE ALLEGASH RIVER.
speechtext:
The question raised by the hon. member is of more far reaching importance than its relation to any particular locality. I take it for granted that many of the boundary streams could be affected by conditions similar to those he has represented in this case. What has been decided by the authorities of the United States having charge of the department which deals with waters of this character ought to be applied here. A question arose of a very similar character with regard to the diversion of waters from the Rainy river. An American company, relying on legislation which it had obtained in the state of Minnesota applied to the department at Washington foT the ratification of plans for the permanent diversion of a portion of the waters of the Birch lake drainage basin which was solely within the state of Minnesota, but in its course discharged southwesterly into the Rainy river which is an international stream. The Waterways Commission dealt with this matter and their report was ratified by the Secretary of War of the United States, and in giving their reasons for their finding and quoting authorities, they quote the opinion of Mr. Evarts, at one time Secretary of State of the United States, on a question between the United States government and the Mexican government with regard to the waters of the Rio Grande river which takes its rise in one country and flows into the other. The complaint in that case was that too much of the water was being diverted for irrigation purposes in the one country to the detriment of the citizens of the other who desired the water for the same purposes, and it was on that point that Mr. Evarts gave his opinion. The Waterways Commission commenting upon Mr. Evart's opinion reports :
It would seem that comity would require that in the absence of necessity the sovereign

power should not be exercised to the injury of a friendly nation or of its citizens or subjects without the consent of that nation.
If I understand aright the contention of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Michaud) it is not that there was diverted into the state of Maine the actual boundary waters of the St. John river, but the waters of a tributary of that boundary stream, and this was a similar case :
The common law protects riparian owners against permanent diversions of waters which injuriously affect their rights, and this law is founded on principles not merely of social necessity, but of justice and right. While the common law is not a part of the law of nations its principles so far as they are founded in justice and equity, ought, where practicable to be applied by nations acting in their sovereign capacity. The Department of State of the United States has adopted this principle in the past and although the application was made in the case of conflicting riparian rights on a boundary stream.
That is very close to the conditions here:
Yet the commission can see no sound distinction between the position taken by the government of the United States in the case referred to, and cases of diversion of water wholly within one country where the diversion injuriously affects riparian owners in another country.
That, I take it to be upon all fours with the situation in this case. Then it says :
This application of the common law was made by Mr. Evarts, Secretary of State.
So that, having Tegard to international law and to the comity between friendly nations and to equity and right as laid down by this authority, it seems to me that the diversion of the waters in this case was not justified. I call attention to this for the reason that it is not happening on the St. John river or on the Rainy river alone, but that it may happen and is likely to happen in very many other cases, affecting vitally the interests of this country. I think, Sir, there ought to be a little more attention paid to this subject and still greater supervision in regard to these matters.
Motion agreed to.

And this is so not only in the province of Nova Scotia, but throughout the whole Dominion of Canada. For that reason I think I am justified in calling the serious attention of this House and of the country generally to anything that may detrimentally affect that very important trade. In the industry of iron and the making of iron and steel and steel rails, which is almost directly dependent on the success of the coal industry we have a capital invested in the Dominion Iron and Steel Company of $30,000,000. I am not in a position to say exactly what the capital of the Nova Scotia Steel Company is, but it is a very large and prosperous company. The Londonderry Drummond Company has $1,000,000 invested in iron in the county of Colchester, and this industry depends to some extent for its existence and growth and prosperity upon the prosperity of the coal trade in the province. I am bound to say anything that I can say in support of this industry from the standpoint of capital, for it is important to us in Canada that every man who invests a dollar in any industry in ithis country should receive attention and protection from this House so far as this House can afford that protection consistent with the general interest of the country.
I am bringing up this question because this House is the tribunal which alone can deal with questions of this wide character, affecting the different provinces. If it could be dealt with by the legislature of Nova Scotia, if that legislature could protect and safeguard this great industry, I would not be troubling this House with any argument on the matter. But this question does not come within the sphere of any provincial legislature, and therefore I am obliged to appeal to the only tribunal which can deal with it. While it is the interest of this country that capital should be safeguarded and capitalists the world over be given the assurance that in Canada we have a parliament and parliamentarians who always keep their eye upon the best interests of those who are willing to invest their capital in this country, it
is equally in our interest that we should likewise keep in mind the men, women and children who are dependent upon this particular industry in every part of Canada, and in doing this we are likewise improving the position of those who invest capital in Canadian industries. We have in Nova Scotia 103,000 people who are depending for their livelihood upon coal cutting and mining. That is a very large number of people. I do not think it would be exaggerating to say that the average family of the miner numbers four and that consequently four people are directly dependent upon every head of a family of every mine operator. I have said in Nova Scotia there are 103,000 people employed in the mines, and taking in those employed directly in the coal mines in other parts of Canada, we have 113,109 miners engaged in the mining of coal. Multiply that by four, and you have 452,436 directly dependent on this work. If you undertake to feed them as they must be fed and estimate the cost at the very small amount of $10 a month, you have $4,524,360 for the feeding alone without saying anything about their housing and clothing. That is an amount of money which even Canada, with its enormous trade, cannot afford to treate lightly, and it is an amount which the traders in Ontario and Quebec, who are directly interested, must not ignore. We are apt, in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, where the great question seems to be to get coal without paying any duty and therefore as low as possible, to ignore] this factor. To get coal cheap seems to be the paramount question of importance in Ontario and Quebec regardless entirely of the trade dependent on the production of coal in this country. I submit that taking the 103,000 in my own province engaged directly in the production of coal, not more than ten per cent of their requirements is found in that province. You would be surprised to know that of these 103,000 people, mostly all are non-productive, that is as far as what they eat and what they require for clothing are concerned. It is important therefore that the large manufacturing centres of this country should realize that the flour, beef, pork, molasses, sugar and other goods which these people consume do not come from Nova Scotia except in a very small proportion. I venture to say that 75 per cent comes from Quebec and Ontario. For that reason it is highly important for those two provinces that the coal industry in the county of Cape Breton and the other parts of Nova Scotia should not be neglected.
There is one point I wish to make in respect to the trade in coal between Cape Breton and the city of Montreal and in respect to the steamers that ply hack and forth between Sydney and Montreal. The idea * seems to be in Ontario and Quebec

that if we had reciprocity the coal from Sydney and Louisburg would go to Boston and other New England ports. But our friends in the upper provinces who are now trading extensively with us in Nova Scotia, must not forget that if the coal trade of the maritime provinces should go to Boston, there also will go the other trade in dry goods and provisions and everything else which the miner requires. To-day the steamers which go to 'Montreal with coal bring back no other goods except those which the miner purchases, and these goods enjoy the advantage of cheap freight rates; whereas if the trade is directed elsewhere, we shall not have that steamer connection and these goods will not be sent to the people of Cape Breton as they now are. That is the point I wish to emphasize. I wish to point cut that this question of protecting coal is not a one-sided one. There is no class of people so profitable to the traders as the coal miners. A farmer may be well off and a merchant or a professional man, but, so far as purchasing powers are concerned, the
coal miner is a much more profitable citizen so long as he has the money to spend. He is not as a rule stingy about spending money. He feeds and dresses his family well and is not at all conservative about his wealth. For that reason the miner and the working men generally in the coal mining district^ are the best kind of customers, and it is well worth the while of our manufacturers and traders to see that the coal miner is in a position to bring up his family well and be of such assistance to the commercial world as he now is. What has startled myself and some others is the falling off of our trade in the St. Lawrence. I am not in a position to say exactly what is the cause, but what we do know is that year ofter year, particularly for the last two or three years American coal is gaining ground along the river St. Lawrence, in the province of Quebec, to the exclusion of our own coal. Now, I wish to bring particularly to the notice of the people that, so far as efforts to bring about reciprocity are concerned, reciprocity in coal in former days has not been a boon to the investors in coal mines in Nova Soctia or elsewhere in Canada. And when I speak of the coal trade of Nova Scotia, I am sorry to say I am not speaking of money invested by the people of Nova Scotia alone. The wealthy men of Quebec, Montreal, Ontario and other parts of Canada, have invested in these mines rather than the people of Nova Scotia. And, when I call upon the representatives in this House of all parts of Canada to take an interest in this question and safeguard the coal Hade in the province of Nova Scotia, I am not asking them to safeguard the interest of the people of Nova Scotia only, but the interest of the people of every part of Canada.
In the year 1865, the coal trade had become such an important factor to the province of Nova Scotia, through the increased coal sales of the new collieries, which were opened out when the leases were granted, outside of the general mining association, that it was deemed necessary to appoint an inspector of mines, who could look after the mining interests of the province. This appointment was the first inspector of mines in America. In the year 1867 the government of the United States imposed a duty of $1.25 per ton on all coals entering their ports. The imposing of this duty very materially affected the output, and expansion of the trade of the whole province of Nova Scotia, as up to this time the New England states had always been their best customers, no other markets being then available, as at that time the local markets were small and restrictive, few miles of railway having been built, and all the coal being water carried by sailing vessels.
From the year 1850 to 1854 coal was admitted into the United States at a duty of 24 per cent ad valorem, and in 1853 the coal shipped amounted to 124,764 tons. From 1854 to 1866 coal was admitted free, when the exports rose from 139,125 tons to 404,252 tons. In 1864, a duty of $1.25 was imposed, when the shipments fell to 165,431 tons. In 1892, the duty was reduced to 75 cents, and the exports gradually fell until 1893, when the entire shipments of Nova Scotia coal to the United States only amounted to 16,099 tons. In 1894 the duty was changed to 40 cents for screened coal, and 15 cents for slack-through i-inch apertures in screen bars. In 1896 the shipments of coal amounting to 174,919 tons. Without saying very much upon this point I think I have shown sufficient of the facts and made out a case strong enough to call the attention of the government and the House generally to this very important question and to impress them with the necessity of taking some steps to preserve to the people of Canada the excellent market which we now have for the coal of Nova Scotia and wherever else coal is produced. I would submit. Sir, that while it may be a hardship in some cases to buy coai, as we sometimes consider it dearer than we would like to pay, we should not forget that the people of the great country to the south of us have pursued the policy which I am advocating. The people in the New England states have no coal, they have to reef ive their coal from the west and they pay a higher price than they would have to pay for Nova Scotia coal. Still, there is enough national spirit to induce them to bear with any little extras they would have to pay in order to develop in the west great coal centres and keep the trade within their own bounds. I submit that in the centre of Canada our people do not view with a proper spirit the necessity of developing the coal of our own country. The proper thing to do in Canada is to develop the coal resources of Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia so that they can be made available for the necessities of the people in the great centres of the west which are now being developed. We heard to-night of the necessity that exists for providing water for the people in the west. I certainly approve of any means that are adopted to bring to their doors those things which are necessary for the purposes of the great development that is now going on there, but if the settler must have water to boil the meal and if he must have water to drink he must also have fire with which to cook his meal, to keep warm his children and for the comfort of his household. It is necessary to have that and it can only be obtained by the proper development, the bringing of that coal to the doors of our people in the west. We have inexhaustible stores of coal in Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia and w'hen the excellent railroads that they are building there with low grades and equipped with big locomotives are completed the loads that can be hauled will be simply enormous and something that we do not calculate upon to-day. For that reason I think it will be quite proper to direct our attention to furnishing fuel to our own people in the west from our own mines. We are expending a great deal of money upon our militia and the development of arms in this country. It is quite proper, but I want to know how long we could stand a war in this country if we had it in mid-winter without the capability of supplying our own people in the west with fuel. The Americans would starve us out in two days. There is nothing said 98
about that. We are furnishing the militia and the arms, but we are making no provision for supplying fuel in winter to our people and ve can imagine what would happen if our fuel supply in the United States were stopped in mid-winter. At no time in winter is there more than a two week's supply in the province of Ontario of the quality of coal which they get from the United States because they depend upon getting it on short notice, and if communication with the mines of the United States were suddenly cut off they would be in a position to which they have not given sufficient thought. I say, after deliberation and after having given the subject a great deal of thought, that 1 believe that with some attention to transportation we can send our coal from the east as far as Toronto, and I submit that with proper attention to the question of transportation that portion of the country west of Toronto can be supplied from the west. I say that as a country that expects to develop, that expects to be independent of the outside world, to as great an extent as any country can be, with reference to the question of power, as power is produced or generated by coal, and as far as everything that is produced or dependent upon coal is concerned, the wise policy on our part is to develop our own coal resources and coal trade and not depend upon the whims of any outside country. As far as Nova Scotia is concerned, so important was this question in 1897 that the premier of that province dissolved the legislature and asked the verdict of the people on the question as to whether or not they wanted the duty retained on coal in the Dominion of Canada. The verdict of the people was almost unanimous in favour of the retention of the duty. I believe that the same verdict would be rendered to-day if that question were to be submitted to the people there. It is important in Nova Scotia and it is also important in every other part of the country, in Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Quebec, because of the great trade which we furnish to the people of Canada and if measures are not taken to protect this industry and to keep the prosperity which we have to-day it may not be so useful to the country as it is at the present time.
Now, I simply want to point out one more thing to the government and to the House and I shall consider that I have put this question, as far as I have any figures or facts at my disposal, before the House to the fullest extent. This government has undertaken to do some things for other industries in this country. , A few years ago the steel industry in Canada was in such a position as to require care, protection and fostering at the hands of this government. The government was equal to the occasion and took steps to safeguard the capital that was invested in that great



industry and also to safeguard the people whose living and every day employment were dependent upon it. As the government has encouraged our steel and iron industry by bounties and duties for protection and assistance, and as we are paying out our good money to assist that industry, there is no reason why some steps should not be taken and even some sacrifices indirectly incurred in order to safeguard our coal mining industry. I have reason to hope that the government will be equal to the occasion and that this House will support the government in inquiring into the cause which is bringing about such a great influx of American coal into Canada to the exclusion of the use of our own Canadian coal, and that whatever steps are necessary to conserve to us our own markets and to exclude American coal shall be taken. I regret that I have been obliged to speak at such length but the question is a very important one. I am not presenting alone the case of the capitalists for whom I can assure you I have no retainer, but I feel that it is my duty as representing a large number of working men to bring their case as near to the foot of the Throne as I can, and so far as I am able to submit to the government and to the people generally that some measures should be taken to enable these working men to have employment every day and to earn sufficient money to support themselves and their families in comfort. I regret that this winter they have not been kept in continuous employment because of this displacement of Canadian coal in the home market by American coal. It is not at all necessary for one to call himself a labour candidate or to sit in this House' as a labour member in order that he should put these issues before the House. Representing as I do a large number of working people, although I do not pose as a labour candidate, I believe that it is my duty to the best of my ability to present to the country and to the House the interests of these people, and to appeal for a remedy to the only institution in the land which has the power to provide a remedy which will relieve us from any further imposition of this kind, and which will hold the markets of Canada for Canadian coal which we are capable of producing just as well as they can produce coal in a foreign country. One more observation Mr. Speaker, and I have done. It has been contended that the price of Nova Scotia coal is too high, that we are making too large profits on it, and that the people who have to buy our coal in Montreal and other cities are obliged to pay too high a price for it. I do not know whether it is a popular suggestion to make or not, but I submit that if the day should ever come in Canada when there is any hardship on the Canadian Mr. D. D. McKENZIE.
consumer because of the high price of coal there is power in this House to put the regulations of the price of that commodity in a commission just as the value of other public utilities is regulated. I consider that the power that is in coal is a public utility, and if ever it should come about that the people of this country are imposed upon, this parliament has the power to protect the consumer so that none but a fair price should be charged. I have presented my views and these statistics to the House in the hope that the government will take into serious consideration the circumstances of those who are dependent on this trade for a means of livelihood as well as those who have had the courage and the enterprise to invest millions of dollars in the development of out coal areas in Nova Scotia and elsewhere in Canada.

Would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Mackenzie) please tell the House the price of coal at the pit mouth in Nova Scotia and the price of the same kind of coal at the pit mouth in the Alle-ghanney Valley or in Ohio?

I do not pose by any means as a coal expert and I only speak of the facts as I know them. I can, however, tell my hon. friend that for domestic use. at the pit mouth in Nova Scotia we pay $3 per ton, although I understand that those who buy in large quantities get it cheaper.
As a purchaser of coal I can tell my hon. friend that the price of soft coal at the pit mouth in Pennsylvania is from 65 cents to 85 cents per ton.
Run of mine?

Yes, run of mine. That coal comes in here and pays 53 cents a ton duty and it competes with Nova Scotia coal which you cannot buy at the pit mouth in Nova Scotia for less than $2.50 per ton. It is quite clear, therefore, that unless there is a reduction in the price of Nova Scotia coal to a reasonable figure or until there is a corresponding increase in the price of Pennsylvania coal, the Nova Scotia coal must necessarily be cut out of the Canadian market. I for one as a consumer of coal in Ontario feel that we would like to use Nova Scotia coal altogether even if we had to pay a trifle higher for it, but if we have to pay $1 or $2 per ton more than for Pennsylvania coal then it becomes another question altogether.

I do not imagine that my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) desires to divide the House on this question to-night, especially as there is a very slim attendance of mem-

bers present. I take it for granted that the purpose of his motion was to have an opportunity of presenting these very interesting statistics to us and to urge, if it be necessary to urge, the importance of this great mining industry. There will be no difference of opinion in that respect. We all recognize that the coal industry of the country, not merely in Nova Scotia but in other parts of the Dominion, is a very great industry and that whatever may reasonably be done to advance the interests of our Canadian miners should be done. It is, however, a very vexed question. It is a question on which there will not be by any means unanimity of opinion. I do not imagine that my hon. friend desires to-night to challenge an opinion, and I would suggest therefore that the debate be adjourned so that at a later date, when there is a better attendance of members, any hon. member who desires may continue the discussion.
Will it ever be reached again?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It may be.
We are all prepared to support his motion on this side of the House, we are all protectionists.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Currie) wants the price reduced before he says very much about that.

I have been very much interested in listening to the remarks of my hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) and I congratulate him upon having made a strong protectionist speech. Sometimes we on this side of the House are taunted by the Minister of Finance with divergence of views on a question such as this, but I think we never have made such a great departure from our political principles as the hon. gentleman (Mr. McKenzie)) has made from his to-night. All I wish to say is that it has delighted me beyond measure to hear my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) free trader as he is make such a strong protectionist speech. It shows just how far a man can get right when his own interests are brought into question.
Mr. ROBERT SMITH (Stormont) moved the adjournment of the debate.

Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
May I ask the hon. leader of the House what the business for to-morrow will be?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We had in contemplation proceeding with the resolutions respecting the loan to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, but by arrangement 981
that goes over till next week. In the meantime, with the view of expediting the passing of the estimates, both for the current year, which will expire in a few days, and for the coming year, the House will be moved into Committee of Supply. I understand that a motion is to be made in amendment, bearing on one branch of the public expenditure. I take it that will not occupy much time, and afterwards we will go into supply and take up the estimates of the Public Works Department and several items scattered through various departments.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11.25 p.m.
Tuesday, March 23, 1909.
